#6468. Security Footage Catches Two Zoo Gorillas Forming a “Living Ladder” To Outsmart an Electric Fence

Two zoo gorillas repeatedly teamed up for food despite rarely spending time together, showing that a shared effort does not always end with a shared meal.

A leafy branch was out of reach for two gorillas at the Ramat Gan Safari, and an electric barrier around the trunk blocked a direct climb. The female western lowland gorillas, half-sisters Amelia and Lisha, formed a “living ladder,” with Lisha providing a steady back for Amelia to stand on.

The most extensively documented event came to light in September 2024, when keepers noticed the pair peacefully eating bark and leaves from a large branch that had previously been beyond their reach. Staff reviewed security camera footage to find out how they had obtained it.

The recording showed Amelia walking over and climbing onto a rock beneath a Peltophorum dubium tree. Lisha joined her and stood firmly on all fours on the rock. Amelia then climbed onto Lisha’s back, stood upright, and reached up to grasp and break off a branch approximately 4.5 meters, or 15 feet, above the ground. The rock, Lisha’s stable posture, and Amelia’s reach together made the branch accessible.

Researchers documented three events involving the same pair in 2021, 2024, and 2025, with each gorilla performing the same role every time. Neither had been trained to perform the maneuver. The team describes their behavior as a rare example of spontaneous cooperation between adult gorillas, with a clear division of roles.

Published in Primates, the study was led by Michael Levitzky and Prof. Israel Hershkovitz of the Department of Anatomy and Anthropology at the Gray Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences and the Dan David Center for Human Evolution and Biohistory Research at Tel Aviv University.

Yehonatan Samocha, Head of the Primate Section at the Ramat Gan Safari (Zoological Center Tel Aviv-Ramat Gan), said, “At the Ramat Gan Safari we have observed and studied animal behaviors for years, closely following their relationships, social bonds, and fascinating capabilities. Particularly among great apes, including gorillas, we repeatedly encounter behaviors that demonstrate high intelligence, learning ability, problem-solving, complex communication, and cooperation.

“This is why we are so thrilled, though not necessarily surprised, by the cooperation between Amelia and Lisha. We are familiar with their abilities and understand how intelligent and curious they are, and how capable they are of learning from one another and working together. Sometimes, our surprise tells us more about our expectations of animals than their actual abilities. The study’s great importance lies in providing scientific documentation and analysis for observations and behaviors we encounter in our daily work, allowing us to enhance our knowledge of gorillas, their social world, and their cognitive abilities.”

In the June 2025 footage, Lisha positioned herself with her back toward Amelia, who was not observed using force. Levitzky, who initiated and led the study, explained how the recording helped the researchers interpret Lisha’s participation.

“When I first watched the footage, it was clear to me that this was something extraordinary. What I find fascinating is that Leisha did more than simply serve as a ‘step’ for Amelia. She appeared to participate actively and willingly in solving the problem, approaching on her own initiative and positioning herself in exactly the right place, without Amelia physically guiding her. This is the difference between using another individual as a tool and true cooperation, in which both individuals work together toward the same goal.

“For years, gorillas were considered less cognitively sophisticated than other great apes. As more observations like these accumulate, we will be able to deepen and refine our understanding of their social and cognitive abilities. Future studies involving systematic documentation and audio recordings could help us decipher how they coordinate with one another, and perhaps also teach us something about the roots of cooperation in our own species.”

The sisters generally spend little time together, sleep in separate night quarters, and rarely groom one another. Their teamwork also had different outcomes at feeding time. Although keepers reported peaceful sharing after the 2024 event, Amelia alone ate the vegetation in the observed 2025 sequence, showing that cooperating to obtain food did not necessarily lead to sharing it.

Hershkovitz said, “Our observations reveal how two gorillas can join forces and assume complementary roles to solve a problem that neither can solve on her own. It is particularly intriguing that this cooperation recurs even though the two do not usually display much closeness, and even when the food is not shared between them afterward. These observations are important for understanding human evolution because they offer an explanation, albeit a partial one, for how we survived on the savanna – through social support and a high level of cooperation that can occur even without language or preplanning. Although the number of observations is small, they offer a window into gorillas’ ability to learn from experience, coordinate their actions, and draw on one another and their surroundings to achieve a shared goal.”

The study involved only two gorillas and three documented events. The available footage could not establish whether they communicated through vocalizations or subtle gestures, or whether they planned their actions in advance.

Reference: “Cooperation in adult female western lowland gorillas: complex problem-solving through learned spatial affordances and mutual agency” by Michael Levitzky, and Israel Hershkovitz, 24 October 2026, Primates. DOI: 10.1007/s10329-026-01297-6

#6467. A Dark Energy Camera Portrait of the Betta Fish Nebula

This is the Betta Fish Nebula, a supernova remnant (SNR) around 6,800 light years away in the Centaurus constellation. This display of illuminated gas came into being when a massive star exploded between 7,000 and 10,000 years ago. When it exploded, it expelled its outer layers. Those layers slammed into the interstellar medium, and are lit up by the energy from the shock, and that's what we see today.

Astronomers love studying SNRs because they can learn a lot about how heavy elements are spread out into the interstellar medium (ISM). These explosions shape the dynamics in the ISM, including how stars form there. SNRs also reveal a lot about their progenitor stars. For these and other reasons, they're rich astronomical targets.

This image is brought to us by a powerful telescope whose main job it is to study dark energy. But that telescope also has a side hustle: capturing stunning images for the rest of us that don't necessarily add anything to scientific understanding.

One of the main efforts to understand dark energy, the puzzling force that drives the expansion of the Universe, is the Dark Energy Survey. It uses a special, purpose-built camera to do its work, called the Dark Energy Camera (DECam.) DECam is a powerful, 570 megapixel, wide-angle camera mounted on the VÃ­ctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile. It used its power to capture this image of the Betta Fish Nebula.

Like many telescopes, DECam sometimes takes a break from its main job and captures images purely for public interest. It's a way for the professional astronomy community to share some celestial wonder with the rest of us. The latest DECam images of the Betta Fish nebula are in that category.

Only part of the nebula actually looks like a Betta, the popular and colourful aquarium fish. They're also known as Siamese Fighting Fish, but whatever name is used, they're popular for their brilliant colours and flowing fins.

This close-up view shows one portion of the Betta Fish Nebula, the part that most closely resembles its namesake. Image Credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA. Image Processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License

What's left of the exploded star is a collapsed, ultra-dense stellar core called a neutron star. It's tiny, only about 20 km across, and is invisible in this image. It's actually a pulsar with unusual properties that has been studied extensively. It's radio-quiet and can only be detected in x-rays, and also lacks a pulsar wind nebula. It's so unusual that some researchers think it may be an example of what's called a 'low-mass bare strange star.'

This is a less visually interesting, more scientific x-ray image of the central portion of the Betta Fish nebula. It shows what's left of the progenitor star that exploded, labelled in the center. Image Credit: Eppens et al. MNRAS 528, 2095â2111 (2024)

But those scientific details take a back seat to the image's visual interest.

These images have been 'dumbed-down' for internet use. There's a version of the image here that lets you zoom-in and explore it in much greater detail.

This zoomed-in image highlights the part of the nebula that gave it its name. A cooperative orange/red star even serves as the Betta Fish's eye. Image Credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA. Image Processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License

DECam has been observing for more than a decade, and over that time its created a nice catalogue of fantastic images. Here's a few of them.

Here are three DECam images the camera has captured over the years purely for public interest. From left to right: the cometary globule CG4, the Rosette Nebula, and the Corona Australis Molecular Cloud. Image Credits: NSF NOIRLab DECam Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License

#6465. Citrus Madeleines

Marcel Proust and madeleines are so intrinsically linked that in France, a madeleine de Proust has become a common expression used to describe a smell, sound, or taste that brings back old memories. Madeleines are small sponge cakes baked in molds shaped like seashells with the signature bump, la bosse, proudly protruding from the top. Freezing the pan and placing it on a hot sheet pan will make the bump pop even more!

As much as I love a plain madeleine, I adore a citrus-scented one. My first madeleine, my Proustian moment, was not at a lovely Parisian pâtisserie. No, my family and I were visiting some of my mother’s friends in Paris and not knowing what they were, I grabbed a bag of lemon madeleines in a local supermarket, simply because I thought the seashell-shaped cakes were the prettiest thing I had ever seen. I could have inhaled them all in an afternoon if I had been allowed.

Seasonal citrus zests—lemons, of course, yuzus, blood oranges, mandarins, or a medley of several—find their way into my madeleines, but the tart-sweet, fruity, floral flavor of Cara Cara oranges is my favorite. Dusting the still-warm madeleines with floral and citrusy coriander-scented powdered sugar just before serving sends them over the top.

Put ½ cup / 115 g unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat and melt, stirring and scraping the bottom with a rubber spatula, until the foaming subsides and the butter smells like toasted hazelnuts and the milk solids are golden brown, 5–7 minutes. Scrape the melted butter and milk solids into a small heatproof bowl and refrigerate until the butter is solid and creamy.

Sift together 1 cup / 125 g all-purpose flour, ½ tsp. baking powder, and ¼ tsp. salt in a small bowl and set aside.

Add ½ cup / 100 g light brown sugar to a small bowl and rub the sugar with zest of 1 Cara Cara orange. Combine the sugar, 1 Tbsp. honey, and 2 eggs in the bowl of a stand mixer, fitted with the whisk attachment. Whisk for 2 minutes on medium-low speed, then increase the speed to medium-high and whisk for another 5–6 minutes, until very pale and airy.

Add the cooled butter to the egg mixture while whisking on low speed, then fold in the flour mixture until just combined.

Transfer the batter to an airtight container and refrigerate for at least 6 hours but preferably overnight.

Grease a madeleine pan with unsalted butter, then dust with all-purpose flour and knock out any excess. Place the pan in the freezer for at least an hour.

Use a 1-Tbsp. measure or transfer the cold batter to a piping bag and fill the center of each cup with 20 g of batter (three-quarters full, or a little more than 1 Tbsp.). Refrigerate the madeleine pan for 1 hour.

Place a sheet pan in the oven and preheat the oven to 350°F / 180°C.

Place the madeleine pan directly on the hot sheet pan and bake for 10–13 minutes, until the madeleines are golden brown and their signature bump springs back when pressed lightly.

Tap the tray to release the cakes and immediately turn out onto a wire rack to cool, turning them bump-side up.

Whisk together ¼ cup / 30 g powdered sugar and ¾ tsp. ground coriander in a small bowl and dust over the warm madeleines.

#6464. The Rise of Astrosociology: What Can Analogue Astronaut Studies Teach us About the Future of Humanity in Space?

It's no secret that some highly ambitious visions for the future of space exploration are taking shape today. Beyond NASA and China's plans to send crewed missions to the Moon by the end of the decade and create permanent infrastructure there, both space agencies hope to put boots on the surface of Mars by the 2030s or 40s. Meanwhile, the European Space Agency (ESA) is active in the Artemis Program and plans to send the ExoMars Rosalind Franklin rover to the Red Planet in 2028. India aims to send the first "gaganauts" to space next year (as part of its Gaganyaan program).

On top of all that, there are plans to "commercialize Low Earth Orbit" (LEO), build infrastructure in cis-lunar space (Ã  la asteroid mining), and even proposals for sending commercial astronauts to "space tourists" to the Moon and Mars. All of this begs the question of how humans intend to live in extraterrestrial environments and among the stars. What is needed to ensure that humans can not only survive the hazards of being off-world, but also flourish? As Mars City Design CEO Vera Mulyani would say, "How can we thrive, and not just survive?"

This is where the emerging field of Astrosociology comes into play, an umbrella term that looks at spaceflight through the lens of the social sciences. In addition to questions related to engineering and astronaut health and safety, astrosociology takes a more holistic outlook and examines the social, cultural, and behavioral patterns of humans related to outer space. Consider Abraham Maslow's "Hierarchy of Needs," which begins with the basics (physiological and security needs) and extends upwards to include the immaterial, such as love, self-esteem, and self-actualization.

This challenge motivated Dr. Jim Pass to found the Astrosociology Research Institute (ARI) in 2008, a California-based nonprofit educational organization dedicated to developing astrosociology as a multidisciplinary academic field. As Pass describes on the organization's website, astrosociology is both a subdiscipline of sociology and a multidisciplinary field that includes (but is not limited to) "psychology, anthropology, economics, social psychology, political science, space history, space law, space policy, philosophy, as well as the arts."

At its core, the ARI's mission comes down to a simple but highly relevant question: "How can social and behavioral scientists collaborate with physical and natural scientists to further the success of space exploration and settlement in the future?" In their latest newsletter, titled "Analog Space Missions: The Astrosociological Factors That Affect Analog Space Missions - Part 1," Pass and his colleagues share the perspectives of analog astronauts who participated in their call for papers and expert commentary by educators, space medics, and systems engineers.

As Mia Belle Parkinson, a postdoctoral student at the University of Edinburgh and ARI's editor-in-chief, wrote in the issue:

When we talk about preparing for space exploration and settlement, we too often default to the technical: propulsion systems, life support, radiation shielding. These things matter enormously. But so do the quieter, harder-to-quantify questions â how do people build trust in isolated environments? How do cultural backgrounds shape group dynamics? What does it mean, psychologically and socially, to live on the edge of the unknown?

While analog astronaut training may seem like a relatively new idea, it's actually part of a long-standing tradition almost as old as the "Space Race" itself. Before astronauts landed on the Moon, NASA conducted a series of training missions known as the "Apollo Geology Field Trips" between 1964 and 1972. The first field trip saw the first two astronaut groups travel to Flagstaff, Arizona, for a two-day mission to Meteor Crater and other locations that resembled volcanic features on the Moon.

Other locations included the Grand Canyon, the volcanic fields in Hawaii, the Nevada National Security Site, and mountain formations in the Sonoran Desert, New Mexico, Oregon, Alaska, west Texas, and Sudbury, Ontario. Additionally, the Soviets conducted the BIOS-3 experiment within the closed ecosystem built at the Institute of Biophysics in Krasnoyarsk in 1965. This was followed by Tektite I and II in 1969 and 1971, which studied human behavior in a confined, isolated, pressurized habitat on the ocean floor near the U.S. Virgin Islands.

JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) astronaut Satoshi Furukawa pedals on the upgraded CEVIS system, keeping muscle and bone density levels during spaceflight. (Credit: NASA)

Since that time, research aboard space stations such as Mir, the International Space Station (ISS), and the Chinese Tiangong space station has provided invaluable knowledge about living in space and the effects of microgravity on humans' mental and physical well-being. However, these studies are not directly relevant to proposed missions that will send astronauts to the Moon, Mars, and other celestial bodies. As Parry writes:

While extremely valuable for zero-gravity spaceflights, living and working at the bottom of a gravity well presents altogether different conditions, including an inability to manufacture drugs or lift heavy objects. Planning for bases and settlements on the surfaces of the Moon, Mars, and eventually beyond can only be simulated on the surface of the Earth to humankind's best approximation even in 2026, because gravity matters!

The second took place in a converted World War II bunker in Poland located inside an old hangar. The hangar itself was filled with sand to simulate lunar regolith, and steel doors sealed the habitat and its six-person crew inside a rather confined space. At the Jules Undersea Lodge, located in Key Largo off the southern tip of Florida, Mund and her colleagues entered a submerged habitat with no escape hatches, accessible only through a "wet room" portal.

Looking back at these three missions, Mund noticed patterns that transcended any single environment. While each had its own geography and logistics, confinement was the common theme. From her experiences, Mund identified four universal human responses that were consistent throughout. The first, she wrote, was the importance of improvisation:

No matter how carefully equipment is designed or schedules are drawn, something always fails... each failure forces us to understand the problem and formulate a response to it in the context of very tight resource constraints. And in adapting, we discover more about ourselves than about the broken machines... These small acts of invention prove that ingenuity is not a luxury in confinement. It is a decisive factor in survival.

Photo of analog astronaut Beth Mund sitting outside the HI-SEAS habitat on the summit of Mauna Kea, Hawai'i. Credit: Beth Mund

The second lesson was the importance of ritual: "At HI-SEAS, our crew naturally gathered each evening for what I came to think of as our 'campfire,' a circle of debriefing, storytelling, and laughter, even in the cold dome with no flame. In Poland, games became our escape valve, a way to puncture the heaviness of the surveys and the claustrophobic walls. Underwater, simply gazing out the porthole together felt like a ceremony. In every analog, the crew instinctively created moments of reconnection that grounded us, even in places designed to isolate."

The third lesson for Mund was continuity, as she and her colleagues inherited experiments started by crews they never met and which would be handled by future analog crews. "It gave weight to our confinement, transforming it from a private trial into a communal contribution," she said. "That continuity across crew "generations" is perhaps the most powerful sociological insight of analog missions. We are practicing not only how to live together, but how to build across time, leaving work - and maybe even some data/ insights - for crews who serve next."

Lastly, there was the inevitability of testing. While every mission includes tests of equipment, plants, and methods for living in space, the experience also tests the limits of human endurance, creativity, and cohesion. This, she wrote, is the true essence of analog astronaut training:

From Mars-like lava fields to a Polish bunker to the ocean floor, I have learned that analog missions are not about pretending to be astronauts. They are about practicing human endurance in places that strip away comfort and certainty. In that practice, in all the different shapes it takes across environments, facilities, missions, and crews, lies the real preparation for humanity to endure no matter the circumstances.

Mund is merely one of many analog astronauts profiled in the Astrosociological Insights Forum's newsletter. To include as many testimonials and experiences as possible, the issue was released in two parts, incorporating perspectives not only from AAs but also from several experts in the burgeoning field of Astrosociology. More to follow, so stay tuned! In the meantime, check out some other articles we have about organizations committed to analog astronaut training:

Further Reading: Astrosociological Insights Forum, vol. 10, issue 1

#6463. America’s Data Centers Have a Hidden Death Toll, MIT Researchers Warn

An MIT analysis estimates that powering America’s data centers contributed to hundreds of premature deaths in a single year, with rural populations facing greater risks than city dwellers.

As artificial intelligence drives the rapid construction of data centers across the United States, concerns about their environmental impact are taking on a new dimension. The electricity needed to keep these facilities running around the clock can increase air pollution in communities far from where the data centers themselves are built, potentially putting the health of people who live nowhere near them at risk.

Researchers at MIT estimate that air pollution associated with data center electricity consumption contributed to approximately 650 premature deaths in the United States in 2023 alone. Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas had the highest estimated rates of premature deaths per capita, even though much of the electricity demand was concentrated in northern Virginia and Texas. Rates in Virginia and Texas were only about half those in most Midwestern states.

“When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors. But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region. Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” says Noelle Selin, senior author of the study, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS), and director of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy.

Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that data centers’ electricity needs accounted for about 4 percent of total U.S. energy demand in 2023 and approximately 4.4 percent of the nation’s overall emissions. Those proportions have likely grown as more facilities have been built.

Determining who bears the health consequences of that growing demand is complicated by the interconnected nature of the nation’s power grid. A data center in Virginia, for example, may increase electricity production at power plants in the Ohio Valley, where a greater proportion of older coal and natural gas plants produce higher levels of emissions.

“Different regions have different mixes of power. If you turn on a major new demand source, by plugging a data center into the grid, you might have to fire up your really dirty power plant to meet that new demand,” Selin says.

The pollution can then travel into neighboring states, where local atmospheric conditions can make matters worse. In agricultural regions such as Iowa and Nebraska, ammonia released from fertilizer promotes the formation of fine particulate matter (PM2.5), microscopic airborne particles that can cause heart attacks, strokes, and lung disease.

The estimated health consequences also extend to Kansas, South Dakota, Missouri, and Arkansas. Overall, the researchers found that rural populations face a significantly higher estimated mortality risk from data center electricity demand than urban populations.

To understand how these risks are distributed, the team developed a model that tracks electricity production and transmission between regions on an hourly basis. While many previous studies relied on average power grid emissions, the researchers assumed that data centers operated around the clock and identified which individual generators would respond to their additional electricity needs.

“Generators that respond to additional electricity demand are often natural gas plants, although the response varies by place and hour,” says Yuang (Albert) Chen, an MIT graduate student and co-author of the study.

“It was a challenge to gather all the data,” Chen says. “There are more than 10,000 generators in the U.S. grid, and we needed to make sure the data provided for each generator is valid and validated across other data sources.”

The researchers calculated emissions of nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide from individual generators. Both pollutants contribute to the formation of fine particulate matter, while nitrogen oxides also help produce ground-level ozone, commonly associated with smog.

Using a separate atmospheric model, the team simulated how these pollutants formed and traveled across regions. They then drew on epidemiological research linking air pollution to premature death to estimate the resulting health impacts.

Of the approximately 650 premature deaths estimated for 2023, 513 were attributed to fine particulate matter and 137 to smog. Together, they represented about 5.3 percent of all estimated electricity-related premature deaths nationwide.

“While it is not surprising that any additional source of air pollution will result in mortalities, with data centers, when and where these deaths are occurring are different than you might expect,” Selin says.

As companies continue to expand their computing infrastructure, the findings suggest that decisions about where to build data centers and how to power them need to account for public health well beyond the immediate surroundings.

“When people are thinking about data center siting and operations, it is important to consider more than just things like land and energy prices. They should also take air quality considerations into the equation,” Chen says. “This is a good baseline to think about where we should build data centers and how we should supply those data centers with electricity.”

The researchers hope to investigate the air quality consequences of a growing industry trend in which data centers incorporate their own on-site power plants. They could also examine whether adjusting when these facilities consume electricity could reduce their impact on air quality.

Reference: “Spatially distributed air quality and health impacts of data center electricity demand in the United States” by Yuang Chen, Shen Wang, Juan Ramon L Senga, Andrew Scott White, Anthony YH Wong, Lyssa M Freese, Michelle L Bell and Noelle E Selin, 19 November 2026, Environmental Research Letters. DOI: 10.1088/1748-9326/aebbd4

This research was funded, in part, by the MIT Energy Initiative Society of Energy Scholars and the MIT Martin Family Society of Fellows for Sustainability.

#6462. The Best Thanksgiving Side Recipes, According to Eater Editors

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table

The sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

While we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever new ideas have been simmering since last year’s big meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director

I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director

Nobody says they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

While more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman

Tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest

This is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated quickly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be said is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

AI has upended the math community with a flood of results. We have to rethink how we assess which questions and answers matter — putting humans back at the center.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An Anthropic mathematician using Claude claims to have proven the most famous problem in math — the Riemann hypothesis — in the latest, but potentially most consequential, example of artificial intelligence (AI) producing stunning math results.

AI has steamrolled its way into the math community. Anthropic's proof will certainly and rightly be scrutinized, but rather than picking apart every single result these models produce, we should respond by changing how we evaluate and reward expertise — placing less weight on the volume of results and more on the human judgment required to decide which questions and answers matter.

Without this shift, we risk drowning genuine insight in a flood of plausible but poorly understood mathematics.

This is a Live Science Pro article that we're putting out for free. If you liked this story, please consider subscribing.

Mathematical judgment is the ability to distinguish a result that is correct, but boring, from one that might fundamentally change how we think about the problem or even the whole area of mathematics surrounding the problem.

AI could generate hundreds of thousands of complex variations on a theorem, but these variations might add very little to mathematical knowledge, each one ultimately proving a dead end. A truly consequential result might settle a long-standing unsolved problem or connect to apparently unrelated areas. It is mathematical judgment that allows us to tell the difference between the two.

Earlier this year, an OpenAI system produced a counterexample to the long-standing planar unit distance problem, overturning a conjecture of Paul Erdős that had resisted mathematicians for decades. More recently, OpenAI announced an apparent solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, a celebrated question about whether equations describing fluid flow can develop singularities, or infinite values. It is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems — a set of seven well-known and complex math problems, each with a $1 million prize attached.

Whether OpenAI's result ultimately stands up to scrutiny remains to be seen. But what is clear is that AI systems are now operating at a level that many mathematicians did not expect to witness for years, if not decades. OpenAI has since released hundreds of further mathematical results, leaving mathematicians scrambling to assess their correctness and significance.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This does not mean that mathematicians are about to become obsolete. But it does mean we need to carefully reconsider what their precise purpose is.

Traditionally, expertise has been closely associated with production: Experts solve difficult problems, prove theorems, construct models and write papers. If AI can generate proofs, conjectures and probe research areas at unprecedented speed and scale, mathematical production is no longer necessarily the bottleneck. Instead, many pure mathematicians would argue that it is mathematical judgment that will become the scarcer resource.

Human judgment remains necessary because proofs generated by AI are not necessarily illuminating, comprehensible or even reliable. Some proofs may be so long or opaque that checking them requires substantial work by specialists and even more work to reinterpret them in a way that is meaningful to human mathematicians.

A proof can be valid without offering insight into why it is true or how its ideas might be employed elsewhere. The job of human mathematicians will be to become arbiters of the correctness of proofs, but also to scrutinize the reasoning and to extract the underlying ideas, determining whether the result says anything that meaningfully advances the field.

Mathematics, as a research community, needs to react rapidly to this change. Mathematicians and journals must prioritize significance over output. Mathematics involves deciding which results are important as well as generating them. A proof can be correct without being insightful. To give a simplified example, AI might "prove" that the square of a number divisible by two is divisible by four and then prove that the square of a number divisible by three is divisible by nine, and so on with ever larger integers. However, each new "proof" isn't an example of insightful mathematics, just a variation on the same elementary idea.

AI can create arguments faster than the community can verify, interpret or absorb them. Existing safeguards were not designed for that imbalance.

In contrast, a significant proof might settle a long-standing question, reveal an unexpected connection between disparate fields or develop a technique which is useful in the solution of many other problems.

Journals should therefore require authors to explain clearly what is genuinely new, why it matters — and what role AI played. Reviewers should judge whether a result deepens understanding, rather than merely verifying that the argument works. That does not mean rejecting work whose eventual importance is uncertain. The history of mathematics is full of ideas whose significance became apparent only decades later, so journals must continue to make room for foundational, exploratory and curiosity-driven research.

But there is a difference between a result with as-yet unknown implications and one that is unlikely ever to be insightful. Mathematical judgement cannot guarantee that nothing valuable is ever overlooked. It can, however, distinguish work that contains genuinely new ideas or possibilities from the automated production of uninteresting dead ends.

Universities and funders should also stop treating publication counts as a convenient proxy for quality. Careers are built around papers, citations, grants and prizes, but these measures were developed when producing sophisticated mathematics demanded substantial human time and effort. In the age of AI, work that might previously have taken years of careful thought could now be produced in weeks or even days.

Consequently, as the cost of generating mathematical results falls dramatically, those measures of quality become less useful. A decreased reliance on traditional metrics may be no bad thing, but institutions need credible alternatives: assessments of a researcher's most important contributions, evidence of intellectual leadership and explanations of how their work has changed understanding. This is urgent because mathematicians are already struggling to evaluate the sheer volume of material being produced.

Finally, mathematical training must continue to reward understanding. Written work alone will become a less reliable guide to individual capability when papers, reports and applications can be written mostly using AI. Seminars, discussions and collaborations can reveal whether someone understands an argument, can defend it and can connect it to other ideas. Demonstrating understanding has always been a more important quality in university students than simply presenting the answer; education and recruitment should now reflect that principle more explicitly.

Critics might argue that this is an overreaction. Mathematical claims still require proof, peer review already evaluates significance, and AI is simply another tool, like a calculator or computer algebra system. There is a degree of truth to each objection. Yet the explosion in the number of published papers changes the nature of the game. A calculator does not generate hundreds of research claims that specialists must spend precious time checking. AI can create arguments faster than the community can verify, interpret or absorb them. Existing safeguards were not designed for that imbalance.

Recent advances have understandably generated both excitement and anxiety. The right response is neither to reject AI nor to unguardedly celebrate every finding it produces. Journals, universities and funders should adapt their incentives now, before quantity overwhelms judgment completely.

In an environment increasingly capable of automatically generating research-level mathematics, the most valuable experts will be those who know which questions are worth asking, which results deserve trust and which ideas are worth our attention.

#6460. A Gigantic Stellar Eruption Spreads Planetary Material Into Space

Highly-evolved stars spread the material for new planets and stars into space with their stellar winds. These stars are called aysmptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, and they're cool, luminous stars that are running out of hydrogen and leaving the main sequence behind. As they age, they can shed as much as 30 Earth masses of material per year into the interstellar medium (ISM).

The material is first emitted in pulses of gas, and eventually that gas cools into dust and the star's radiation pressure pushes it away with its stellar wind. Carbon and silica are important parts of what's emitted, and silica is the main building block for rocky planets, while carbon feeds into organic particles. So these stellar winds from AGB stars clearly play an important role in the formation of planets, other stars, and even potential life.

Researchers at Chalmers University in Sweden have been observing Mira, an AGB star about 300 light years away. It's the prototype and namesake of what are called Mira variables, pulsating AGB stars that are oxygen-rich. Their results are challenging the long-held understanding that stellar winds driven by radiation pressure are what spread heavy elements into the interstellar medium (ISM).

The research is "A giant magnetic eruption from the asymptotic-giant-branch star Mira A," and it's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics. The lead author is Wouter Vlemmings, Professor in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology in Gothenburg, Sweden.

"Mass loss during the advanced evolutionary stages of low- and intermediate-mass stars is traditionally attributed to dust-driven winds, whereas the influence of magnetic fields remains poorly constrained," the authors write. "This mass-loss process is crucial for the chemical enrichment of the Universe."

Since this type of mass-loss is so fundamental, it's attracted a lot of attention and is the subject of a huge amount of research. In this work, the researchers used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observations to study how Mira's magnetic fields might shape its mass loss. ALMA can't directly observe magnetic fields; instead it observes them indirectly through their polarizing effect on radio emissions.

âFor decades, astronomers have believed that the winds from stars like this must be powered by starlight. Light from the star shines on grains of dust in the starâs outer atmosphere, and that gives them a push. But this star is showing us something different: that strong magnetic fields can also shape and power stellar winds. That changes a fundamental part of the origin story of the atoms we ourselves are made of," lead author Vlemmings explained in a press release.

This schematic shows the structure of an AGB star, from its degenerate core to its circumstellar envelope. It shows it during its thermal pulse stage, when pulses drive gas outward, where it cools and forms dust in the envelope. Radiation pressure generates the stellar wind that drives the dust away into the ISM. Image Credit: Lu et al. Front. Astron. Space Sci., 23 July 2025. Sec. Astrostatistics

Astrophysicists have detected strong magnetic fields in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars like Mira, and researchers have suggested that they may play a role in driving their mass loss. But the researchers explain that there's been no empirical evidence of the role magnetic fields play in the process, and that wind-driven mass loss models don't include magnetic fields.

Recent observations, however, are challenging the overall understanding of the wind-driven mass loss scenario. Some AGB stars show mass-loss but also show insufficient dust to explain it. These stars are oxygen-rich AGB stars like Mira. Since Mira is the nearest of its type of dusty, pulsation-driven O-rich AGB stars, it makes sense to study it.

Both ALMA and the Very Large Array recently observed Mira A, the AGB star, and its companion Mira B, a white dwarf, in August 2025. But observations go back ten years, and both sets of data combine to reveal dramatic changes on Mira A's surface.

"During the past decade, high-angular-resolution observations of Mira A at visible, millimetre, and submillimetre wavelengths have revealed several unexpected phenomena related to the stellar atmosphere and mass-loss process," the authors write.

This ten-year study of Mira's surface is the longest study of any star other than the Sun.

This time-lapse shows ten years of changes on the surface of Mira A. Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

âWe were astonished to see how the starâs surface is constantly changing. The brightest areas were different every time we looked, and the brightest patches are amazingly bright. We realised that star is flaring, releasing vast amounts of energy each time," said study co-author Miora Andriantsaralaza, a postdoctoral researcher in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology.

Some of the hotspots in the video have brightness temperatures of 8,000 Kelvin. That's far higher than the average 2,000 K brightness temperature.

But the main finding is what researchers call SiO (silicon monoxide) masers. They're often found in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars, just inside the dust formation zone. But Mira A's masers are at a much greater distance, where the gas is too thin for a strong SiO maser to form. So the researchers say the masers trace a shock moving outward, and that it has much higher density than expected. In short, a flare that expanded into a huge loop of expelled material.

âIn 2023, we saw one of these flares appear on the starâs surface, but it didnât stop there. Over the next two years, this eruption on the surface created a vast, expanding loop of gas around the star, which we captured in an image in 2025. The loop was much bigger than the star, extending as far out as the distance of Saturn from the Sun. We hadnât seen anything like that before," said co-author Behzad Bojnordi Arbab, a doctoral student at Chalmers University.

Masers aren't always polarised, but these ones are linearly and circularly polarized. Linearly polarised means its polarisation is organized, and the polarising is shaping it. Circular means it rotates in a corkscrew pattern. Taken together, the astronomers used those features to map Mira's magnetic field geometry. That in turn let them understand how the magnetism is shaping its wind and its mass loss.

The loop and its polarisation is the key in this work.

âIn the loop, thereâs a strong magnetic field, which must also influence the starâs wind. That showed us a connection between the flare and the loop, and reminded us also of phenomena we can see on our Sun," said Vlemmings.

This figure from the research shows a three-dimensional representation of the adopted magnetic-loop ejection model anchored to the surface of Mira. The structure is colour coded according to line-of-sight velocity. Image Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

For now, the source of these magnetic fields isn't entirely clear. "The origin of the magnetic fields responsible for the observed ejections remains uncertain, although several mechanisms have been proposed," the authors write. A turbulent dynamo deep in Mira's convective envelope could be responsible, or differential rotation between the star's core and envelope could be behind them. Making progress understanding how the magnetic fields drive mass loss will depend on understanding how they're generated.

The flares and magnetic fields are evidence of a new element in mass-loss. On our Sun, flares are generated by magnetic fields, and they're associated with coronal mass ejections, where material is sent speeding away from the Sun. But our Sun is young, and isn't an aged AGB star experiencing the same level of mass loss. Still, these findings draw a parallel between the two.

âNow we see that magnetic storms on Miraâs surface are continually creating bright flares. Even more surprisingly, each of these is strong enough to lift parts of the starâs outer layers and launch them into interstellar space,â said Andriantsaralaza.

This research shows that our understanding of AGB mass-loss has to take into account magnetic fields, not just radiation-driven stellar winds.

"The discovery of coronal-mass-ejection-style eruptions from an AGB star redefines our understanding of late-stage stellar evolution," the authors write. They can help explain some of the features of AGB mass-loss, like clumpiness, asymmetry, and time variability. They can also help explain some of the morphologies of planetary nebulae, the beautiful shells of ionized gas ejected by aged stars.

"Consequently, magnetic activity must be integrated into models as a dynamically dominant force in initiating mass loss and shaping circumstellar environments," the authors conclude in their study. And since AGB mass loss spreads the stuff of planets into the ISM, that could explain, at least partly, why we're here.

âOur study has consequences for our understanding of the whole of the galaxyâs ecosystem. Perhaps, Earth wouldnât be here if it wasnât for magnetic storms on a red giant star, billions of years ago before the Sun was born," said Vlemmings.

#6459. Earth’s Lakes Are Changing in Unison – and Scientists Are Worried

Lakes play an important role in regulating Earth’s carbon cycle, and scientists warn that environmental changes occurring across many lakes at once could amplify global climate risks.

Lakes around the world are increasingly changing in step, a trend that could weaken a natural buffer against environmental disruption. A new study found that this synchronization has accelerated markedly since 2000.

The characteristics of a lake’s watershed, the land that drains into it, have historically helped buffer its ecosystem against broader environmental changes. Lakes fluctuated independently, a pattern known as “spatial asynchrony” that spread ecological disturbances across time and space.

A team led by Prof. Ke Zhang of the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (NIGLAS) combined century-scale sediment records with continuous satellite observations from approximately 2,000 lakes. Alongside growing synchrony, the researchers found a significant decline in network modularity, meaning the lake network was becoming less divided into groups with distinct patterns of change.

The researchers used water clarity and phytoplankton biomass, the mass of microscopic organisms that use sunlight to make food, as proxies for lake metabolic activity. These indicators provide an indirect view of how lake ecosystems process energy and nutrients. Their growing synchrony suggests that the underlying carbon, nutrient, and biodiversity dynamics they reflect may also be becoming more synchronized.

The study attributes this shift to environmental telecoupling, connections through which climate extremes such as heatwaves and socioeconomic pressures link changes across distant regions. The authors describe this increasingly linked response to large-scale environmental change as a new hallmark of the Anthropocene, a term used to describe a world profoundly shaped by human activity.

Although lakes cover less than 2% of Earth’s surface, they help regulate global carbon and nutrient cycles and biodiversity. Losing the differences in how they respond to environmental pressures could therefore have consequences well beyond individual watersheds.

“This loss of buffering capacity transforms lakes from passive, regionally distinct systems into active amplifiers of global environmental risks. Synchronized lakes can concentrate biophysical fluxes, potentially triggering high-amplitude global pulses, such as simultaneous greenhouse gas emissions or widespread aquatic hypoxia, thereby exacerbating the triple planetary crisis,” Zhang said.

Aquatic hypoxia means a shortage of oxygen in the water. The “triple planetary crisis” refers to climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution.

Water management has traditionally treated lakes as isolated local resources, creating what the researchers describe as a “scale mismatch” between governance and the processes shaping these ecosystems. Zhang and his co-authors propose treating interconnected lake networks as a dynamically coupled “Planetary Commons.” Their objective is to protect the local ecological processes that maintain variation across landscapes, without seeking to eliminate synchrony.

To put that idea into practice, the team introduced a framework called Strategic Planetary Lake Areas (SPLAs). By tracking large-scale measures of synchrony and modularity, policymakers could identify priority regions, including regional groups of lakes whose behavior is rapidly converging. These areas could become candidates for targeted polycentric governance, an approach involving multiple centers of decision-making.

“This research not only redefines the critical importance of inland waters in global change studies but also introduces a macroscale dimension to international sustainable development agendas,” Zhang said. “The work emphasizes that preserving the diversity of ecological responses is essential for maintaining long-term Earth-system stability in an increasingly interconnected world.”

Reference: “Global lake synchrony signals rising planetary-scale ecological coupling” by Ke Zhang, Yaoyao Han, Lindsey Gillson, Xiaoling Zhang, Suzanne McGowan, Michael E. Meadows, Yuan Jin, Luki Subehi, John A. Dearing, David P. Hamilton, Yan Zhao, Lian Pin Koh and David Taylor, 16 November 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2611874123

Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter.Follow us on Google and Google News.

“The authors describe this increasingly linked response to large-scale environmental change as a new hallmark of the Anthropocene.”

The article doesn’t really support their claim of “increasing synchrony.” This sounds more like assigning a scapegoat than explaining what is driving the alleged changes. It appears to me that the relationship is best described by a U-shaped function rather than a linear, long-term trend. The index graph that is most U-like is the one going back farthest in time, suggesting some periodicity related to time.

The R^2 value in all cases is less than 0.5, and in most cases less than 0.2. That means that the variance in the dependent variable that is explained by the changes in the independent variable is less than the probability of getting a ‘Head’ in a coin flip. That doesn’t convince me that they really understand what is going on. But the buzzword salad had all the right words and conclusions to get published!
