#6458. The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor

The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

We update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor

The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

We update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

As Jonathan Nunn wrote in his guide to north London’s best-value restaurants, “Durak, a tantuni salonu run by Dogan Yesil on West Green Road, is the superior late night snack template.” Only the tantuni, a speciality which originates in the city of Mersin on the southern coast of Turkey, is served here. Beef is boiled, seasoned with the likes of tomato, pul biber, sumac, and cumin and subsequently fried in cotton oil before being loaded, meat juices aplenty, inside a thin lavash with chopped parsley, tomato, and onion. It is then given a pleasing bend before being eaten; a selection of high-acid accompaniments — pickled chiles, lemon — provide the necessary cut-through.

Best for: A snack on the way home after a long day.

Mukaddes Yadikar’s restaurant near Walthamstow Central station opened in London in summer 2017. It was London’s first strictly Uyghur restaurant, and has become perhaps E17’s finest neighborhood restaurant. To start, go for the Chaomian, a stir-fry of short noodle snippets wokked with chunks of beef, spring onion, and tomato. Third, and most importantly, get the signature da pan ji (“big plate chicken”): a remarkably deep, savoury, and spicy chicken and potato stew, teeming with Sichuan peppercorns, served with flat hand-pulled noodles. This is a warm, homely, and treasured space to eat in east London.

Open for: Lunch and dinner on weekends, dinner only during the week

Eater London’s Restaurant of the Year 2022 comprises three discrete yet intertwined endeavors. Downstairs in the basement kitchen, George Jephson butchers whole animals, repurposing them as immaculate charcuterie, while upstairs, chef Mike Murphy uses excellent ingredients to prepare simple plates that lean French and southern European — think trout poached in butter with roe and sorrel; or a roast game bird with quince and bitter leaves. Sommeliers Tom Beattie and Fran Roberts, the duo behind the wine importer bearing both names, run the bar and the floor with a small team. Cadet is a wine bar, a restaurant, a charcutier, and a shopfront; it feels French and it feels London; and, from the moment it opened, it has always felt just right.

This diminutive Vietnamese shop on Hackney’s Graham Road serves one of the city’s best sandwiches — inside one of the city’s best baguettes. Although the spot has just one table and three or four seats, it’s difficult to think of warmer hospitality than at Bánh Mì Hội-An. The duo behind the counter prepare fresh sandwiches to go, and while the pork classic is excellent, don’t sleep on the turmeric-heavy fried catfish on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays; fragrant with coriander, mayo, fermented chile paste, sriracha, and pickled vegetables, it is an object lesson in flavor, texture, and balance.

Ex-Noma sommelier Yukiyasu Kaneko’s wine bar, set in a cozy space beneath a railway arch close to London Fields, may yet become the new template for natural wine bars, a category that has grown a little tired and derivative. Few other businesses can rival Yuki’s assured sense of self and pleasing ambience. An extensive (and fairly priced) list includes highlights from the Jura, Savoie, and Loire regions, as well as bottles from elsewhere in the Old World. Food is secondary but not an afterthought, with snacky dishes such as eggs with tahini, house-made potato crisps dressed with sansho pepper, cured beet tops, silken tofu with mushrooms, and made-to-order beef tartare.

Must-try dish: Ask Yuki for his best wines from the Jura or the Savoie.

These days, London has no shortage of excellent new-age wine bars. It’s been a signature category in the city since the days of P. Franco and the likes of Terroirs before. But in more recent times, spots like Cadet, Hector’s, and Yuki Bar have raised the standard of wine bars sharply. At Goodbye Horses, which opened in the second part of 2024 (and where I enjoyed one of my favorite nights out last year), sommelier Nathalie Nelles oversees one of the most interesting wine lists in the city. Nelles has a penchant for excellent French wines from the Jura, Loire, and Burgundy. Go in the evening to enjoy a selection of small plates, which might include an avant-garde beef tartare, some carefully arranged crostini-like toasts, and a cheese plate. But you’re here to drink, really, and to take in the quite extraordinary interior, hand-painted curtains and long, organically shaped wooden bar — which lend the room a World of Interiors vibe in the best way.

Must-try: Complex savagnins from the Jura, elegant chenin blancs from the Loire Valley, grower Champagnes, and a mix of modern and classic wines from regal Burgundian producers.

East Ham is home to London’s largest Kerala community and its greatest concentration of South Indian restaurants. The pick of them is Thattukada, run by chef-owners Biju and Preeti Gopinath. Curries and roasts have a depth of flavor and spicing that belie their simple descriptions, and they should be mopped up with crisp parottas or snow-white appams. But it’s the legendary fries that are unmissable: half a chicken cut into segments, then aggressively and skillfully fried with chiles and crispy onions; little netholi (anchovies) cooked and eaten whole; or battered mussels that pop thrillingly in the mouth.

This elegantly designed wine club beneath a Haggerston railway arch now firmly belongs in the top bracket of (French) restaurants in London. Chef Seb Myers and his modern-ish, playful take on French country cooking fits perfectly with the fascinating and broad wine list owned by patron Jonathan Alphandery. With dishes such as a red mullet tartine; grilled leeks vinaigrette with Tunworth cheese; a duck offal choux farcis; and mackerel with coco beans and greens; as well as a caramel tart with blue cheese, Planque has nearly everything that makes a great modern European restaurant great.

Best for: Pairing some of London’s cleverest cooking with some of the best wine in the city.

Open for: Lunch and dinner, with brunch on weekends

Since Cafe Cecilia opened in 2021, it has maintained a steady flow of plaudits from all the coolest places, in part because of chef-owner Max Rocha’s connection to the world of fashion (father John and sister Simone are designers). However, there’s a surfeit of substance as well as style in this stark, minimalist cafe-bistro. And playfulness, too, seen in the likes of recreations of chicken Kievs or deep-fried bread-and-butter pudding in a pool of cold custard. Rocha and his staff are direct descendaents of the ingredients-obsessed tradition of St. John, the River Cafe, and Quo Vadis. Like peer Anna Tobias’s cooking at Cafe Deco, Rocha’s can be colored a bit beige, but it deserves the attention it has received.

Must-try dish: Do not miss the steak and chips with peppercorn sauce, nor fruit tart at dessert.

This quaint place close to King’s Cross hasn’t been open long, but has been a conversation starter the likes of which the London restaurant scene hasn’t seen for years. Chef and Belfastman Hugh Corcoran’s sub-20-seater venue is open only at lunchtime (midday and 2 p.m. sittings are offered), reservations must be made via the restaurant’s landline (or postcard, honestly), it is cash-only, and the wine menu is all kept inside the faintly grumpy, periodically affable proprietor’s head. You can skip the starters (save, perhaps, the homemade soda bread and butter); just head straight to the mains, where you might find a slice of game bird pie with mash, a portion of braised guinea fowl with cabbage, or a fantastic rendition of a Dublin classic — coddle: boiled, peppery white sausages in a salty broth with root vegetables and lots of allium. This place eschews everything that the London restaurant industry has become, while bringing forth some (if not all) of the good things it once offered. And you can say, “I was there then.”

The area around Euston station is replete with no-frills, delicious places to eat. This little Malaysian basement setup from chef Sugen Gopal on Doric Way may be the best. Two pieces of freshly made, high-moisture roti canai — to eat in or take away — are best served with curry dal. Roti King has a few other locations throughout London as well.

Know before you go: The new online queueing system makes for a seamless experience.

Chef Ed Wilson’s hearty French Italian menu is a showcase for his own personal love of food. To eat here is to share that passion, especially now with an increased emphasis on fresh pasta and spectacular comfort food. Wines are predominantly natural and biodynamic. Illustrated wine posters, art, and curios on whitewashed brick walls also make the two relaxed dining rooms on Columbia Road among London’s most handsome and cool.

Vibe check: This place has the city’s smallest and most beautiful bathrooms — among the very first to use Aesop, too.

At the late chef Kate Armah’s outstanding neighborhood Ghanaian restaurant in east London, the sharing platter — which includes tsofi, chicken wings, kebabs, plantains, and more — might be the definition of generosity in hospitality. Other highlights here include akonfem (guinea fowl), red red (fried plantain with black eye bean stew and gari foto), and any of the soups, which come served with choice of starchy sides such as fufu, kenkey, kokonte, or rice.

Vibe check: As the venue of choice for many visiting musicians and performers, Kate’s might be London’s least-appreciated celebrity restaurant.

There is no shortage of decent pizza in this town, but reliably excellent New York-style slices are harder to come by. Tom Vincent’s Vincenzo’s, which has been a bona fide IYKYK destination in Bushey, Watford for the last half decade, made its arrival in central London at the end of 2025 and since then has been treating the city to an excellent roster of classics and innovative pies. There are cheese, tomato, and pepperoni pizzas, all featuring low-moisture mozzarella, good tomato sauce, and a delightfully crisp base. U.S. colleagues might even admire the resistance to tip dip. Beyond the classics, look out for a spanakopita slice featuring feta, creamed spinach, and a Scotch bonnet honey; and the lesser-seen, thicker-based grandma pie for the heads, sometimes topped with vodka sauce, other times with pepperoni and hot honey.

Best for: Probably the best pizza slice in town.

After a refurbishment of both kitchen and premises, this haven on Farringdon Road is back to the form that has made it one of the most essential of the city’s essential kitchens in recent years. Chef Nick Bramham’s cooking now leans more towards the Aegean, with the likes of giouvarlakia bringing herbed meatballs bobbing in avgolemono. The menu will change weekly and will travel across southern Europe, but look out for Bramham’s clever riffs on BLTs, lobster rolls, and perfectly seasoned pasta dishes, after peerless gildas, before flawless sour cherry cannoli.

Must-try dish: When Nick does pasta or Nick does a sandwich, you must order it.

Clerkenwell’s Sushi Tetsu might be the hardest reservation in London. It also pound-for-pound serves the best (value) sushi in the city. To observe Toru Takahashi’s knife skills and to eat his omakase menu while receiving Harumi Takahashi’s gently flawless hospitality (the two are married) is to experience one of London’s most complete and completely brilliant restaurants.

Know before you go: There are only seven seats in the restaurant, all at the sushi counter.

While the original St. John is rightly regarded as the most important British restaurant in a generation, Bread and Wine, the sibling site in Spitalfields, is a better and more interesting restaurant today. If food were a religion, then this would be its church. Welsh rarebit, bone marrow and parsley salad, foie gras on toast, mussels with cider, deviled kidneys, half a dozen madeleines, and a whole pie, which might be filled with pheasant, bacon, and trotter. Praise be.

Best for: Lunch is one of the purest, most heavenly restaurant experiences in London.

Joké Bakare’s small, two-story central London venue is no secret to anyone interested in restaurants: The chef’s modern recreations of classic dishes from Nigeria and the broader West African region have earned recognition from across the globe, including from the Michelin guide, which awarded Chishuru a star. As well as the chef’s immense presence, inventiveness, and ability to convey her love of food, the brilliance of Chishuru’s menu is rooted in age-old practices of fermentation, which lend many of the dishes a deep and lasting umami. It’s there in dishes like beef sirloin and dawadawa short rib with Tokyo turnip and a bitter leaf sauce, as well as grilled guinea fowl breast with celeriac cake, jalapeño, and egusi sauce.

Must-try dishes: Be sure to try Bakare’s jollof rice, and leave room for dessert.

Given the pace at which restaurants are modernizing and as the internationality of food becomes ever more commonplace, the Ledbury’s tablecloths and Franco-modern European style might be classified as old-school-ish. But that would be to ignore the level of craft and conscientious sourcing, and its application of Japanese ingredients and techniques in dishes like Cornish bluefin otoro with miyagawa and black sesame; or veal sweetbread with parsnip, liquorice, pear, and sansho pepper. And, finally, to consider the Ledbury a relic would be to overlook the profound influence chef-owner Brett Graham has had on the professional development of many of London’s best modern chefs — from BRAT to the Clove Club and beyond.

Best for: Birthdays, anniversaries, and one of the most special fine-dining experiences in the city.

Chef Meedu Saad’s hotly-anticipated Soho restaurant feels all at once brand new, a fixture of Soho and primed to remain in situ for years to come. Super 8, the group behind it and celebrated venues like Kiln, Brat, and Mountain, has a knack for creating the restaurants that Londoners (and tourists) really want, before they know they want it. Impala embodies the qualities that give the group its edge — a buzzy, handsome dining room, thoughtfully curated playlists, attentive and cool service, plus clever dishes prepared with fine, carefully-sourced produce. The group also promotes its best talent to give them a platform; in Saad, backed by development chef Songsoo Kim, they have a star. This north Londoner, British Egyptian chef is cooking his own food: North African leaning with French and modern British accents, most of it over hot coals or from a wood-fired oven. Try the aish balady with Tunisian harissa, ftira with egg, a grilled squid and green leaf salad, sheftalia, molokhia with lamb, Cantonese-ish-style roast duck with fig sauce, or an elegant pilaf. And save room for the one dessert: a pistachio and date custard tart.

Must-try dish: Cantonese-style roast duck with molasses and fig sauce. (Get it with the pilaf.)

Shuko Oda’s little bar in Soho is among London’s most acclaimed Japanese restaurants. Over a long, blond wooden counter, chefs calmly and politely pass hot bowls of steaming broth containing noodles made on-site, topped with proteins like tempura prawn or smoked mackerel, or seasonal green vegetables from Sussex farm Namayasai. The traditional Japanese breakfast is the most steadying in London.

Know before you go: The specials board of small plates changes every day and exhibits some of the city’s best modern British cooking.

Bar Italia remains one of London’s most precious institutions, a relic of the mid-20th century sitting indomitably on Soho’s Frith Street. More than almost anywhere else in the capital, Soho is a victim of change, fads, and nonsensical restaurants. (True story: A half decade ago this same street played host to a venue called Flavour Bastard.) But Bar Italia never changes. And for that, we must be grateful. Its consistency and sense of self is what makes it so steadying and reassuring in a world of flux and uncertainty. At Bar Italia you always know your espresso will be bitter, your Peroni will be cold, and your bacon ciabatta will be better than almost anything else you can get in this storied but spoiled patch of the city.

Best for: An iconic, reliable breakfast and espresso.

For my money, Ikoyi may be the choicest special occasion venue in the city. Chef Jeremy Chan and restaurateur Iré Hasan-Odukale’s venue has evolved since its inception in St. James’s in 2017. It now occupies a sleek location in the bowels of 180 The Strand and has matured accordingly, elevating the food yet further to match its fancy new surroundings. While it is still philosophically rooted in the culinary traditions and flavor profiles of Nigeria and the West African region, Ikoyi is now an archetype of the Ultra-Modern European genre. Recent meals have featured the seductive savory deliciousness of Chan’s signature smoked jollof rice, and the precise application of spice and chile heat to immaculately cooked protein will blow you away, whether it’s sweetbread suya, dry-aged turbot, or charcoal-grilled lobster. A special restaurant, deserving of its two Michelin-starred status.

Gerrard Street’s Cantonese institution needs little introduction. Wong Kei is a decades-old London restaurant famous for its multistory dining room, roast meats (duck, char siu), wontons, red-ringed plates, and the now-cult (if much overstated) brusque service. Its enduring appeal — in spite of newer, trendier, regionally diverse restaurants in central London’s Chinatown — is its faithfulness to the traditions of dependable and delicious Cantonese cooking in the U.K., the stuff of a bygone era. In other words, it’s a giant, 500-seat living monument to a time before bubble waffles and Instagram-first openings.

Best for: A nostalgic UK-Cantonese meal with a group.

Chef Normah Abd Hamid and her family team offer a Malaysian comfort menu that makes the restaurant one of the best in the city from a nook of a unit in Queensway Market. Sour, hot assam pedas; roti to rival London’s King in Euston; and beef rendang or nasi lemak to go alongside. Normah’s is quaint and Normah is brilliant; this remains one of central London’s best restaurants to visit with a small group of friends and one to take out-of-towners visiting the city.

Know before you go: The food is halal, and no alcohol is allowed on site.

Mayfair’s two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of a few places in London that manages to straddle the line between celebrity hype and quality cooking. Tandoori masala lamb chops, chicken butter masala, and the trademark wild muntjac biryani remain standouts 13 years after it arrived on Albemarle Street. The prices match the level of cooking and the illustrious surroundings, making this one for special occasions.

Best for: Special occasions, atmosphere, and some of the finest curries in the city.

Together with Saikei, this is one of the great places in London to eat dim sum — particularly, with a big group on a Sunday lunchtime for the whole experience, driving out to the Docklands, walking up the wooden staircase to above a mixed martial arts gym, and putting your name down among the dozens of others to wait for a table. Once inside and seated, it’s a procession of tea and food. Be sure to order extra of the prawn and chive dumplings, and the special fried cheung fun with XO sauce (one of the best rice noodle dishes in the city). You might plump for sui mai, tripe, or some ribs. Barely anything you choose will disappoint. And from there, it might be a selection of sticky-sweet roast meats, or a Cantonese-style steamed seabass with ginger and spring onions and rice to share for the table. There is no way you’ll leave unsatisfied; lunch at Yi-Ban is pure nourishment.

Best for: Sunday lunch with a group (and plane spotting at City Airport).

There’s something lazily obvious about including the Ritz on a list of essential restaurants in London, but credit where credit’s due. The chef in charge comes fully garlanded: John Williams MBE is the master of niche, old-school French fine dining, delivering dishes of exceptional precision, yet never at the expense of deliciousness. Despite much frippery and eye-watering expense, when you get down to the brass tacks of a meal at the Ritz, it’s really quite simple: immaculately seasoned ingredients, assembled into balanced dishes, cooked adroitly. That’s true across the menu, but nowhere more so than in the Dorset crab with creme fraiche and Imperial caviar; filet of veal with white asparagus and lovage; the classic beef Wellington; and the theatrical crepe suzette.

Know before you go: The restaurant will make sure you comply with the formal dress code.

A treasure. Unmoved by the comings and goings of trends, Bermondsey’s 40 Maltby St is a 40-cover answer to the question, pejorative as it may often be: What is British food? Steve Williams is a chef’s chef, cited by James Lowe, Brett Graham, and Florence Knight in their top five in the city. Raef Hodgson of distributor Gergovie Wines — which features low-intervention styles — runs the front-of-house without hubris. Recent dishes included winners such as pork schnitzel with raw celeriac, mustard, and braised potatoes, onion, and thyme, or a chestnut and brown sugar meringue.

Know before you go: Check Instagram for the menu, which always features an in-joke or two.

This vast restaurant dining room sits quite inexplicably on the ground floor of a Holiday Inn Express budget hotel just off the A102 on the south exit of the Blackwall Tunnel. But this is a destination dining room of tremendous pedigree. A mid-length, high-quality dim sum menu features a must-try fried prawn and Chinese chive number that stakes a fair claim to being the best single-bite hot item in the city — a crispy, fatty, sweet, salty umami nugget. Among the noodle plates to share, king prawns are excellent, with the noodles taking on the requisite smoke from the wok, seasoned judiciously. Saikei is a close-to-perfect family and group dining experience.

Best for: Sunday lunch, preferably with a large group.

Open for: Dinner to late night during the week, lunch to late night on weekends

In his guide to the city’s best East African restaurants, Riaz Phillips says Adulis’s “palatial setting has to make it one of the finest east African and Eritrean restaurants in the capital.” The dark wooden fixtures give every meal here a sense of occasion. The restaurant is well-suited to solo or group dining, with a menu offering selections for one, two, four, and eight persons. Look out for kwanta fitfit, smoked, dried beef with green chile and injera; zilzl assa, grilled red snapper seasoned with Eritrean herbs; and the entire range of vegetarian and vegan stews, comprising spinach, beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all eaten with more of the excellent, subtly tangy, and moreish injera.

Best for: A special occasion with vegetarians and vegans.

Open for: Dinner on weeknights, brunch through dinner on weekends

The second branch for this south London institution, Nandine — “kitchen” in Kurdish — is run by Pary Baban, husband Pola, and sons Rang and Raman. During the day it serves a menu of brunch dishes, meze, and intricate pastries. Technicolored and abundant meze platters served in the evening include kubba (minced beef and rice patties), onion dolma, and qawarma. Pastries like borek, made with a Kurdish pastry called galgali, and baklava are not to be missed.

Best for: Go for brunch and get the meze, for yourself.

Bruce Poole’s Wandsworth Common institution is best summed up thus: technique, decadence, and salt. There’s skill and execution here that no longer feels commonplace in restaurants in London (explained, perhaps in part, by how out-of-London it feels). It’s classical in almost every sense; the dining room has the breezy, impressionist art-covered air of a destination neighborhood bistro in which Michelin’s inspectors would feel welcome. But what it lacks in new-wave imagination over the course of a meal, it makes up for in professionalism and elan. My favorite dish during a recent visit was a “homemade” (you’ve gotta shout about these things in buzzy Wandsworth) cavatelli with duck and morteau sausage ragu, showered with Parmesan: rich, moreish, sumptuous — a flawless small plate of pasta.

Best for: Special occasions, especially including a glass or two of vintage Champagne.

Possibly London’s best Jamaican jerk shop. On the edge of Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park, with a smoky aroma detectable from many hundred meters, this stark room is dedicated to one thing: immaculately, judiciously seasoned protein grilled without remorse. The age of these oil drums and the time-honored expertise of chef Murphy Lawrence and his team result in jerked pork belly, chicken, goat, and even lobster, all penetrated with smoke and lifted by allspice, Scotch bonnet, and salt. Tasty Jerk is a heady, intoxicating, and remarkably good-value eating experience.

Know before you go: Buy a bottle of the home-made pepper sauce to take away, but use with caution and keep it in the fridge.

Fascinated by British meats and Thai cooking preparations, restaurateur Ben Chapman opened this homage to northern Thailand on Brewer Street in Soho 10 years ago this year. It has always been a dynamic showcase for rare-breed British meat in spicy, piquant laabs, Cornish dayboat fish in bright seafood curries, and complex, herbaceous salads (a mix of British leaves and Thai herbs), the like of which are seldom found anywhere in the capital. Almost all of the cooking here is done not with electricity or gas, but over charcoal.

Must-try dish: Claypot glass noodles. Don’t skip the wine list.

Despite the proximity of France to Britain, the restaurant traditions and contemporary scenes have little in common. There is just something – the je ne sais quoi – about bistros in France which isn’t often found in venues on this side of the channel. But there are those who manage to recreate the mythos and romanticism of the bistro-proper. Chef Henry Harris’s longstanding practice in the field of French cooking lends him a rare level of expertise. His Bouchon Racine sits above a pub close to Farringdon station, and it feels like a bistro – tables are close, there’s little in the way of frippery, the menu is written out in chalk on a blackboard, which is moved around the dining room. It’s difficult to choose, but a good place to start is with a plate of paté or terrine, followed by one of the finest versions of rabbit in mustard sauce; confit de canard; or a côte de boeuf to share. It would be rude not to finish with a crème caramel and a pate of cheese.

Best for: Lapin à la moutarde, French bistro classics.

Open for: Lunch and dinner during the week (but check opening hours; reservations by email only.)

Best for: The most delicious, hyper-seasonal cooking in the city right now.

Canada’s smallest province is big on fresh produce, pristine seafood, gorgeous views, and warm conviviality.

Where to eat in Barcelona, Spain, according to a local gastronomic tour guide

All-inclusive escapes have never looked — or tasted — so good

Today guests expect more than a Michelin-starred restaurant. They want to get into the kitchen and out in the field.

No more generic resort food. These culinary-savvy properties bring a distinct sense of place to the all-inclusive experience.

Where to go to rest, relax, recharge, and eat well while doing it

#6457. A Brief-ish History of METI. Part IV: Millennial METI Experiments

Welcome back to our ongoing series on the Brief-ish History of Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence (METI). In our previous installments, we examined the inspiration and earliest experiments in this field. We then looked at how it co-evolved with the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI), leading to the first true attempt to send a message of greeting to the stars (the Arecibo Message). We followed up with a look at two of the brightest minds in the business (Frank Drake and Carl Sagan), the brains behind the first interstellar messages (the Pioneer Plaques and the Voyager Golden Records).

Today, we'll look at experiments conducted since the end of the Space Age and the turn of the century. And just like SETI, the number of experiments has grown considerably, thanks to renewed interest in space exploration following new efforts to explore Mars and the Solar System. This included the first orbital observatory, the venerable Hubble Space Telescope, and deep space probes like the Galileo, Cassini-Huygens, Magellan, and Venus Express missions.

This era also saw revitalized efforts to search for signs of past (and maybe present) life on Mars. These included orbiters like the Mars Odyssey and Mars Express missions, and rovers and landers like Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, as well as Spirit and Opportunity. These experiments also reflected the changing nature of space exploration, which included missions from emerging space agencies, non-profits, and private entities.

All of these experiments built on the legacy of the Arecibo Message, adding additional information and personal touches where the creators desired.

An explanatory diagram of a message transmitted in 1983 by Masaki Morimoto and Hisashi Hirabayashi to Altair. Credit: ShizuShizu/Wikimedia

In 1983, astronomers Masaaki Morimoto and Hisashi Hirabayashi used the Stanford Dish radio telescope at Stanford University to transmit the Message to Altair (or the Call to the Cosmos 83'). The message was produced in collaboration with the Japanese publication Weekly Shonen Jump and transmitted on August 15th, 1983, to commemorate the publication's 15th anniversary. The destination was Altair, an A-type blue-white giant star located 16.7 light-years from Earth, which represents the Shinto deity Hikoboshi in the Tanabata legend.

Like the Arecibo Message, the content was a symbolic, graphic message meant to convey information about humanity, life on Earth, and peace. Unlike the Arecibo message, the Message to Altair consisted of several pages rather than a single, long pictograph, each dealing with a different subject. The first page included mathematical information, such as the numbers 1 to 12, prime numbers, powers of 3, formulas for indicating addition and multiplication, and chemical elements essential to life.

For this, Morimoto and Hirabayashi chose hydrogen, helium, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen, the building blocks of stars and planetary systems. Several other molecules were included, including hydroxide, water, nitrous oxide, formaldehyde, hydrogen cyanide, and their respective wavelengths. All of these chemicals play a central role in prebiotic chemistry and the formation of organic molecules that give rise to life.

Page two included information on the Solar System, including (from top to bottom) the Sun, the planets in order of distance, some of the larger moons, and their equatorial radii and mean distances from the Sun. Pages three and four included the chemical formulae for DNA compounds, as well as showing DNA structure and replication. This was followed by a series of drawings that showed different types of life forms on Earth, and they were arranged to convey the process of biological evolution.

They begin with pictures of early primitive life, followed by jellyfish, fish, amphibians, lizards, early mammals, apes, and then humans. Like the Pioneer Plaques, this image shows a man and a woman with two children between them. This was followed by a close-up illustration of the woman's face waving hello. The last page showed the transmission parameters: the total number of bits, the transmission wavelength, and the radius of the radio telescope that beamed the message.

It also contained the Japanese and English spelling for the word "toast," followed by the chemical formula for ethanol alcohol - in short, the message concludes with the raising of a toast with an alcoholic drink.

The thirteen pictures that make up the Message to Altair, listed in order (left to right, top to bottom). Credit: Shinya Nurasawa

As Altair is approximately 17 light-years distant, the message would have arrived around 2000, and the window for a reply would open by 2017. In 2023, Hyogo University astronomer Shin-ya Narusawa (who knew Morimoto before his death) asked the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) to help search for a possible reply. JAXA obliged and used the radio antenna at the Usuda Space Observatory to observe Altair for an hour at 10 p.m. on August 22nd, 2023.

The date was significant because it also fell on Tanabata in the old Japanese calendar and is the only day of the year when the deities Orihime and Hikoboshi (represented by Vega and Altair, respectively) are allowed to meet. The observations detected no signals, but Narusawa said he intends to continue observing and collaborating with other research institutions.

Between 1999 and 2003, three METI experiments were conducted using the Evpatoria Planetary Radar (EPR), a Soviet-era facility located in the Crimea for deep-space communications and radio astronomy. All four projects were organized with help from famed Soviet-Russian radio engineer, astronomer, and SETI researcher Alexander Zaitsev. As we addressed in part I of the series, he coined the term METI in his 2006 paper, Messaging to Extra-Terrestrial Intelligence.

The first project to use the EPR RT-70 radio telescope was the Cosmic Call, which included two broadcasts, one sent in 1999 and the other in 2003. The venture was a crowdsourced effort by Texas-based startup Team Encounter, Canadian astrophysicist Yvan Dutil, Russian scientists (including Zaitsev), and Eastern European radio engineers.

The message included contributions by Dutil and his fellow physicist StÃ©phane Dumas. Their primer was inspired by Hans Freudenthal's 1960 book Lincos: Design of a Language for Cosmic Intercourse, which describes a language designed to be understandable to an extraterrestrial intelligence (ETI). Using Lincos, Dutil and Dumas' message (DDM) was carefully structured to include pictograms showing mathematics, physics (the hydrogen spectrum), and related concepts.

The second part consisted of a series of pictograms created by Richard Braastad of Team Encounter, the Braastad Message (DM). It used mathematical symbols to describe a solar sail (another project Team Encounter was working on), including its dimensions, payload, trajectory, and projected launch time. This was followed by the original Arecibo Message (AM), the company's Team Encounter 2001 Staff Message (ESM), and a message composed with input from the public - the Public Part (PP).

The second page of the primer prepared by Dutil and Dumas, denoting mathematical concepts (part of the Cosmic Call). Credit: Dumas, S.

The broadcast was broken into four sessions, lasting a total of 40 hours, with each session targeting a different Sun-like (G-type) star system. These included 16 Cygni A on May 24th, 1999, a G-type star in a triple-star system located 69 light-years from Earth. On June 30th, 1999, the target was 15 Sagittae, another G-type star about 58 light-years from Earth in the Sagittarius Constellation. Lastly, and again on June 30th, 1999, the team transmitted to HD 178428, a G-type star located 69 light-years away, also in the Sagittarius Constellation.

Each session of Cosmic Call 1 transmitted the scientific parts (DDM, BM, AM, and ESM) three times at 100 bits per second, followed by the Public Part (PP), sent once at 2000 bits/s. The full message was structured as:

DDM â BM â AM â ESM â DDM â BM â AM â ESM â DDM â BM â AM â ESM â PP

The second Cosmic Call, in 2003, followed a similar structure. For this message, Dutil and Dumas presented an updated version of their Lincos pictographs (DDM2), the Arecibo Message, the Bilingual Image Glossary, and the same Public Part. The structure was as follows:

DDM2 â DDM2 â DDM2 â AM â AM â AM â BIG â BIG â BIG â BM â ESM â PP,

The destinations for this message included five more stars, with all transmissions occurring on the same day (July 6th, 2033). They included GJ 49, a G-type star located 32 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia, on July 6th, 2003. This was followed by Gliese 208, an M-type (red dwarf) star 37 light-years away in the constellation Orion; 55 Cancri, an M-type star 41 light-years away in Cancer; HD 10307, a binary star system with a G-type primary and an M-type companion 42.6 light-years away in Andromeda; and 47 Ursae Majoris, a G-type star located 45.3 light-years away in Ursa Major.

The Cosmic Calls were the most ambitious public SETI/METI effort mounted to date. While Team Encounter went bankrupt in the years that followed, their messages established a precedent that would be joined by several more METI efforts in the new millennium. Zaitsev would play a key role in several, and his work with his colleagues would culminate by 2008 in the creation of METI International. More on that soon!

Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. He lives in beautiful British Columbia with his wife and family. For more information, check out his website.

#6456. Maybe Dark Energy Isn't so Inexplicable After All

The Universe as we know it is comprised of three "things": baryonic matter (planets, stars, galaxies, us), dark matter (still unexplained) and dark energy (really, really still unexplained). Of the three, dark energy remains the most challenging. It's "something" that's driving the acceleration of the expanding Universe but that's all we know about it. We can't see it, or even put a description to it, other than "it's mysterious".

This cosmic component accounts for about 70 percent of the known Universe's energy budget. Physicists have spent a lot of time trying to explain it, often invoking some hitherto-unknown fields, or exotic physical particles, or some kind of "cosmological constant" that is the same everywhere in space and time. Despite these and other attempts at explaining dark energy, physicists still don't know exactly what it is. However, there's hope that an explanation will come in our lifetimes. A team of scientists at Canada's University of British Columbia and the University of Sheffield (in England) have come up with a possible model that provides an explanation. They think dark matter may be a product of the same physics that governs the strength of the atomic nucleus. If that's true, then they could use the standard model of particle physics to understand this mysterious thing that is pushing the Universe apart.

Dark energy has many descriptions, which reflects our incomplete understanding of it. It could be a negative pressure that pushes space outward, although thereâs no proof of that. It could be vacuum energy, which is an idea that thereâs a background of energy that permeates all of the Universe. Itâs also been called âquintessenceâ, which is a sort of imaginary âfluidâ that fills space. Or it could be a combo of dark matter and dark energy, both yet unexplained. The wildest idea is that dark energy could be a wrinkle in the fabric of space-time, or even something leaking from another universe. All those explanations are fairly wild, and oftentimes in science, the simplest is the best explanation. Thatâs where the work in Canada and England is coming in handy, if particle physics can provide insight.

According to lead scientist Ariel Zhitnitsky of UBC, using particle physics means we don't need exotic explanations for dark energy. âOur theoretical framework suggests no new particles may be required at all,â said Zhitnitsky, who developed the theoretical ideas explained by the team. âThe characteristic energy scale predicted from the QCD vacuum and gravity comes out close to the observed dark-energy scale today without having to introduce an ad hoc new field nor new parameter.â

What Zhitnitsky and others are talking about is a theory called quantum chromodynamics (QCD). It focuses on the strong nuclear force that holds quarks inside the protons and neutrons that make up atoms. QCD describes the actions of the strong force. Those actions could be affecting space, and in particular what it contains.

A NASA illustration of the strong force at work in an atomic nucleus. Credit: NASA

Space is never empty. Rather, itâs filled with subatomic fields and something called quantum energy. That's energy that exists in individual packets called âquantaâ. This creates a âquantum vacuumâ with properties that can affect space over large distances. Now, add in the fact that the Universe is expanding, and that has implications that need further explanation. The team, led by scientist Dong Ha Lee, proposed the following: as the Universe expands, the subatomic structure in the quantum vacuum responds differently as time goes by. That response generates a small energy shift that is just enough to drive the acceleration of universal expansion. The team points out that you donât need new particles or other exotic things for this: the current particles are just fine, Lee suggested. âThe idea that the quantum vacuum as described by QCD could have the right properties to account for the accelerated expansion of the universe is very intriguing,â said Lee.

So, if this idea holds up, it means that dark energy could have a connection to the strong nuclear force. Scientists could create models to test this using currently available physics models. The big test would be to compare it to cosmological data, according to Lee. âOur analysis shows that such a model can reproduce the evolving dark energy behaviour suggested by current observations. This motivates further theoretical work to better understand how the QCD vacuum responds to cosmic expansion and to develop predictions that can be tested with future observations.â

When tested against real astronomical data including light from distant supernovae and leftover radiation from the early Universe, the team found that their model matched observations just as well as standard cosmological models. In addition, it offers a possible way to explain what is causing dark energy. The next step for the team is to keep refining their model and calculations in order to build as robust a model as possible. By that time, observations and data from the next generations of telescopes, such as the Nancy Grace Roman telescope, could prove very useful in testing ideas about the true nature of dark energy and its effects on the expanding Universe over time.

#6455. Losing Weight but Getting Less Healthy? Study Reveals a Dark Side of Keto

Mice that lost weight on a very low-protein keto diet also developed fatty liver and lost muscle, highlighting the limitations of weight as a measure of health.

Ketogenic diets have become a popular approach to weight loss, despite conflicting research on their metabolic benefits. A new study in mice suggests that two often overlooked factors may help explain these inconsistencies: the amount of protein in the diet and the genetic makeup of the animals eating it. The findings also raise questions about whether losing weight on a keto diet necessarily means becoming healthier.

The research, published in Cell Metabolism, began when first author Zhaoyue Zhang, a postdoctoral fellow in the Friedman lab, noticed considerable variation in the protein content of ketogenic diets. Although these diets are generally high in fat and extremely low in carbohydrates, their protein content could be contributing to differences in metabolic outcomes.

Zhang and her colleagues systematically tested diets containing different proportions of fat and protein. After four weeks on a ketogenic diet containing just 5% protein, mice belonging to C57Bl/6J, the most commonly used laboratory mouse strain, reduced their food intake by approximately 40% and lost weight. Mice fed an otherwise similar diet containing 10% protein ate more and gained weight. Both groups produced ketones, molecules generated when the body relies heavily on fat for fuel, suggesting that ketosis alone could not account for the difference.

“The result was so striking,” Zhang says.

A closer look at the mice that lost weight revealed a more complicated picture. Although their glucose tolerance, or ability to manage changes in blood sugar, improved, they also developed fatty liver. Much of their weight loss was associated with reductions in lean mass, including muscle.

To understand what was suppressing the animals’ appetite, the researchers investigated GDF15, a hormone released in response to cellular stress that can act on the brain to reduce food intake. When they conducted an experiment using genetically modified mice lacking GDF15, even the control mice unexpectedly failed to lose weight on the low-protein diet.

“At first, I was a bit panicked,” Zhang says. “We had repeated the same experiment many times, and all of a sudden it didn’t work.”

Retracing her steps, Zhang discovered that the genetically modified mice belonged to a different substrain, C57Bl/6N, which shares approximately 99.9% of its genome with the mice used in the earlier experiments.

“This realization was key, and it became the starting point for the rest of the study,” Zhang says.

The researchers eventually identified two genes that helped explain the difference: NNT, which protects cells against oxidative stress, and NLRP12, which helps regulate inflammation. The mice susceptible to weight loss, known as B6J, carried mutations in both genes. Feeding them the low-protein ketogenic diet triggered stress and inflammatory responses in the liver, accompanied by rising levels of GDF15 and an inflammation-associated protein called LCN2. Both proteins can influence appetite through their effects on the brain.

Restoring NNT function in B6J mice caused them to eat more and lose less weight. Conversely, disabling both genes in the genetically similar B6NJ mice, which normally carry functioning versions of both genes, caused them to eat less and lose weight. Treatment with N-acetylcysteine, an antioxidant with anti-inflammatory properties, also lowered circulating levels of GDF15 and LCN2, increased food intake, and reduced weight loss.

Zhang cautions that the findings cannot be directly applied to humans, particularly because the 5% protein diet contained substantially less protein than most ketogenic diets used in clinical trials. Future trials could benefit from paying closer attention to both dietary protein content and genetic differences among participants, while looking beyond weight loss and blood sugar control when assessing metabolic health.

The researchers now want to investigate whether other genetic factors influence responses to ketogenic diets and whether the changes they observed can be reversed once the diet is discontinued.

Reference: “Macronutrient composition and genetic background determine the response to a ketogenic diet in mice” by Zhaoyue Zhang, Alexandre Moura-Assis, Shanshan Liu, Alon Millet, Jordan Shaked, Divya Rajan, Katelin Chen, Anduena Toci, Chloe Schaefer, Ijeoma Obi, Sebastian Carrasco, Sandra Kelly Atkinson, Francois Marchildon, Hanan Alwaseem, Michael Isay-Del Viscio, Henrik Molina, Paul Cohen, Kivanc Birsoy and Jeffrey Friedman, 18 November 2026, Cell Metabolism. DOI: 10.1016/j.cmet.2026.10.017

#6454. The Gifts Chefs and Bartenders Actually Want This Year

Streetwear cooking shoes, a perfect pepper mill, and more

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

This is not your average “gifts for foodies” round-up. We know that you’ve probably been given a few too many wine glasses and cookbooks. “As a professional, I don’t want to be gifted introductory-level items that will ultimately go unused,” says Storm Brunni, private dining director at Barolo Grill in Denver. That’s why, for our guide, we’ve consulted you, the hospitality pros, about what you actually would like to receive this year.

New shoes for service. “I’m getting all of my favorite people the new high-top kitchen shoes by Chuck Taylor in leather anti-slip. They’re cool enough to complete your streetwear look, functional enough to wear in the dining room, kitchen, or work, and comfy enough to wear as a commuter.” —Jonathon Sawyer, chef at Kindling in Chicago

An industry-favorite hand cream. “Between constant handwashing, citrus, chiles, and hot pans, hospitality hands take a beating. Add a heated neck massager to use on the couch after a midnight close, and you’ve basically given someone a spa day.” —Antelmo Ambrosio, executive chef at Casa Oaxaca in New York City

Something for the coffee nerds. “It’s definitely a splurge, but I buy myself the Onyx Coffee Advent Calendar every year. A lot of hospitality pros nerd out about coffee, and Onyx is one of the best roasters. They fill the calendar with individual portions of beans (enough for two people) with different origins, roasts, and processes every day. Everything is roasted on a schedule so that when you’re brewing each one, the coffee is at its peak that day. The calendar has some of their signature coffees, alongside one-offs that you’ll never be able to get again, and I’ve tried some of the best coffees of my life in past calendars.” —Katie Renshaw, owner of Bar Bambi in Chicago

An upgrade for kitchen organization. “I love this automatic tape dispenser. Gift it with a nice fresh box of Sharpies.” —Kevin Beary, beverage director of Gus’ Sip & Dip, Kitty’s Cosmopolitan Club, Three Dots and a Dash in Chicago

The gift of longer-lasting produce. “Vejibag is a family-owned business, run by a small team of women who create 100 percent organic cotton bags designed to keep produce fresher for longer at home. They genuinely work and are an amazing addition to any kitchen.” —Lauren DeSteno, executive chef at Ai Fiori in New York City

A tool for operators who know there’s always something that needs fixing. “I was given a precision screwdriver from HOTO Tools and now I’m obsessed with the brand and their design aesthetic. So many things in the restaurants need little fixes all the time and the 3.6V Electric Screwdriver Kit Pro has all the bits you could need. I also love their rotary drill for polishing plateware with chips/scratches for work.” —Zach Engel, chef at Galit and Cafe Yaya in Chicago

Gifts with a personal touch. “As a general manager some of the top staff requests I’ve received are for nice wine keys (it’s an even nicer touch if they’re engraved) and custom server books.” —John Schneekloth, general manager at Toro in Chicago

Nice dishware is worthwhile at home, too. “I’d love to receive items from Ivo Angel, a beautiful ceramics company out of Italy. I am a huge fan of the splatter design and always want a pinch bowl; I can’t have too many. Also the olive bowl with an attached vessel for pits is perfect for hosting.” —Julia Jaksoc, chef and owner of Bar Roza, Cafe Roze and Roze Pony in Nashville

The pepper mill that chefs swear by. “It’s one of those tools that gets used constantly, makes a real difference, and is something every cook or bartender would appreciate having.” —Marco Torres, Chef at Brass and The Tusk Bar in New York City

Fun socks. “Being locked down in heavy black pants, unforgiving non-slip shoe leathers, and a stiff chef coat means you have to find your personality somewhere. A pair of loud, ridiculous socks underneath always makes me feel a little more human. I’ll never forget getting this pair of bright yellow Spam socks as a Christmas gift one year. Honestly, it’s one of the best presents I’ve ever unwrapped, and it brings a little joy each time I slip them on.” —Soo Ahn, chef/partner at Adalina Prime, Arla and Adalina Italian in Chicago

Something to take the edge off. “For the industry pro who enjoys a little puff puff and a good nap (especially after a Saturday morning shift with lines out the door), you can’t go wrong with Tokin’ Jew rolling papers. We sell them at the deli because, come on, but they’re also a fantastic gift. And for the pipe people, their pickle pipes are another way to keep it kosher.” —Jake Schneider, chef and co-owner of Schneider Deli in Chicago

A beautiful book for recipe writing. “I would gift this brown leather journal cover from Shinola along with this 12-pack of pens. I think the notebook is a worthwhile splurge, and while I know the idea of a more expensive and elegant pen is both compelling and sexy, it is also impractical for when you’re on the go or as prone to losing nice pens as I am. These ones write fluidly and beautifully.” —Róbert LeBlanc, creative director and founder of LeBlanc + Smith in New Orleans

The kitchen fit of your dreams. “I could wear this jumpsuit 24/7! It’s comfortable, easy to move around in, and perfect for those long days in the kitchen when I’m constantly running around and want something that looks as good as it feels.” —Andrea Belfiore, chef and founder of EVÈNTO in New York City

A tool for foraging. “I love my ARS pruning shears. I take them pretty much everywhere when I’m out foraging, and they’re great for everything from cutting herbs to collecting branches and other ingredients for drinks. They’re one of those tools I use all the time.” —Danny Childs, co-owner of Field Day in Philadelphia

A trio of pastry chef staples. “On any given day, a pastry professional will produce dozens of recipes, and we need tools to measure mass/weight, time, and temperature. Even when we have our own, backups or better ones are always welcome! My top picks include: this scale, which has a pull-out screen when you’re scaling on to sheet trays or large bowls; this kitchen timer has four color-coded channels for timing multiple projects at once; and this thermometer, which is fast-reading, accurate, and has a magnet on the back for easy access on any magnetic surface.” —Orlando Soto, executive pastry chef of Le Bernardin in New York City

The perfect vessel for an industry-favorite amaro (or 50/50 shot). “Some of the best hospitality happens in an ounce and a half: a pour of Cynar for a regular who had a long week, a welcome taste for someone new at the bar. I’d recommend these little ceramic artichoke shot glasses to make that moment feel even more considered.” —Steven Waters, owner and operator of Fino in Denver

Many knife options. Patrick Dooley of Harry’s Bar in Paris recommends Le Grand Tradi, which is sized between a paring and chef’s knife, making it a great workhorse option, while Nancy Santiago, beverage director at NYC’s IGC Hospitality, recommends a Japanese petty knife “for precise citrus work and garnish prep.” Amir Babayoff of Ophelia Lounge in NYC is partial to Tojiro’s chef knives.

And knife storage and upkeep options. Schneekloth of Toro recommends a knife backpack, while Devin Denzer, chef at Atsumeru in Chicago, recommends a whetstone and ceramic sharpening rod, especially for newer line cooks.

A thoughtful gift card. “Here are a few gifts that I have received that stood out to me: a hefty gift card to a sought-after restaurant with guaranteed reservations on a night off, which is such a good way to give someone a night out; a gift card to a shoe store that carries high-quality work shoes, like Red Wings, Dansko, or Blundstones; and a gift card to something wellness-related—my business partner Jesse got me three sessions at a body-stretching spa downtown.” —Phila Lorn, chef and co-owner of Mawn and Sao in Philadelphia

#6453. Striped Malted Pound Cake

My earliest dessert obsession was the malted milkshake, which I indulged in every time I had enough babysitting money. My oldest, best friend, Toi, was equally obsessed with Whoppers, and we both wondered why malted sweets were so good. Turns out, the secret is in the combination of malted barley, wheat flour, and evaporated whole milk that gets toasted to caramelize the sugars contained in it.

This cake is my latest malted creation. Layering the malted vanilla and chocolate batters so they create a striped pattern isn’t just an aesthetic choice. Doing so really does keep the flavors distinct. Starting off in a cold oven allows the cake to bake evenly without overbrowning and results in a smooth, fine, melt-in your-mouth crumb. For extra malted flavor, use a pastry brush to brush the top of the cake with malted vanilla syrup in several additions, letting the syrup sink in after each addition.

I originally made this syrup to give my milkshakes that nostalgic, malt-shop flavor. But honey, it’s no one-hit wonder. It is a beautiful sweetener and is terrific when brushed on top of still-warm Striped Malted Pound Cake.

I also drizzle it over roasted fruit and mix it into buttercreams, glazes, and frostings. For breakfast, I stir it into coffee or lattes, smoothies, yogurt, and oatmeal. And it’s got savoy game, too. Try it on a dinner plate, spooned over roasted sweet potatoes or carrots alongside roasted chops or chicken.

More delicious loaf cake recipes this way.

Grease a 9x5" loaf pan with softened butter or cooking spray. Dust the pan with all-purpose flour, shaking out any excess.

In a medium bowl, whisk together 1¾ cups / 220g all-purpose flour, 1⁄4 cup / 34g cornstarch, 1⁄2 tsp. fine sea salt, and 1⁄2 tsp. baking powder.

In a stand mixer fitted with the paddle, combine 16 Tbsp. / 2 sticks / 226g unsalted butter, at room temperature, 1¼ cups / 273g granulated sugar, and 1⁄4 cup / 37g malted milk powder. Beat, starting on low speed and increasing to medium-high speed until lightened in color and fluffy, 5–7 minutes, scraping down the sides of the bowl once or twice.

On medium-low speed, add 3 large eggs, at room temperature, one at a time, scraping down the sides of the bowl after each one is incorporated.

Add one-third of the flour mixture and beat on the lowest speed until just combined. Add 2 Tbsp. heavy cream and beat on low speed until just combined. Add another one-third of the flour mixture, beating until combined, and another 2 Tbsp. heavy cream to combine. Add the remaining one-third of the flour mixture and beat until the batter is smooth, scraping down the sides of the bowl as necessary. Mix in 1½ tsp. vanilla bean paste or pure vanilla extract and 1½ tsp. whiskey or bourbon (if using).

Transfer 1½ cups of the batter to a medium bowl. Sift in 3 Tbsp. unsweetened cacao powder or cocoa powder and add the remaining 1⁄4 cup heavy cream, stirring to form a smooth chocolate batter.

To create the striped layers, drop 1 cup of the vanilla cake batter into the center of the loaf pan and then drop ½ cup of the chocolate batter on top of the vanilla batter. The alternating layers do not have to totally cover each other and let the layers spread naturally. Continue to drop those same-size portions of batter directly on top of each other, alternating the vanilla and chocolate, until all the batter is used. The batter should have spread to the corners, but if not, gently rap the pan on the counter to help it even out. Smooth the top with a small offset spatula.

Place the cake in a cold oven and set the temperature to 300°F. Bake until the loaf is golden, its top is slightly cracked, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean, 1 hour 20 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes.

Let the cake cool in the pan on a wire rack for 10 minutes, then run a knife around the edges to release it. Invert the cake onto a wire rack, reinvert, and cover the warm cake loosely in plastic wrap until completely cooled. If desired, use a pastry brush to brush the top of the cake with ½ cup Malted Vanilla Syrup several times, letting the syrup sink in after each addition. The cake will keep, wrapped in plastic at room temperature, for up to 5 days.

In a small saucepan, combine ⅓ cup / 73g granulated sugar, ½ cup / 120g water, 2 Tbsp. malted milk powder, and pinch of fine sea salt. Cook over medium heat until bubbling, whisking until the sugar and malt powder dissolve and the mixture becomes glossy, slightly thickened, and evenly beige, 2–3 minutes.

Remove from heat and whisk in 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or pure vanilla extract. Let cool slightly before using. This will keep in a covered jar or airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

#6452. Scientists Uncover a Potential Root Cause of the Global Allergy Epidemic

Scientists have identified a potential biological mechanism that could explain how seemingly unrelated environmental factors contribute to the growing prevalence of allergies.

Allergies may begin with an energy crisis inside the cells that protect the body from the outside world, rather than a malfunction of the immune system. An extensive analysis led by Griffith University researchers challenges decades of conventional thinking about allergic diseases and proposes a potential biological origin for conditions ranging from eczema to food allergies.

The researchers identified abnormalities involving mitochondria, the structures responsible for producing much of the energy cells need to function. Their findings suggest that epithelial cells, which form protective barriers along the skin, gut, nose, lungs, and esophagus, may struggle to meet environmental and metabolic demands, triggering an excessive immune response.

“For 60 years, we’ve taught that allergies start with the immune system and the barrier breaks as a consequence, but our work suggests it may be the other way around,” said study lead Professor Peter Smith, a clinical immunologist from Griffith’s School of Medicine and Dentistry.

The team examined what it describes as the largest collection of multi-omic allergy data known to the researchers, drawing on 116 case-control cohorts and data from 3,776 patients. Multi-omic analysis combines different types of molecular information to identify biological patterns that might otherwise go undetected.

Scientists may have discovered the hidden cause of allergies. Credit: Professor Peter Smith, Griffith University

“Allergy diseases, which now affect up to one in three children, may start one step earlier as a power failure in the mitochondria of the epithelial cells which form the body’s barrier surfaces,” Professor Smith said.

“The barrier cell can’t meet the energy and stress demands of the modern environment so raises the alarm too easily, and the immune events we recognize as an allergy, follow.

“It could help to explain why some children have eczema, food allergies, hay fever, asthma and related conditions.”

The strongest evidence emerged in eosinophilic esophagitis, an allergic inflammatory disease affecting the esophagus. Across all 13 independent patient cohorts, researchers found reduced activity in the cellular process responsible for removing damaged mitochondria.

In patients with eczema, abnormalities affecting the skin’s protective barrier and antioxidant defenses appeared even in areas without inflammation. This finding is consistent with the possibility that cellular dysfunction precedes visible symptoms.

However, the mitochondrial signature was not universal. Researchers found only partial evidence of it in hay fever, while the pattern was absent in established asthma and nasal polyps.

The researchers propose that several environmental factors associated with allergies could converge on the same biological vulnerability: the ability of epithelial cells to generate sufficient energy and withstand stress.

Potential contributors include highly processed diets, air pollution, microplastics, detergents, declining dietary fiber intake, and antibiotic exposure early in life.

Associate Professor Nic West, a molecular immunologist from Griffith’s School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences and co-author of the study, said the wide range of factors associated with allergies has made it difficult to develop a unified explanation for their rapid increase within a single generation.

The proposed mechanism could also explain why allergic diseases frequently recur after treatment. Inflammation itself can damage epithelial cells, potentially creating a self-perpetuating cycle of barrier dysfunction and immune activation.

“The research also explains why allergies can relapse,” Associate Professor West said.

“Once inflammation is established it damages the barrier further.

“Today’s drugs act downstream, so the disease often returns when treatment stops as they do not reach the root cause.”

The researchers emphasize that their findings support a hypothesis rather than establish a definitive cause of allergies. Direct measurements of epithelial cell function before symptoms appear will be needed to determine whether mitochondrial dysfunction initiates allergic disease.

“We have spent our careers managing the smoke and for the first time we think we can see the fire, and it is not where everyone was looking,” Professor Smith said.

“This is not a cure but is something we have never had before – a logical starting point.

“The next step is to measure these cells directly in infants before the allergy develops.”

Reference: “The Origins of Allergy: An Outside-In, Bioenergetic Hypothesis” by Peter K. Smith, Nicholas P. West, Stanley Du Preez, Hugh A. Sampson, Peter W. Hellings, David Price, Liam O’Mahony, Carina Venter, Cezmi A. Akdis and Gil Yosipovitch, 29 October 2026, Allergy. DOI: 10.1111/all.70532

Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope followed up on years-old observations to confirm the first recorded act of a giant star swallowing its companion. The stellar cannibalism occurred just next door, in the Andromeda galaxy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the first time, astronomers have caught two stars — a supergiant and a star slightly smaller than the sun — in the act of merging. After orbiting each other for thousands of years, the pair came together in just under seven years — a span short enough that researchers could watch the drama play out from start to finish. The discovery was described in a study published Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

"Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict," Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University and first author of the study, said in a NASA statement. "However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do."

The stars' imminent merger was originally picked up by NASA's now-retired Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer — a spacecraft that was designed to spot asteroids but also discovered many other interesting changes in the night sky.

Researchers noticed that a previously stable binary star system in the Andromeda galaxy, the closest major galaxy to ours, had begun to brighten. Follow-up observations from the Wide-Field Infrared Transient Explorer ‪—‬ a near-infrared instrument at the Palomar Observatory in California — revealed that the galaxy had also started spewing dust. Karambelkar’s team backed up these observations with data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) in December 2025.

The researchers dubbed the binary pair "Bao" (after its formal name, AT 2025abao) and started keeping tabs. They found that sometime in 2018, the smaller component of Bao bumped into the surface of the supergiant Bao. From there, things escalated quickly. The stars started exchanging gas in a process known as common envelope evolution. The larger Bao dragged its smaller companion closer and closer, until it was finally sucked into the supergiant's core, releasing a gigantic burst of energy.

Views of the stellar merger in Andromeda (left) captured by the NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and James Webb space telescopes (right).

This dramatic culmination was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," study co-author Kishalay De, an astronomer at Columbia University, said in the statement.

The researchers were surprised by not only the speed of this interaction but also its outcome. Bao could have easily exploded into a supernova, transformed into a neutron star or collapsed into a black hole. Instead, it seems to have settled back into a single massive star. Future observations will give scientists a sense of how the new, rejuvenated Bao is holding up after its act of cosmic cannibalism.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team's analysis could also help inform future studies of supergiant stars and binary systems. Getting a clearer picture of how common envelope evolution works could allow astronomers to reconstruct how previous mergers went down. Thanks to NASA's new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, Karambelkar predicts Bao will be far from the last merging stars scientists spot.

#6450. Comet Encke's Shape and Heat Revealed in Thermal Glow

Comets are time capsules of the origins of the solar system, containing materials that have existed for billions of years. While comets primarily orbit in the farthest reaches of the solar system, specifically the Kuiper Belt or Oort Cloud, some make their way closer to the Sun. When this happens, the increased heat cause cometary icy material to evaporate, producing a spectacular tail while also revealing the rocky material underneath, known as a cometâs nucleus. But how well can astronomers use telescopic observations to study the composition and temperatures of a cometary nucleus?

Now, a team of researchers from Japan might be one step closer to scientists better understanding comets, specifically a cometâs nucleus. Through findings recently published in The Astronomical Journal, the researchers presented new analyses regarding the shape and temperature of a comateâs nucleus, providing researchers with key observations that could be used to understand both the formation and evolution of comets and the solar system.

For the study, the researchers analyzed archival data on Comet 2P/Encke originally obtained from the Cooled Mid-Infrared Camera and Spectrometer (COMICS) on the Subaru Telescope in November 2003. During this time, Comet 2P/Encke traveled as close as 0.26 astronomical units (AU) from Earth, or about 37 million kilometers (26 million miles), enabling several ground-based telescopes, including the Subaru Telescope, to conduct mid-infrared observations of Comet 2P/Encke. This distance from Earth also put Comet 2P/Encke about 1.09 AU from the Sun, or about 163 million kilometers (101 million miles). Unfortunately, COMICS was retired from Subaru in 2020, leaving Subaru without a mid-infrared instrument, thus limiting its studies to archival data.

The primary goal of the study was to ascertain the composition of Comet 2P/Enckeâs nucleus while isolating its signal from the surrounding ice, gas, and dust that envelopes the comet and becomes larger and denser as the increased Sunâs heat evaporates it. In the end, the researchers found the nucleus of Comet 2P/Encke measured about 7 kilometers by 3 kilometers (4.3 miles by 1.9 miles) while its surface temperature is estimated to be about 328 Kelvin (55 degrees Celsius/131 degrees Fahrenheit).

"Our study of Comet Encke showed that mid-infrared observations can directly capture thermal emission from the nucleus itself," said Dr. Takafumi Ootsubo, who is assistant professor in the Department of Basic Sciences at the School of Medicine at the University of Occupational and Environmental Health in Japan, and lead author of the study. Despite COMICS retiring in 2020, Dr. Ootsubo is actively working to restart the program. "By restarting COMICS, we hope to study the shapes, temperatures, and surface materials of many more cometary nuclei in detail and get closer to revealing their true faces."

As noted, comets originate from the far reaches of the solar system, specifically the Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud, with Comet 2P/Encke originating from the former. However, some comets periodically migrate inward and become whatâs known as a Jupiter-family comet, which is what happened to Comet 2P/Encke. This means Comet 2P/Enckeâs orbit has been both captured and reshaped by Jupiterâs massive gravity, resulting in its orbit becoming significantly shorter than traditional comets at only 3.3 years. This is in stark contrast to traditional comets, which can take anywhere from decades to millions of years to travel from the outer solar system to the inner solar system and potentially be observed from Earth.

While its orbit is only 3.3 years, this doesnât mean it encounters Earth every 3.3 years. Instead, Comet 2P/Enckeâs orbit is constantly reshaping, meaning it has only had a limited few encounters with Earth in the last few decades. Along with the November 2003 encounter, Comet 2P/Encke came within only about 0.19 AU (28.5 million kilometers/17.7 million miles) from Earth in July 1997 and is slated to come within 0.62 AU (93 million kilometers/58 million miles) from Earth in February 2027.

What new insights into Comet Encke and other comets in our solar system will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!
