#6415. AI Helps Three Powerful Supercomputers Simulate The Milky Way In Extraordinary Detail

In the early days, astronomers kept sketchbooks close at hand when they looked through their telescopes. They drew what they saw and shared their drawings. Modern astronomy, with its enormous segmented lenses, gigabyte cameras, and cryogenically-cooled infrared space observatories, makes those days seem more distant than they really are. But one of the latest efforts in astronomy makes astronomy's sketch-pad days seem so far in the past, they're almost red-shifted.

In an impressive technological maneuver, astronomers have harnessed three different supercomputers together to simulate the Milky Way at a level of detail never before achieved. They used the supercomputers and AI together to simulate the Milky Way down to the level of individual stars. Up until now, the smallest level of detail in simulations, called particles, was clusters of stars with the mass of about 100 Suns. The behaviour of individual stars was averaged out in those simulations (Auriga, FIRE, etc.)

These results are in a paper titled "Architecture-Agnostic Exascale Star-by-Star Simulation of Our Galaxy," from the SC26: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis. The lead author is Keiya Hirashima, from RIKEN in Japan.

In simulations, achieving a level of individual stars means that individually simulated particles have one solar mass. So it's like a proxy for the population of stars. But regardless of that important distinction, the new simulations are extraordinary.

"Our highest-resolution Milky Way simulation used 5.4 trillion particles, â¼ 10, 000Ã those in the state-of-the-art simulations," the authors write.

âWe expect better simulations as computational power increases, but this still requires work on improving resolutions, and for a Milky Way-sized galaxy, itâs not straightforward,â said Professor Michiko Fujii from the Department of Astronomy at the University of Tokyo. âWhen we look at smaller regions in detail, we encounter areas where the gas is denser and changes rapidly. This means the simulation needs to take much shorter steps in time, which greatly increases the amount of calculation required."

This figure from the paper shows different structures of disk galaxies at different scales, emphasizing the complexity necessary for accurate simulations. Top left and middle: NGC 4414, a disk galaxy similar to the Milky Way Galaxy, taken with the Hubble Space Telescope. Top right: NGC628, a disk galaxy with spiral arms and bubble structures taken with the JWST. Bottom left: Carina star forming region taken with the JWST. Bottom middle: Cassiopeia A supernova remnant taken with the JWST. Bottom right: turbulent innterstellar gas around Cassiopeia A taken with Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer. Image Credit: Hirashima et al. 2026. SC2026.

To achieve this fine particle resolution, simulations need ever shorter time steps, and time steps are like simulation currency; the shorter they are, the more computing resources they demand. To supply the resources for that, the researchers harnessed the power of three exascale supercomputers together: Aurora, Frontier, and JUPITER. Each one ran the same software on different hardware: Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD graphic processing units (GPUs) and central processing units (CPUs).

But linking three supercomputers was only part of the solution.

"We overcame this problem by using an AI model to predict how gas around supernova explosions evolves," said Fujii. "This allowed us to carry out the simulation more efficiently and achieve a level of detail where individual stars can be represented."

By using this model, the larger simulation was able to skip over many small timesteps. It's called PHEASANT, and it was developed by postdoctoral researcher Keiya Hirashima from RIKEN. Supernovae are complex and require their own detailed simulations with very small timesteps. By plugging PHEASANT into the larger simulation, it relieved that simulation of a lot of work.

"With trillions of particles, we resolve individual stars and model their SN feedback self-consistently within a galactic-scale simulation," the authors write. "Such a simulation reveals how individual stars, such as the Sun, contribute to the overall structure of the MW through multiple physical processes."

This image from PHEASANT shows the Milky Way's disk. Galaxies are complex structures, with different types of structures at different scales. They have thin and thick disks, bulges, halos, spiral arms, star clusters, nebulae, and individual stars and gas clouds. In this work, the researchers divided the galaxy into smaller regions that could be processed by different parts of a supercomputer. Â©2026 PHEASANT/Hirashima/Fujii CC-BY-ND

âOne of my parts was to develop an AI model that predicts how the gas surrounding a supernova explosion changes over time. If we calculate this process directly, we need time steps of around 100 years,â said Hirashima. âMy model predicts gas distribution after 100,000 years. This means that, rather than having to calculate every small step, we can use a much longer time step for the entire galaxy simulation. Making this work efficiently on different supercomputers was a challenge because each system uses different AMD, Intel, or NVIDIA CPUs and GPUs. Achieving good performance across all three systems required some specific optimizations.â

These panels are snapshots from PHEASANT. The panel on the left shows the distribution and temperature of gas across a model galaxy. The panel on the right is a close-up view, where individual stars are visible as dots. Image Credit: Â©2026 PHEASANT/Hirashima/Fujii CC-BY-ND

We can't understand the Milky Way, or galaxies in general, without a detailed understanding of how its gas and stars behave. Stars are born, drift away from their clusters, and evolve. Depending on their masses, they can remain on the main sequence for trillions of years, leave the main sequence after a few billion years and then linger as white dwarf cinders, or exhaust their fuel rapidly and explode as supernovae.

Gas is also complex. It collects in clouds where stars form, can be funnelled into the galactic center and "recycled" by supermassive black holes, or blasted away by explosions. Stars and gas are linked, and there's an extraordinary amount of detail involved.

Supernovae are among the most complicated events. In some regions, the massive young stars that eventually explode as supernova are born in the same region. When they exhaust their fuel, they explode and carve massive bubbles in the interstellar medium. That can drive gas away to form more new stars elsewhere. They can even propel gas outside of the galaxy. It's all part of the life of the Milky Way, and simulations that struggle to recreate all of the detail in supernova explosions can lead astronomers astray.

This is LHA 120-N44 (N44) in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the ESO's Very Large Telescope. It features a massive bubble excavated in the interstellar medium by exploding young stars in its center. Some of the stars are still there, and they're still expanding the bubble with their powerful winds. Simulating all of the complexity involved is an enormous challenge. Image Credit: ESO/Manu Mejias

âSomething we want to understand is how events on the scale of individual stars connect to the larger structure of the Milky Way,â said Fujii. âWith this simulation, we can investigate how individual supernovae affect the number of stars that form, the size of these giant gas bubbles and the material that flows out of the galaxy. We can also study how groups of stars form and how they may eventually develop into star clusters.â

The PHEASANT AI surrogate model plays a critical role in this work, and that's part of a broader trend in science.

"The surrogate modeling approach can also be generalized beyond astrophysical problems to other research fields," the authors write.

"AI surrogate modeling accelerates simulations and bridges wider physical scales, opening new pathways in various real-world applications, including climate modeling, space forecasting, and low-temperature plasma," the authors conclude.

#6413. Hidden Viruses in the Human Gut Offer New Clues to a Disorder Affecting Millions

Many gut viruses were found at lower levels in people with irritable bowel syndrome, offering new clues to a poorly understood condition that affects roughly one in ten people.

Scientists have identified more than 116,000 groups of viruses living in the human gut, over 99% of which had no close match in the largest existing catalog of gut viruses. These largely unexplored microbes could offer new clues to how the digestive system functions and why it changes in people with conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

Research into the gut microbiome has traditionally focused on bacteria, leaving much less understood about bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria. Scientists from King’s College London, Helmholtz Munich, and the University of Nottingham are now filling that gap with two studies published on November 17, 2026, in Nature Communications and Gut.

Professor Ana Valdes and Dr. Afroditi Kouraki from the University of Nottingham said, “For a long time the viral part of the gut microbiome has been a kind of dark matter: we knew it was there but couldn’t see it. Advances in sequencing and computational methods mean we can now start to map it properly, and this study shows just how much has been hidden.”

For the Nature Communications study, researchers analyzed genetic material from stool samples collected from more than 1,000 participants in TwinsUK, the largest twin registry in the United Kingdom. Using data on gut bacteria, health measurements, and diet, they examined how populations of viruses and bacteria varied together. Certain viruses were consistently more abundant alongside particular bacteria, while others showed the opposite pattern.

Dr. Panayiotis Louca, a research associate at King’s College London who led the study, said, “Gut viruses are difficult to study, so most of what we found simply isn’t in existing catalogs. What stands out is how closely they track with gut bacteria and with the chemicals those bacteria produce. We can’t yet say whether the viruses are driving that, and testing it is our next step.”

Studying twins also allowed researchers to estimate how much genetics and the environment shape the gut’s viral community. Genetic factors accounted for an estimated 47% of the variation in overall viral diversity, although most individual viral populations appeared to be influenced primarily by environmental factors.

The researchers also discovered a small group of viruses carrying genes linked to harmful bacterial behavior. These viruses were more commonly found alongside bacteria that can sometimes cause infections and less commonly alongside bacteria that break down dietary fiber.

Such relationships could be relevant to IBS, a condition that affects around 10% of the population and can significantly disrupt daily life. Its underlying causes remain poorly understood.

In the second study, published in Gut, researchers used TwinsUK data to identify 50 viral groups associated with IBS, most of which were less abundant in people with the condition. Relationships between bacteria and viruses also differed, with many viruses infecting bacteria previously linked to IBS. This suggests that the condition may involve changes across the wider microbial community rather than in bacteria alone.

Senior author Dr. Cristina Menni, who leads the metabolomics research group at the Department of Twin Research, Ageing and Genomic Epidemiology at King’s College London, said, “Our research highlights that to fully understand the gut microbiome and its links to health and disease, we need to look beyond bacteria and consider the viruses that live alongside them. We reveal a fascinating and largely unexplored dimension of the gut microbiome—discovering that viruses are not only closely associated with bacterial communities, but also with the metabolites that connect the microbiome to our health. This opens exciting new avenues for understanding how the gut ecosystem works.”

Future research will examine whether gut viruses actively influence bacterial metabolism and how these interactions change in health and disease. Understanding these relationships could eventually help researchers develop better biological markers and treatments for IBS, as well as more personalized approaches to gut health.

Dr. Louca added: “The study is observational, so it cannot show that the viruses cause these effects, but it provides greater understanding of a largely unexplored area of the human gut. It would also be beneficial to replicate the study on a more diverse cohort, as participants were mostly older women of European ancestry.”

“Population-level characterization of the human gut phageome and its association with microbial metabolites” by Panayiotis Louca, Mohammadali Khan Mirzaei, Afroditi Kouraki, Erfan Khamespanah, Yu Lin, Xue Peng, Robert Pope, Alessia Visconti, Francesco Asnicar, Daniel Kirk, Ricardo Costeira, Nicola Segata, Mario Falchi, Jordana T. Bell, Tim D. Spector, Lindsey A. Edwards, Li Deng, Ana M. Valdes and Cristina Menni, 17 November 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79230-0

“Large-scale shotgun metagenomic analysis of gut bacteria–phage interactions in IBS” by Daniel Kirk, Erfan Khamespanah, Panayiotis Louca, Alessia Visconti, Robert Pope, Francesco Asnicar, Sarah E Berry, Jonathan Wolf, Nicola Segata, Tim D Spector, Mario Falchi, Frances M K Williams, Mohammadali Khan Mirzaei, Li Deng and Cristina Menni, 16 November 2026, Gut. DOI: 10.1136/gutjnl-2026-338807

This research was funded by the Chronic Disease Research Foundation (CDRF) and in part by the Wellcome and Medical Research Council (MRC).

#6412. Slingshot Earth: NASA's Europa Clipper Will Gain Speed and Tests Its Instruments During Its Earth Flyby

NASA's Europa Clipper will soon bid farewell to Earth. On December 3rd, it will conduct its propellant-saving gravity assist maneuver and head for Jupiter. These types of maneuvers are a common part of missions beyond Mars.

Gravity maneuvers can be used to either accelerate or decelerate spacecraft, depending on their desired trajectories. When a mission requires acceleration to the outer Solar System, a spacecraft passes behind a planet's orbital path, and the planet's gravity pulls on it and accelerates it relative to the Sun. The maneuver also changes its trajectory. These maneuvers are the norm for missions beyond Mars.

The relative velocity is illustrative and does not represent Europa Clipper's velocity. Credit: Made with AI.

âWeâre coming down into the gravity well of Earth, following its curve, and shooting out again,â said Robert Pappalardo, Europa Clipperâs project scientist at NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory. âThe spacecraft is able to get pulled by the gravity of the planet and continue on its way â now with a slightly changed trajectory and moving faster than it was before.â

When a mission needs to decelerate into the inner Solar System, the spacecraft passes in front of a planet's orbital path, and the planet's gravity decelerates it relative to the Sun. Bepi-Colombo, for example, relied on multiple gravity-braking maneuvers to slow down enough to orbit Mercury. The Europa Clipper performed one of these earlier in its mission, to set it up for the gravity-assist with Earth.

The relative velocity is illustrative and does not represent Europa Clipper's velocity. Credit: Made with AI.

The Europa Clipper is NASA's largest deep space mission, and this Earth flyby is critical to accelerating it toward Jupiter. So was its gravity braking maneuver at Mars in March, 2025, which slowed it down so it could perform this upcoming flyby of Earth.

The Clipper's closest approach to Earth will be within 3,140 to 3,450 kilometers on December 3rd, above West Africa, at at 3:14 p.m. EST. In Africa and southern Europe, it should be visible in backyard telescopes.

Even though about half of the Clipper's launch mass is propellant, it needs these flybys to complete its mission. The flybys get it to Jupiter, and the spacecraft is conserving its propellant for orbital insertion at Jupiter, the single largest burn of its mission. Jupiter's gravity well is powerful, and even with all of this propellant to place it in orbit, the Clipper will still perform a gravity breaking maneuver at Ganymede hours before insertion to save a little more propellant. It will enter its Jupiter orbit in April 2030.

The flyby of Earth serves another purpose, too: instrument calibration. All 11 of the Europa Clipper's science instruments will be active during the flyby. The mission has nine science teams organized around the 11 instruments, and each team will take the relevant data and compare it to known data about Earth. That will let them calibrate their instruments to a very fine degree.

âWeâre practicing the intricacies of the operation, but weâre also practicing how to work together to produce the best science,â said JPLâs Erin Leonard, Europa Clipper project staff scientist. âThe things we practice now will set us up for success at Europa.â

Since Earth's magnetosphere is so well-understood, this is an especially important opportunity for Clipper to calibrate one of its most important instruments, the Europa Clipper Magnetometer. The central goal of Clipper's mission is to determine if Europa truly does have an ocean under its icy shell, and the magnetometer will be able to do that after multiple flybys. It can also determine the ocean's depth, and even its salinity. It can also help measure the thickness of the icy shell.

This illustration shows what Europa's ocean could be like. Scientist know it has an icy shell, and they know it has a rock core and mantle. There are enticing hints that it has a subsurface ocean, but they aren't sure. Europa will find out. Image Credit: NASA/(Europa Lander Study 2016 Report)

Europa sits inside Jupiter's vast and powerful magnetic field which varies and oscillates as Jupiter revolves and Europa orbits. If Europa has a salty ocean, that will generate a separate magnetic field, because a salty ocean is conductive. The strength and orientation of these fields are always changing. There's also a large body of magnetospheric plasma that co-rotates with Jupiter at its magnetic equator, and its effects need to be accounted for, too. It's like a big, multi-faceted puzzle of magnetic fields that the Clipper's magnetometer is built to solve.

âThe magnetometer measures variations in the magnetic field as weâre orbiting Jupiter, but we need to pin these observations to something we know to understand the actual value that itâs measuring,â Pappalardo said. âThe flyby will enable us to calibrate the instrument absolutely, using its observations at Earth to refine other calibrations done before launch and in flight.â

Measuring Europa's magnetic field is also complicated because the Europa Clipper has its own unavoidable magnetic field. The spacecraft has more than 300 separate magnetic sources that its magnetometer must account for. Those range from magnets used in valves in its propellant system, to electrical current loops from its solar arrays. The magnetometer is mounted on a boom, called the Magboom, as far away from most of these sources as it can get, but it still needs to take them into consideration.

The Europa Clipper's magnetometer isn't its only important instrument. They're all important, or they wouldn't have survived the mission's rigorous design process. They'll all be active during the spacecraft's upcoming Earth flyby.

The E-THEMIS (Europa Clipper Thermal Emission Imaging System) instrument will scan Earth every eight hours as the spacecraft approaches. Its purpose is to find hotspots on Europa's surface where water from its subsurface ocean may be closest to the surface, or even escaped above the ice. Then other remote-sensing instruments will follow up those observations. The MISE (Mapping Imaging Spectrometer for Europa) can examine that water and map its composition.

The Europa-UVS (Europa-Ultraviolet Spectrograph) will also scan Earth during the flyby. It's job is to to study Europa's surface and its atmosphere. It will compare its Earth observations to similar observations from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbit (LRO). When the Clipper is measuring Earth, the LRO will point at Earth and do the same with one of its instruments. Then the mission team can use both results to calibrate their instrument.

âItâs super-exciting when we actually do get to collect data thatâs really meaningful to the instruments, and get to share it with other people,â Leonard said. âThis is Earth, and everyone understands what that data means. Imagine what itâs going to be able to show you about Europa.â

The Europa Clipper is scheduled for a four-year mission at Jupiter. If there's no mission extension, then it will likely be crashed into Jupiter, Ganymede, or Callisto. NASA doesn't want to risk it crashing into Europa because of potential contamination. In 2022, Pappalardo suggested crashing it into Ganymede, because the ESA's Juice mission, which is also on its way to Jupiter, can observe that crash and use it to learn more about that moon's surface chemistry.

After this upcoming Earth flyby, the Europa Clipper will begin a long cruise phase. Not much happens during these cruise phases, which is good because it means nothing's gone wrong. Barring any significant problems, we may not hear much from the Europa Clipper until it reaches Jupiter in 2030.

Some time after that, we may finally get an answer to a long-burning question: Does Europa have a subsurface ocean with the right environment for life?

A new positioning technology could make autonomous vehicles and robotaxis more reliable at recharging themselves.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers in Japan have developed a new technology that could enable electric vehicles (EVs) to charge "simply by parking".

Wireless charging is still relatively nascent in the EV market, but scientists hope that integrating more wireless charging devices into roads and parking spaces will move the EV industry away from bulky plug-in infrastructure. It uses the same wireless power transfer technology found in modern smartphones and consumer electronics: a transmitter coil inside in a ground pad generates an oscillating magnetic field, which induces an electric current in a receiver coil underneath the vehicle. This current recharges the EV's battery cells.

However, small misalignments between the two coils can affect how quickly and efficiently the battery recharges. This new system uses short-range radio signals to determine the position of the vehicle's magnetic charging coil relative to the charging device in the ground, including its distance and angle. This helps the EV and its driver get into the optimal position for efficient charging.

The technology could be particularly useful for driverless "robotaxis" and other autonomous vehicles that need to be able to recharge quickly and efficiently without human assistance, the researchers said. They detailed their findings in a study published Aug. 26 in the IEEE Open Journal of Vehicular Technology.

"We hope this research will lead to a future where EVs charge simply by parking, much like smartphones placed on wireless chargers," Ryotaro Hada, first author of the study and a master's student at the University of Osaka's Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, said in a statement.

Existing methods for aligning an EV's charging coil with a wireless charging pad use magnetic sensors or cameras. Magnetic systems work best when the coil is close to the pad, while cameras can struggle in rain, poor lighting or when dirt obscures the pad, the researchers explained.

This new system uses four ultra-wideband radio devices mounted around the vehicle's charging coil to communicate with four antennas around the charging pad.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By measuring how long radio waves take to travel between the ultra-wideband devices and the antennas, as well as detecting tiny differences in how the signals arrive at each of the vehicle's sensors, the system can pinpoint the position and angle of the EV's charging coil relative to the ground pad.

The same technology is used in some digital car keys. They use short radio pulses to detect when the driver is close by, allowing the driver to unlock their vehicle without requiring a physical key.

In laboratory experiments using a scaled-down vehicle model, the system worked out where the vehicle's charging coil was to within 0.09 inches (2.32 millimeters) of its actual position and which direction it was facing to within 0.25 degrees. Correcting for distortions in the radio signals reduced the positioning error by around fivefold, the team said.

The researchers noted that the system still needs to be tested outdoors, on full-size EVs and under real charging conditions.

#6409. Astronomers Discover a Hidden Binary in a Star System Used to Calibrate the JWST

When observatories like the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) conduct observation campaigns, they often start by observing star fields to calibrate their instruments. These stars must have precisely characterized spectra so that their radiant energy (or fluxes) can be measured accurately. However, some stars that appear as single objects have a binary companion that has not been resolved, altering their predicted stellar flux. In fact, a star that is used for JWST calibration (HD 158485), which was thought to be an A-type star, has been identified as a binary system.

The discovery was made by a team from the Xinjiang Astronomical Observatory of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), who found the binary while reviewing long-term observations from NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). Their study, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, provides the first orbital solution and dynamical mass ratio for the system. HD 158485 is an example of a pulsating, variable, or Delta (Î´) Scuti star, which experiences brightness changes at a regular frequency (typically every 18 minutes to 8 hours)

From the TESS data, the team noticed that HD 158485 was pulsing in six distinct rhythms, otherwise known as Î´ Scuti pulsation modes. They further noticed that these pulses fell into two groups with opposing light-travel-time variations, meaning that the light from these pulses reached Earth at different times. This could only be explained by the presence of a binary companion. The team used the variation between the two signals to trace the star's orbital motion with HD 158485, which showed that they orbit each other every 382.8 days.

Pulsation timing results for HD 158485. The two groups of pulsation modes show opposite time delays, revealing the orbital motion of both stars. Credit: Chenglong, LV et al. (2026).

The data also allowed them to constrain the orbital parameters and the star's mass. According to their calculations, the companion has an eccentricity of 0.242, indicating a moderately elongated, closed elliptical orbit, and is about 80% as massive as its primary - making it a likely F-type (yellow-white) main-sequence star. Their findings are independently confirmed by an orbital model built from earlier TESS data, which accurately predicted the timing variations that were detected by a separate observation campaign.

The team further compared a two-star atmosphere model with a conventional single-star model using the system's mass ratio, which showed a flux difference of about 1.6% between one and five micrometers (Î¼m), and 2.5% between five and 28 Î¼m. These findings could have significant implications where JWST calibration is concerned. While they do not represent a measured error, they do show how mistaking a binary system for a single star can shift predicted fluxes, thus throwing off readings.

In essence, the team's results show that stellar pulsations can reveal binaries that conventional observations leave unresolved. It also underscores the need to account for hidden stellar companions when evaluating calibration standards for our instruments.

Further Reading: Chinese Academy of Sciences

#6408. Semiconductor Breakthrough Cracks a Longstanding Solar Energy Problem

An unusual material could help us make better use of the sun’s energy, offering new possibilities for more efficient solar power and fuel production.

Generating more electricity from sunlight does not necessarily mean installing more solar panels. Finding ways to extract more energy from the light that already reaches them could make solar power a more practical source of electricity. Part of the challenge lies in what happens inside a solar cell in the moments after it absorbs sunlight.

Solar cells contain materials called semiconductors, which use the energy from sunlight to free negatively charged electrons, leaving behind positively charged gaps known as holes. Both charges must be collected to generate electricity. If an electron and a hole meet and cancel each other out, a process known as recombination, the energy they carry is lost. Unfortunately, materials that are particularly good at absorbing sunlight also tend to lose these charges more quickly.

A study led by the University of Oxford has identified a promising exception in a semiconductor called bismuth sulfide. Published October 28, 2026, in Nature, the research examined how the material’s unusual electronic structure could help overcome this longstanding limitation in solar energy technology.

To investigate how long electrical charges survive in bismuth sulfide, the researchers exposed thin films of the material to extremely short laser pulses. They then tracked how quickly the charges disappeared using a technique called ultrafast terahertz spectroscopy, conducting measurements at temperatures ranging from room temperature to just above absolute zero.

“One of the longstanding challenges in developing efficient solar-energy materials is that the properties which make a semiconductor very good at absorbing sunlight also tend to make the resulting electrical charges disappear quickly,” said corresponding author Professor Laura Herz (Department of Physics, University of Oxford). “Our work shows that this trade-off is not inevitable. By uncovering how an unusual electronic structure can combine strong light absorption with much slower recombination, we have identified a new principle for designing semiconductors that could help us harvest solar energy more efficiently.”

Electronic structure calculations by Professor Marina Filip’s group in Oxford’s Department of Physics helped explain why bismuth sulfide behaves differently. The material has two closely spaced routes through which electrons can move between energy levels. One allows the material to absorb light strongly, while the other sits at a slightly lower energy and allows charges to disappear much more slowly. Because the two are so close together, charges spend much of their time in the lower-energy states, which effectively serve as a temporary storage reservoir.

Cooling the material provided further evidence for this explanation. In most semiconductors, electrical charges disappear faster as temperatures drop. In bismuth sulfide, more charges settled into the reservoir as the material cooled, allowing them to survive longer. The results matched the team’s model of what physicists call a pseudo-direct semiconductor.

Even at room temperature, the researchers estimate that this arrangement reduces the rate of charge loss by about 75% compared with conventional semiconductors that absorb light equally well.

Giving electrical charges more time to be collected could improve the efficiency of solar panels without compromising their ability to capture sunlight. The benefits could also extend beyond electricity generation. Longer-lived charges could provide more time for the chemical reactions needed to produce fuels using sunlight.

“What makes this discovery particularly exciting is that we are not simply improving an existing semiconductor property but identifying a different way in which semiconductors can behave,” said Professor Herz. “Understanding this mechanism gives us a roadmap for discovering and potentially engineering other materials with similarly advantageous properties.”

The team’s calculations suggest that researchers could search existing materials databases for semiconductors with similar properties or engineer new ones. However, the study demonstrates the underlying physical mechanism rather than the performance of a finished solar cell. Further research will be needed to determine how these properties can be put to use in solar energy technologies.

Reference: “Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor” by Marcello Righetto, Debalina Banerjee, Zhenglin Jia, Joshua R. S. Lilly, Vincent J. -Y. Lim, Snigdha Lal, Siyu Yan, Jae Eun Lee, Jay B. Patel, Michael B. Johnston, Qianqian Lin, Marina R. Filip and Laura M. Herz, 28 October 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11223-x

#6407. Physicists Discover a Strange New Form of Magnetism in a Simple Metal

Electronics can use more than electrical charge, and evidence of unusual magnetism in europium silicide could help researchers explore how to put electron spin to work.

At very low temperatures, a simple metal made from europium and silicon develops a spiral pattern of magnetism that leaves it with no overall magnetization. Its electrons nevertheless appear to favor opposite spin orientations when they travel in opposite directions, an unusual relationship that could offer researchers new ways to explore and control electronic behavior.

An international team has found compelling evidence for this state, called p-wave magnetism, in europium silicide, or EuSi. The findings, published in Nature, provide an experimental foothold in a field where suitable materials have been difficult to find.

Spin is a quantum property that gives electrons a magnetic character, somewhat like tiny compass needles. In a conventional ferromagnet, spins tend to align in the same direction, producing net magnetization. In EuSi, between approximately 33 and 62 kelvin, or about −400 to −348 °F, the magnetic moments of europium atoms instead form an ordered spiral. The individual moments are substantial, but their contributions cancel overall.

The predicted relationship between opposite directions of electron motion and opposite spin polarizations is known as an odd-parity spin texture. Finding a material in which researchers can investigate it has been challenging. Previous candidates include electrical insulators and metals that develop magnetic order only at very low temperatures or have additional symmetry complications. EuSi combines a fixed chemical composition with a spiral magnetic phase that has the required symmetry, and researchers can grow high-quality single crystals for experiments.

Dr. Erjian Cheng grew those crystals approximately three years ago at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Physics of Solids (MPI CPfS) in Dresden. Initial photoemission experiments, which use light to eject electrons and examine their properties, showed that magnetism had an unusually large influence on EuSi’s electronic band structure, the pattern of energies electrons can occupy inside the material. That raised the possibility that its magnetic order might link spin to the direction of electron motion.

The investigation brought together 38 researchers from 19 institutions, including ShanghaiTech University, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, the Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

Combining theoretical calculations with several experimental techniques, the researchers examined both the atomic magnetic arrangement and its effects on electrons. Neutron diffraction revealed the spiral of europium magnetic moments and confirmed that its symmetry met the conditions for p-wave magnetism. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, which maps electron energies and momenta, showed that magnetism substantially reshaped the electronic structure, producing energy separations exceeding 100 millielectronvolts.

Measurements that also resolved electron spin supplied a more specific test. The spin polarization changed sign across successive magnetic Brillouin zones, repeating regions in a map of electron momentum defined by the magnetic order. It also weakened sharply near regions where the predicted p-wave spin texture should vanish. Together, these observations provided spectroscopic evidence consistent with the theoretical state.

“When we first measured the electronic structure of EuSi, we were surprised by the exceptionally large effect of magnetism on the electrons,” explains Cheng. “That observation led us to investigate whether this simple compound could host a much more unusual magnetic state. The combination of crystal growth, neutron scattering and spin-resolved spectroscopy now provides compelling evidence for p-wave magnetism.”

The proposed spin pattern arises predominantly from magnetic exchange interactions, which influence how spins arrange themselves, and from the symmetry of the magnetic spiral. That distinguishes it from familiar spin-splitting effects driven mainly by spin-orbit coupling, an interaction between an electron’s spin and its motion.

The spiral also introduces handedness, or chirality. EuSi’s underlying crystal structure is centrosymmetric, meaning that it looks the same when inverted through its center. Its magnetic spiral, however, can twist in either of two opposite senses. Using magnetic force microscopy and spatially resolved photoemission spectroscopy, the researchers identified magnetic domains approximately ten micrometers across.

When examined with circularly polarized light, domains with opposite magnetic handedness showed distinct electronic responses. The results demonstrated that the spiral’s handedness is coupled to the electronic structure, connecting the organization of the atomic magnetic moments with the behavior of the electrons.

“What makes EuSi particularly exciting is that an unconventional electronic spin structure emerges from the magnetic order of a chemically simple metal,” says Prof. Claudia Felser, Director at MPI CPfS. “This demonstrates how the discovery of new materials can reveal entirely new electronic phenomena. EuSi now gives us an experimental platform to investigate how magnetic symmetry and chirality can be used to control electronic properties, with potential implications for future spintronics and unconventional superconductivity.”

Spintronics uses electron spin as well as electrical charge in electronic devices. The findings could inform that field, along with research on topological quantum materials and unconventional superconductivity. They also illustrate how a solid’s properties depend on its magnetic order and electronic quantum states, alongside its chemical composition and crystal structure.

Reference: “Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi” by Erjian Cheng, Yixing Yang, Yifan Gao, Jan Priessnitz, Yiqing Hao, Jieyi Liu, Rui Lou, Alexander Fedorov, Mengyu Yao, Yuri Prots, Houke Chen, Ralf Koban, Xuemin Shi, Ying-Ting Chan, Ulrich Burkhardt, Berit H. Goodge, Walter Schnelle, Vicky Hasse, Jaafar Ansari, Zhuocheng Lu, Peter Bencok, Gerrit van der Laan, Makoto Hashimoto, Donghui Lu, Jacek Osiecki, Zhanfeng Liu, Shengtao Cui, Jaime Sánchez-Barriga, Oliver Rader, Yulin Chen, Hua Wang, Jiadong Zang, Leila Noohinejad, Weida Wu, Libor Šmejkal, Junwei Liu, Zhongkai Liu and Claudia Felser, 18 November 2026, Nature. By inserting human genes into lab mice, scientists were able to study the underlying mechanics of a disease that's been notoriously difficult to research.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have unraveled the workings of a rare disease by putting a large chunk of human DNA into a lab mouse.

The incurable disorder, called X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP), mostly affects men of Filipino descent and leads to early death. The new mouse studies revealed previously unknown aspects of the disease's biology that could point to new avenues for treatment.

The condition has long been thought of as a disease of neurons, as it triggers neuron death in a part of the brain that's key to controlling movement. But the new findings highlight an unsung role of neurons' support cells, called glial cells.

"This had never been described in this disease before," study co-author Shane Liddelow, an associate professor in the Institute for Translational Neuroscience at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, said of the new findings. "It really sort of upended this idea of the disease" as primarily affecting neurons.

The two studies, published Thursday (Nov. 19) in the journal Cell, not only shed new light on this rare disease but also showcase a powerful technique for mimicking human conditions in laboratory animals. Known as "SwAP-In," it enables researchers to rewrite large portions of an organism's genetic code by inserting big chunks of synthetic DNA. In this case, the approach was used to insert a human gene into lab mice.

"It is kind of a generic method that can be used to make extensively humanized mice," said study co-author Jef Boeke, director of the Institute for Systems Genetics at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a lead developer of the SwAP-In technique.

Liddelow anticipates that this new method for humanizing mice, or tweaking their biology to more closely match that of humans, will prove useful for studying a wide range of diseases, from common conditions like Alzheimer's to "orphan" diseases like XDP, which are rare, underresearched and lacking effective treatments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

XDP is a neurodegenerative condition that particularly impacts the striatum, part of the brain that's crucial for movement. The disease causes symptoms such as slowed movements, tremors, muscle stiffness and involuntary muscle contractions.

On average, symptoms emerge around age 39 and patients live for 13 to 16 years after their symptoms appear. In late stages of the disease, problems with breathing and swallowing can lead to deadly complications such as malnutrition, aspiration pneumonia and respiratory failure. Historically, XDP has also carried a lot of social stigma, which has contributed to high rates of depression and suicide among those with the condition.

"Patients get sort of shunned and hidden away," Liddelow said. That, among other factors, made XDP difficult to study.

XDP shows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern (depicted above).

Although XDP isn't fully understood, its underlying genetic cause is known. It stems from a mutation in TAF1, a gene on the X chromosome that helps translate DNA sequences into new proteins. Because males carry only one X chromosome — and thus have no backup copy of the gene — the condition affects far more males than females.

The mutation first appeared in a person on Panay, an island in the Philippines. Due to a phenomenon called the "founder effect," it has risen in prevalence among people of Filipino ancestry but is not seen in other demographics, Boeke explained. Studies suggest there are about 5.7 cases per 100,000 people in the Philippines.

XDP's rarity and associated stigma have made the condition difficult to study, but there's another layer of complexity: The mutation in TAF1 was originally caused by a "jumping gene" ‪—‬ a bit of DNA that changed its position within the genome. In this instance, the DNA happened to jump into the middle of TAF1 and disrupted its function, Boeke said.

But the jumping gene in question is found only in primates. Ideally, if you wanted to study the disease in lab mice, you'd have to insert that jumping gene into their DNA — and that's exactly what the researchers did in the first of their two new studies.

Using SwAP-In, the team inserted 78,000 "letters" of human DNA code into mouse embryonic stem cells. This code included part of the human version of the TAF1 gene and the relevant jumping gene that causes XDP. In both lab dishes and living mice, this gene insertion triggered the telltale signs of XDP: low levels of the TAF1 protein, cell death and holes in the brain, especially in the striatum.

One big difference between mice and humans is that the mouse version of XDP progresses very quickly, with symptoms appearing in just 1.5 months, whereas the human disease takes years to show up. That may be because human bodies have safeguards to help offset the jumping gene's effects — at least for a while — while mice lack this safety net, the study authors theorized.

That difference in disease progression is actually a "huge advantage" for researchers, Boeke noted. "Because it's so sped up, it's possible to do experiments on therapeutics," he said. For instance, if an experimental drug is successfully fighting the disease, that should be obvious in the mice, whose condition would otherwise progress very quickly.

I think that is, one, interesting from a biological standpoint, but two, profoundly important for how you might develop therapies to help these patients.

In the second of the team's new studies, they took a closer look at the new mice with XDP, to see how the disorder affected their brain cells. Through a battery of tests, they realized that glial cells known as oligodendrocytes showed dramatic changes in both their overall numbers and their gene activity.

These cells would normally make a fatty insulating material called myelin, which wraps around the outgoing wires of neurons to help them send signals. To see how the cells were faring in the XDP mice, study co-author Priya Prakash, a postdoctoral scholar in Liddelow's lab, used a blue stain to label the cells within the mouse brain tissue.

"Where you would normally see this beautiful blue brain, full of lipid, full of myelin, you essentially see a white brain, with none of this lipid there," Liddelow said. This was especially apparent in the striatum and the prefrontal cortex.

Further experiments revealed that the mutation was preventing oligodendrocytes from fully maturing, and that reduced the amount of myelin made in these parts of the brain. They backed up these findings in brains of people with XDP that had been donated after death.

The researchers think this extensive loss of insulation may leave neurons vulnerable to dying early, Liddelow said. In short, "this is a neurodegenerative disease that may not first be manifesting in neurons themselves," he emphasized. "I think that is, one, interesting from a biological standpoint, but two, profoundly important for how you might develop therapies to help these patients."

Together, the studies raise several ideas for treating XDP. One treatment could involve cranking up the activity of the TAF1 gene to boost the levels of its related protein. This idea showed promise in experiments with mouse cells in the team's first paper. The second paper points to oligodendrocytes as potential targets for future therapies, and myelin loss as a potential early sign of the disease that might be useful for diagnosis.

There's still much more to learn about the biology of XDP and what types of treatments might reverse the drivers of the disease, Liddelow and Boeke emphasized. But now, other scientists have access to a brand-new mouse model that can help them solve the disease's remaining mysteries.

#6405. Donkeys help families survive droughts, but governments often overlook them

Donkeys help East African families survive severe droughts, yet governments and aid organizations often overlook their essential needs.

Families in East Africa depend on donkeys for many everyday tasks. The animals carry water, feed for livestock, and household belongings. They have also been part of local culture for generations.

In a drought their job gets even more important. Once the water close to home has dried up, donkeys trek long distances to bring it back.

Yet when drought relief arrives, donkeys are rarely part of it. Aid has tended to go to the food-producing animals, and donkey-owning households end up worse off for it.

A team from the University of Portsmouth, Maasai Mara University and Haramaya University looked at how far that neglect goes.

They went through 77 documents and talked with 41 people on the ground. Donkeys, it turned out, are mostly missing, from the policies right down to the vet schools.

From 2020 to 2023 East Africa was hit by drought. Crops failed widely and some places lost up to 70% of livestock.

Around 26 million people were threatened with food shortages, and conflict over the dwindling resources went up.

Many of the worst affected families are pastoralists, meaning their living depends on herds that often move with them.

Donkeys have been part of that life since they were domesticated in Africa thousands of years ago.

When nearby sources dry up, the water a donkey brings back keeps people, crops and herds going. Donkeys also get people to health facilities, aid distribution centers and markets.

Kenya and Ethiopia both rely heavily on them. Ethiopia has about 10.8 million donkeys, and Kenya around 1.2 million.

Professor Leanne Proops works on animal behavior and welfare at the University of Portsmouth and supervised the project.

“Working donkeys are a lifeline for many communities during drought, helping people access water, transport essential supplies and sustain their livelihoods,” said Proops.

“Yet their contribution is largely overlooked in the policies and support systems designed to help communities cope with these crises.”

Of the 77 documents, 51 were Kenyan and 26 Ethiopian, issued anywhere from 1964 up to 2025.

Animal health, agriculture, climate change, disaster risk and water were the areas covered. Equids, that is donkeys, horses and mules, came up in just 17.

Quite often the donkey got one mention in a species list and was absent from the rest of the policy.

“Livestock” was a word used a lot, but most documents never said what species it took in. In reality it meant cattle, sheep and goats.

Donkeys, on the occasions they did appear, sat outside conventional livestock under labels such as “working animals” or “emerging livestock.”

Not one of the documents made a link between donkeys and drought, even though camels were mentioned in that role.

On welfare the picture is not much better. Kenya’s Animal Welfare and Protection Bill has been in deliberation since 2019 without being enacted.

Up until 2025, Ethiopia’s criminal code only made cruelty an offense when it happened where the public could see.

A 2025 proclamation now prohibits overloading or overworking any working animal, though no penalties are set out in that part.

References to animals in the policies were heavily based on use, with meat, milk, hides and exports driving them. Kenya’s 2024 Livestock Bill does define donkeys as draught animals but welfare hardly features.

The interviews pointed the same way. If a drought is forecast, preparedness plans kick in with worming and vaccination for the other livestock.

“The donkeys were generally left out. Nobody was thinking about them,” one participant in Kenya told the researchers.

Later on, supplementary feed rations get handed out in both countries and again the donkeys are not counted.

A participant in Ethiopia said that when fodder runs short, “the priority is not for donkeys, not for mules, just for animals with salvage value.”

In the only program one Kenyan participant had worked on with donkeys included, they got rabies vaccination and no food. The rest of the animals were counted for supplementary feeding.

Participants also noted that droughts are far more frequent than before. Money often comes towards the end, when much has died.

Pastoralists summed this up in their own words: “money comes with the vultures.”

Dr. Emily Haddy, lead author of the paper, did the work at Portsmouth and is now at the University of Nottingham.

“Recognising donkeys in livestock and disaster planning is not just an animal welfare issue,” said Haddy.

“By including working donkeys in drought preparedness and emergency responses, governments and aid organisations can help protect animal welfare and strengthen community resilience.”

The veterinarians taking part spoke of getting little or no training on donkeys. One participant in Kenya said they try to extrapolate from horses, which does not always hold.

“We try to extrapolate what we know from the horse to the donkey, which is not always true,” the participant said.

Vets specializing in donkeys are few and tend to be in urban areas such as Nairobi. Pastoralist communities therefore often have no access, and lose animals that could have been treated.

Medications suitable for donkeys are also in short supply, particularly anesthesia and pain relief.

“I don’t even think there is any company in Kenya which makes feeds for donkeys,” another participant said.

It should be noted the vets interviewed were older graduates. Donkey medicine in the Kenyan vet curriculum has recently improved, though its effect on the ground may take time.

According to participants, the priority for government is animals bringing in foreign currency directly, through sale of meat and hides.

The services of a donkey are largely invisible. That makes them hard to quantify and keeps them out of national economic reports.

One participant described a child-focused relief scheme for milk. Donkeys play a vital role in that milk chain, but they were not taken into account.

“They see the human being first, and they see the cattle, the producer of the milk, and the consumer of the milk, the in-between connection they don’t see,” the participant said.

Donkey deaths are also not systematically recorded, so they usually do not appear when authorities list the animals that died.

International guidelines do mention working equids. The Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards, aimed at livestock projects in humanitarian crises, include them as pack animals.

The World Organisation for Animal Health gives advice on managing equids during feed shortage too. These were poorly reflected in the national documents.

Professor Tesfaheywet Zeryehun of Haramaya University put the two kinds of welfare side by side.

“Our findings reinforce the fact that donkey welfare cannot be separated from human wellbeing,” said Zeryehun.

“In drought-prone communities, protecting working donkeys is equally about protecting the livelihoods, resilience and dignity of the families who depend on them.”

“Their contribution must therefore be recognized in policies and emergency preparedness programs.”

Documents had to be online and in English to be included. That likely cut the Ethiopian count, as many are in Amharic.

Only one pastoralist representative from Ethiopia was interviewed, so those views are probably underrepresented. Fewer than 15% of participants were women.

People were found by snowballing through the authors’ own contacts, and that could bring some selection bias with it.

What’s missing above all is hard evidence on how much donkeys are worth economically. Several interviewees felt numbers on that are what would capture the minds of policy makers.

The authors recommend that equids be explicitly included in livestock definitions. Doing that would make donkeys eligible for the feed and veterinary support that other livestock can get.

They also suggest fodder reserves kept for donkeys, donkey modules in vet training and welfare laws that are actually enforced.

The impact of severe drought on donkey health is named as a research priority.

Dr. David Obiero of Maasai Mara University said the gaps reach beyond policy itself.

“The lack of recognition of working donkeys extends beyond policy into veterinary training, access to healthcare and vaccination programmes,” said Obiero.

“These animals are vital to community livelihoods, yet the systems designed to support livestock often overlook them. Addressing these gaps is essential to supporting pastoralist communities during time of drought and beyond.”

With recurrent droughts expected to intensify, the animal fetching the water is still largely outside the plans to help.

The full study was published in the Journal of Rural Studies.

#6404. Mathematicians Find a Brilliant Shortcut to a 174-Year-Old Math Puzzle

A faster way to color maps using only four colors has revealed hidden mathematical patterns that could help solve puzzles involving far more complex shapes.

In 1852, English mathematician Francis Guthrie noticed something curious while drawing a map of England’s counties. He needed only four colors to ensure that no two neighboring counties shared the same color. Could the same be true of every flat map, regardless of how complicated its borders were?

What seemed like a simple observation became one of the most famous problems in mathematics. It took 124 years to prove Guthrie right and another half century to discover the most efficient way to assign those four colors. In solving the latter problem, an international team of mathematicians has uncovered something previously unknown about the mathematical structures underlying maps.

The history of the Four Color Problem is filled with frustrated attempts. A proof presented in 1879 stood for 11 years before an error was discovered. When mathematicians finally succeeded in 1976, their proof was controversial because it relied heavily on computer calculations that were difficult for others to verify. A more accessible proof followed in 1997, although finding a suitable coloring for large maps remained computationally demanding.

“The previous proofs showed that it is always possible to color a map using four colors. But they are not very good at actually finding the colors for each individual region on a map. The new algorithm is efficient and provides a much faster way of coloring,” says Professor Mikkel Thorup from the Department of Computer Science at the University of Copenhagen.

The achievement marks the first major breakthrough on the problem in nearly 30 years. The first part of the research paper was presented at FOCS’26, one of the world’s leading conferences in theoretical computer science, where it received the Best Paper Award.

Mathematicians can represent a flat map using what is known as a planar graph. Imagine replacing each country or county with a dot and drawing lines between those that share a border. The challenge then becomes assigning colors to the dots so that no two connected dots have the same color.

Within these graphs are small arrangements called reducible configurations, which allow mathematicians to simplify the coloring problem. The researchers discovered that graphs contain far more of these useful arrangements than anyone previously realized.

“Think of reducible configurations as handles you can grab hold on to start four coloring. We show that graphs do not contain just one handle, but an astonishing number of them. Nobody knew that before,” says Professor and co-author Carsten Thomassen from DTU.

Where earlier methods could often identify only one suitable starting point, the researchers can now work from many different parts of a graph. The advantage becomes particularly pronounced as maps grow larger.

“We have gone from what mathematicians call quadratic time to linear time. This means that if a map contains ten times as many regions, the computation only becomes about ten times slower. With the previous algorithm, it would have become about 100 times slower,” explains Carsten Thomassen.

Finding this solution occupied Thorup and his colleagues, including Thomassen, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, and Bojan Mohar, for around a decade. Thorup has a name for the peculiar fascination that has kept mathematicians returning to the problem for 174 years: “the four-color disease.”

“The disease is believing that there must be a simple proof for such a simple statement. I would guess that at least 1,000 mathematicians have caught the four-color disease, spending months trying to make it work but never quite succeeding. It is the disease people have suffered from since 1852.”

Thorup is equally candid about the appeal of devoting years to an apparently modest mathematical puzzle.

“Because mathematicians are slightly crazy. Most of what mathematicians work on consists of very nerdy questions. We become obsessed with this type of problem because it challenges the human intellect. And if we find the answer, we’ll probably also find answers to other mathematical puzzles,” says Mikkel Thorup.

That possibility is already emerging from the team’s work. The abundance of reducible configurations could help mathematicians investigate more complex graphs and surfaces whose geometry differs considerably from that of an ordinary map.

“The remarkable thing is that because there are so many handles, the idea can also be applied to other kinds of surfaces besides a flat map. For example, surfaces with holes, such as a swim ring or a piece of Emmental cheese. That is why we believe the result could have significance far beyond the Four Color Theorem,” says Mikkel Thorup.

Reference: “The Four Color Theorem with Linearly Many Reducible Configurations and Near-Linear Time Coloring” by Yuta Inoue, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Atsuyuki Miyashita, Bojan Mohar, Carsten Thomassen and Mikkel Thorup, September 30, 2026, arXiv. DOI: 2603.24880

#6402. Artificial intelligence could fundamentally change how we grow our food

A new review explores how generative AI could transform crop breeding and help address future agricultural challenges.

Modern plant breeding runs on genome data and decades of catalogued crop genes. For all that, it still takes 10 to 15 years to turn a promising cross into a variety a farmer can plant.

Conventional crossbreeding largely relies on existing genetic variation.

A new review says the next round of breeding won’t start with a plant at all. It will start with a model that writes DNA no plant has ever carried, and a lab that builds the sequence to see whether it works.

Feng Xu, Jun Yan, Xiangfeng Wang and their colleagues at China Agricultural University went through 67 generative AI tools built for biological design.

They sorted the tools by the part of breeding each one could serve, and hardly any were made with crops in mind.

Most were trained on microbes or mammalian cells, and the authors wrote that carrying them over to a maize or wheat genome is unfinished work.

The appeal lies in what the older tools couldn’t do.

Yield that holds up in a dry year is controlled by many genes at once, and a model that only ranks the variants nature supplied has a short reach.

Plant breeders mark their own history in stages, and the review counts four before this one. Choosing by eye and crossing came first.

Molecular markers came next, then genomic selection, then the omics work of the past decade, which filled catalogs with crop genes and the traits attached to them.

Every stage improved the odds of picking well. None of them changed the basic move, which was to choose among variation that already existed in a species.

Breeders have worked those catalogs for particular traits, from tomato flavor to seed size to crops that fertilize themselves.

Breeding 5.0, the authors’ name for what comes next, is meant to change the move itself. Design the genetic part first, then build it.

Artificial intelligence in plant science has mostly sorted things. It scored variants, predicted traits and ranked candidates a breeder could already have grown.

Generative models work the other way around. Trained on enough DNA and protein structures, they produce new examples that fit the patterns they learned.

That buys two things the authors care about: sequences beyond anything in nature, and screening that happens before a seed goes in the ground.

Four kinds of model do most of this work. One compresses sequences into a map a researcher can move through in small steps, which suits fine-tuning how strongly a gene switches on.

One trains two networks against each other. The first writes sequences, and the second tries to spot the fakes.

A third starts from noise and strips it away a step at a time, which gives tight control over three-dimensional shapes.

The fourth treats DNA as a language, with bases as letters and genes as sentences.

Those language models are the ones that can take an instruction in plain words.

The clearest results involve the short stretches of DNA that decide when a gene switches on and how strongly. Biologists call them promoters.

In cyanobacteria, 95% of the promoters one model designed turned out to be active. In E. coli, a second model wrote promoters that worked 70.8% of the time and looked little like anything in nature.

The authors call that design from scratch. Designs can be tuned as well as built. A third model raised promoter activity by as much as 33.43-fold, and in yeast a fourth moved expression across a thousandfold range.

Of that fourth model’s designs, 57% beat the strongest natural promoters they were measured against. Not one of those organisms is a crop.

That pattern runs through the review. The proof exists, and it exists in microbes. Plant-specific models are appearing, and most of them still score sequences instead of writing them.

Genome editing lets breeders change a gene directly, and Cas9, the enzyme behind most of that work, came out of bacteria.

Profluent Bio fine-tuned a protein language model until it produced OpenCRISPR-1, the first openly available Cas9 designed this way.

It cut DNA about as well as the standard enzyme, with better specificity, and it still read the short tag that marks where to cut. A separate model produced another Cas9 variant that worked in mammalian cells.

Protein design has gone further outside plants. One model produced 310 proteins that folded as predicted once made, and tools like AlphaFold made that check routine.

In plants, almost all the published work is redesign of existing proteins, including a refined enzyme in Arabidopsis and an improved potato protein.

The authors said design from scratch has rarely been validated in crops.

The authors also raised safety and regulatory questions about AI-designed proteins in crops, including their potential unintended effects, how long they persist under field conditions, and whether they are safe to consume.

So the authors suggested starting small, with designed proteins used as laboratory probes rather than put straight into a crop.

The authors’ own contribution is a framework they call DESIGN, named for six capabilities: discover, engineer, simulate, integrate, generate and navigate.

In plainer words, find the patterns in existing data and pull together information of different kinds.

Then design molecules that fit a set of constraints, make parts nature does not, test candidates in simulation, and weigh competing goals.

The authors set out two worked cases. One designs a maize promoter that stays quiet in a watered field and drives a drought-response gene hard when water runs short.

The other designs a protein that traps a molecule the stripe rust fungus uses to switch off the defenses of wheat.

Neither case is a finished experiment. Both are plans, detailed enough to name the tool at each step and the filter a candidate must clear.

The six capabilities don’t run in a line, the authors wrote. They run as a loop: learn, design, build, test, then feed the results back into the model.

Three problems sit between the framework and a field. Plant datasets are scattered across species and growing conditions, and well-annotated ones are thin for most crops.

Many models don’t transfer between domains or explain their output. Testing in plants is slow, so designs pile up faster than anyone can check them.

Plant genomes make the data problem worse, being larger and more repetitive than the genomes most of these models learned from.

The same gap shows up in single-cell work. One plant model, built for Arabidopsis, labeled cell types it had never been shown with 0.91 accuracy.

The goal is to simulate how a root cell handles salty soil before planting.

The authors emphasized that AI is not meant to replace plant breeders. Breeders will continue to set agricultural goals and evaluate real-world results, while AI helps explore new possibilities.

What hasn’t happened yet, by the authors’ own accounting, is the validation of even one designed protein or regulatory element in a greenhouse or a field.

They named the benchmarks and shared datasets that would get the field there. That greenhouse result is the thing to watch for.

The full study was published in the journal Science China Life Sciences.

#6400. Why Some Farts Can Clear a Room While Others Barely Smell

A microbiologist reveals the surprising gut chemistry behind room-clearing farts, why some stink more than others, and how their terrible smell may serve a useful purpose.

A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day. Altogether, that’s enough gas to fill a super stinky party balloon.

Farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut. These organisms have an important job: They help chew up food that your stomach cannot break down on its own. In the process, they act like mini chemical factories that provide you with nutrients while releasing waste gases into your gut. These gases mix with air you swallow and other gases that you make during digestion. After passing through the intestines, they come out in bursts as farts.

As a microbiologist, I study communities of bacteria, called microbiomes, in various regions of the human body. The microbiome in your gut plays an important role in your health. Producing gases is a sign that bacteria in the gut microbiome are doing their job properly. Farting also relieves pressure in your belly and prevents painful bloating and cramping.

So you might wonder: Why does a normal and healthy body process cause such a bad stink?

Farts are mostly made up of the same odorless gases found in the air we breathe.

Anywhere from 20% to 90% of a fart’s volume consists of nitrogen, which makes up more than three-quarters of air. Up to 10% of a fart is oxygen, which humans need in order to breathe. Up to 30% is carbon dioxide, up to 50% is hydrogen, and up to 10% is methane. Microbes produce most of the carbon dioxide, hydrogen, and methane, though some of the carbon dioxide is made when digestive juices mix with stomach acid.

But wait: These are not the gases that give farts their delightful array of aromas. What makes farts so malodorous is other gas molecules that contain the element sulfur. Pure sulfur has no smell on its own, but when combined with other elements it makes molecules that reek.

One key culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which is famous for smelling like rotten eggs. Others include methanethiol, which has a bouquet of cabbage, sewage or skunk spray, and dimethyl sulfide, which hits the nostrils with scents of cooked corn, algae or seafood.

Only tiny amounts are required: One molecule of hydrogen sulfide among 1 million other gas molecules has enough power to do the job. That’s equivalent to one kernel of corn in a truckload of about 1,250 ears, or 10 bricks out of all the bricks that make up the Empire State Building in New York City. Other sulfur-containing gasses can be sniffed out at even more minuscule amounts.

Your farts’ aroma depends on what your microbiome gets to eat.

The main thing that determines which gases and how much of them are in your farts is what food your gut microbiome gets to eat.

Some types of foods often referred to as junk food, including candy or diet foods containing artificial sweeteners or syrups, can change the way microbes digest food. High-fiber foods such as beans and grains also have this effect. These foods can cause your body to produce more farts that often are bigger and louder.

However, the loudest fart is not always the stinkiest one. It’s the ones that contain sulfur that pack a smelly punch.

Food is a key source of amino acids, nutrients that build proteins the body needs to function and grow. Two amino acids, methionine and cysteine, contain sulfur, and they are plentiful in meat, dairy, eggs, and to a lesser degree, beans and grains. Some foods – most notably, vegetables such as cabbage, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower – contain other molecules that also have sulfur in them.

When you eat sulfur-rich foods, your gut microbes digest them to produce sulfur-containing gases. That can lead to some putrid farts, with the precise smell tuned to your diet – as well as your overall health. In fact, persistent foul-smelling gas can be a sign of illness, such as irritable bowel syndrome or food intolerance or sensitivity, which you might need to see a doctor about.

As you might know from experience, it’s impossible to hold in a fart until it goes away. It will come out somehow – sometimes at speeds up to 10 feet per second, according to back-of-the-envelope estimates, including my own. This rush of gas exiting the body makes the surrounding tissue vibrate, often causing an embarrassing noise.

Farting has been the butt of jokes for millennia. According to the Guinness Book of World Records, the oldest joke ever written down was a popular proverb dating back about 3,900 years that warned new husbands about their wives’ farts. The popularity of fart jokes remains strong. In the 2010 movie “Despicable Me,” for example, mad tech wizard Dr. Nefario mishears his boss’s demand for a dart gun, instead creating a fart gun, or Fart Blaster, that’s now a real-life popular toy.

But sometimes this natural body process can be a real bummer – like on an airplane. Cabin pressure in flight is often lower than normal air pressure on the ground, which can cause the gas in your gut to expand, spurring more farts. To protect the noses of travelers trapped together in the friendly skies, researchers designed seat cushions and blankets that contain sulfur-absorbing substances, such as activated charcoal. So far, no airlines have adopted these funk-reducing technologies, but you can buy them yourself.

Despite farts’ assault on the senses, your ability to detect them means your nose is doing exactly what evolution designed it to do: act as a chemical sensor for sulfur-containing gases. People can detect hydrogen sulfide and methanethiol at minuscule concentrations, even when there is less than one molecule of these compounds amid billions of other molecules.

These smells can signal the presence of rotting substances and bacterial activity that might harbor pathogens that can make you sick, or deadly environments such as swamps, stagnant caves, and volcanic vents that can suffocate and kill you.

So the next time you lay a fart that’s pungent enough to clear the room, don’t apologize – just say you’re conducting a live demonstration of natural chemistry that took eons of evolution to perfect.

Written by Brenda A. Wilson, Professor of Microbiology, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

Adapted from an article originally published in The Conversation.
