The new Ring Floodlight Cam Wired Pro builds on that solid design with extra features, including support for dual-band WiFi and a “bird’s-eye view” feature that tracks a recorded subject as they move within the camera’s view, showing it on a top-down layout of the area.

The camera’s 1080p video resolution and 140-degree field of view are the same as the previous model, but image quality is enhanced with high dynamic range (HDR) support, which improves visibility in both low light and extremely bright conditions.

The lights themselves are also quite bright, 2000 lumens each, and the fixtures are adjustable so you can angle the light as you please.

The Ring Floodlight Cam Wired Pro also features two-way audio support, with a 110-decibel siren that sounds when the system detects motion. It also offers customizable motion zones and 3D- motion radar for you to tailor to your property.

In practice, the security camera is great at sensing motion more than 100 feet away, so it could potentially double as a nature cam. It lacks some of the features other, similarly priced models on this list have, but the biggest drawback is that the field of view is only about 50 feet wide.

The Arlo floodlight has everything we love from our top pick, including Arlo's superior app and software, but adds on a large floodlight, as well as a need for wired power.

As with the Arlo Essential XL, you get quality motion detection software and color night vision. Spring for Arlo Secure, and you get AI target recognition that can point out passing cars or faces, and highlight packages.

The floodlight also has some interesting features: Each light is individually adjustable, so you can angle them for the best possible coverage. That includes creative solutions like angling one light toward your back door, while pointing the other toward the steps leading to your back porch. It's a small touch, but a very appreciated one. It also includes a loud, 110-decibel siren.

If you're looking for a low-maintenance outdoor security camera system, eufy's S330 "eufycam 3" is a dynamic wireless option that supports solar charging and doesn't require professional installation.

Once installed and set up, we did not have to take either of the cameras down for recharging once over months of use. The solar panels kept them perpetually charged as long as they got exposure to a few hours of sunlight per day.

It was similarly easy to connect the cameras to the greater home security. The outdoor cameras works through the home hub which after initial installation using an ethernet cable, works comfortably through your home WiFi. The cameras can then be set up anywhere within several hundred feet of the hub without losing connection.

A big benefit we also loved is the camera system requires no monthly subscription to access its features. This includes AI-powered face recognition, customizable activity zones, and of course, motion detection.

The only drawback for this camera set is the placement of the solar panels. While the panels being integrated directly on top of the camera makes it less cumbersome, it also means you need to install them in a spot with direct sunlight or they won't properly charge.

The Reolink Argus 4 Pro gives you a sweeping 180-degree field of view, which allows you to cover large open spaces with as few cameras as possible. Properly positioned, you can achieve a near-complete view of an area with just two cameras.

This 4K camera features a dual-lens design that covers larger areas without blind spots or fishbowl-style warping. You'd think that might lead to complications with position or usage, but we found it easy to operate.

It features discrete solar panels for power, which allows for more placement flexibility: For example, you can install the camera under a ledge or rooftop, then secure the solar panel above, where it will get direct sun. That makes it easier to get the perfect shot and optimal power.

In terms of storage, the Argus 4 Pro records footage locally and connects to a home hub. You don't have to pay a monthly fee for cloud storage or additional features. Simply turn it on, connect it the hub, and in theory, it should run without issue in perpetuity.

There are two types of consumer-grade home security cameras: wireless battery-powered cameras that you can set up easily nearly anywhere, but require you to occasionally replace batteries, and wired models that connect directly to your home's electrical system.

Wired cameras are generally more expensive and require an electrician's help unless you're comfortable with home wiring, but require far less maintenance once they're installed. Their placement is also restricted to locations where you can wired them in.

Battery-powered cameras, by contrast, are only restricted by the range of your WiFi router. Of course, you'll need to access them every few months to replace their batteries. Some models feature solar panels, giving you renewable energy, but panels also impose some placement restrictions. (Namely, access to sunlight).

Wired cameras do fall short of battery-powered models in one niche scenario—when the power goes out. Unlike, say, wired smoke or carbon monoxide detectors, which have reliable battery backup, you can't count on a wired security camera to provide surveillance footage during an extended period of time if there's a power failure. It varies from model to model, but most wired cameras can only last for 30 minutes to, at most, a few hours before they go dark.

To avoid recording 24/7, which wastes power and storage space, outdoor security cameras usually feature motion sensors that trigger recording whenever there’s activity. Many cameras will also an alert to your companion app whenever they start recording.

Most cameras give you the ability to calibrate the motion sensor by setting motion zones in spots where you expect frequent false alarms, like a sidewalk. Others offer smart features that can differentiate between people, animals, and vehicles. You should also have the ability to customize your notifications, so you’ll only receive an alert in certain situations, like if it detects a person.

Furthermore, some cameras feature microphones, enabling audio detection, which can trigger recording and alerts based on nearby sounds that may be out of view (like a window breaking). Audio detection is a useful extra layer in a few specific situations, like when a single camera can’t cover the entire side of your home, but may also lead to more nuisance alerts. If you decide to use one, we recommend customizing your audio alert sensitivity if possible so you aren’t constantly getting notified when the neighbor’s dog barks.

The best outdoor security cameras record video in "Full HD" (1920 x 1080p) resolution, which captures enough detail to identify facial features or a car’s license plate. More expensive cameras record at higher resolutions, such as 2K or "Quad HD" (2560 x 1440p) or 4K Ultra HD (3840 x 2160) video, which deliver better detail. While higher resolution may help, 1080p video is usually clear enough to give you more than enough information in most situations.

Your camera’s field of view (FOV) is just as important as its resolution. Field of view refers to how wide of an angle the lens is and therefore, how much of your yard or porch is in view. With a wider FOV, your camera can see a wider area around your property, providing more coverage. For the best results, we recommend a model with a field of view between 130 and 180 degrees.

Many outdoor cameras also feature an integrated spotlight that can illuminate the surroundings if motion is detected, improving visibility in low-light situations. A spotlight also acts as a deterrent by making potential intruders more visible. Similarly, the majority of outdoor cameras offer some kind of night vision feature, which uses infrared (IR) lights to record a high-contrast black and white video in the dark. Top-of-the-line cameras are capable of recording standard video in low light, minimizing the need for night vision.

There’s no point in recording camera footage if you can’t store it for when you need it. Many manufacturers offer free cloud storage for a limited time—typically seven days–after which video is overwritten with new recordings. You can always download and save that footage, so long as you do during that initial window.

If you want to save your footage for a longer period, there are a couple of options. Many companies provide additional cloud storage for a subscription fee. There are also cameras that feature a microSD card slot for storing footage locally. This does require a bit of extra maintenance in the form of occasionally removing the card and either deleting or downloading the recorded data to free up more space on the card.

Security cameras are more than just their features. Nearly all security cameras are built to connect with other smart home devices. So, before buying any specific option, make sure it is compatible with the devices you already own. For example, Amazon makes it easy to pull up a live feed from your Ring camera(s) on an Echo Show or Fire TV. There are many brands that work with the majority of the smart home software available such as Apple, Google Nest, and Ring. Some have limited functionality on other smart home software systems outside of their brand, but still work with them. Furthermore, most security camera brands require a monthly subscription to gain full access to many of their features. These monthly subscriptions range in price and overall necessity with some basically essential to operate the cameras and store footage in the cloud while others are designed as a bonus add-on to the base product. Prior to purchase, make sure to take a close look at both the smart home compatibility as well as what comes with and without the monthly subscription service.

Most of the outdoor security cameras we recommend are sold individually or as part of a larger set. The number of cameras you need for your property will vary, based on your home security plan and how much camera coverage you want. A well-installed camera with a wide field of view can cover an important and vulnerable area on your property, such as a back door or garage.

That said, even a small home will need at least a few cameras to achieve full coverage on every ground-level door and window. You may need multiple cameras to reveal tricky blind spots created by corners, lawn features, and anything else that might impede a single camera position.

Don't freak out about needing a fleet of surveillance gear, though. Not everyone wants or needs to have every single square inch of their property under constant watch. It’s up to you to decide where you want an extra eye. The important thing is to make sure you know what you need before making a purchase.

Of course. There are no features of an outdoor security camera that would prevent it from working inside. That said, many companies make indoor cameras that are cheaper, and may feature a stand or mounting options that make more sense for blending in with your home or office.

You should always be careful when considering home security. Over the years, there have been multiple reports of strangers accessing live video feeds and recorded videos from home security cameras.

Luckily, there are simple ways to protect yourself. As with other devices, adhering to digital security best practices, such as keeping your smart home devices’ firmware up to date, creating a strong password and activating two-factor authentication wherever possible, will help prevent a breach.

You may also have concerns about who has access to video that’s stored in the cloud. Most companies ask for permission to review recordings for research and development purposes. Depending on the company, this request often comes in the form of an “opt-in” setting in the camera app, though some may turn it on by default unless you “opt out.”

Some may also share recordings with law enforcement. In some cases, they will only do so when compelled by a search warrant. A couple manufacturers, specifically Amazon (Ring) and Google (Nest), have said they will provide footage without a warrant if law enforcement claims it is an emergency.

#6388. Electrons usually flow freely through metals, but Columbia scientists just found a way to trap them in place

Physicists trapped electrons at a missing atom inside a metal crystal, where quantum interference left them no route out.

A metal conducts electricity because its electrons spread through the whole crystal, the way a ripple spreads across a pond rather than staying where it started. There’s nowhere in a metal for one to hold still.

However, in a palladium compound made at Columbia University, two of them hold still anyway, pinned to a single missing atom.

Morgan Thinel, Simon Turkel and colleagues in Columbia’s Department of Physics and Department of Chemistry found them with a microscope that feels a surface atom by atom.

Two of the authors also work at Brookhaven National Laboratory, and the group’s theorists reproduced both states on paper.

The trap is not a wall around the electron. It is the metal crystal’s own geometry cancelling every route out.

The material is Pd5AlI2, a palladium-aluminum-iodine compound that Xavier Roy’s chemistry group at Columbia built a few years ago. It is a van der Waals crystal, which means it comes apart into sheets the way graphite does, and the sheets stay metallic.

The compound’s electrons moved more slowly than anyone expected, and the group published the reason last year. Call it gridlock: an electron has competing routes to the next atom, and the routes cancel.

The cancelling is the whole mechanism here. A quantum particle does not take one path; it takes every available path at once.

The paths add up like waves, reinforcing in some directions and wiping each other out in others. When the wiping-out is complete, there is no route out at all.

Physicists call the result a bound state in the continuum. The particle is stuck in place even though it is surrounded by an unbroken range of energies into which it could escape.

Light does this. Over the past decade, engineers have etched patterns into materials to catch photons that way, and the trick now drives lasers and sensors. In a metal, it had stayed out of reach.

The team split a crystal open in vacuum and cooled it to about 7 degrees above absolute zero. Then a scanning tunneling microscope measured how easily electrons flow into the surface, point by point and energy by energy.

Across a clean stretch, the answer was much the same everywhere, which is what a metal crystal looks like. Over one kind of flaw in the lattice, two sharp peaks appeared. One sat 475 millivolts above the metal’s own energy floor and the other 620.

Comparing the images with simulations identified the flaw: a single palladium atom missing from the layer buried inside each sheet. Vacancies like it turned up across the crystal at roughly two trillion per square centimeter.

Both states hug the vacancy inside a single nanometer, a span a few atoms wide. A normal defect in a metal only nudges the passing electron waves. These two were not passing.

“Bound electrons shouldn’t occur in a metal, but they do in Pd5AlI2,” said Raquel Queiroz, a theoretical physicist at Columbia who built the models behind the result.

“What we have observed is the first clear evidence of quantum interference trapping a state in a metal.”

Mapping each peak across the surface produced two pictures. The lower one has four lobes, like a clover. The upper one is a plain circle.

Those are the shapes of orbitals around a single atom, which is an odd thing to find around an absence.

The team’s model is a stripped-down version of the layer with one atom removed. It produced both shapes, and put them a few hundred millivolts above the energy floor, where the microscope found them.

The circular one only appears once the model includes the iodine atoms sitting above and below the gap.

The team also answered the obvious objection. The gridlock in an idealized version of this lattice is perfect, and perfect conditions are not what a real crystal offers.

Loosening the model so the electrons are not quite frozen keeps the two states tightly bound across a wide range of settings, including the ones that match the real material.

When two palladium atoms were missing from neighboring sites, the pair of states became four. Each of the original two had split, into a slightly lower energy and a slightly higher one.

That is what happens when two atoms bond into a molecule. The resemblance runs even further. For the four-lobed state, the lower version piles electron density between the two gaps at 440 millivolts. The higher one, at 510, leaves the middle empty.

Move the vacancies two lattice spacings apart and the splitting disappears.

So the trapped states behave like the orbitals of atoms that are not there, and two of them nearby make something like a molecule out of two holes.

No one is placing these on purpose yet. Every vacancy here arrived by chance while the crystal was growing.

That is the sharpest difference from the light version of the effect, where the pattern goes exactly where the designer wants it. Roy’s and Abhay Pasupathy’s groups are working on putting flaws where they choose.

What a trapped electron is good for is also open. The authors note that photonic bound states have essentially unlimited lifetimes, and suggest these might carry charge without loss at their own energies, but nothing here measured current through one.

“And if you trap a particle, you can manipulate it,” Roy said. The uses he and his colleagues point to, from quantum sensors to quantum computers, are a long way past what was measured.

The prediction worth testing is that the lattice did this, not the material. If gridlocked hopping is the ingredient, other crystals with the same frustrated geometry should trap electrons the same way.

The authors name two common lattice patterns to look at next. That is a recipe, and the next paper either finds one or does not.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6386. Dams may be getting blamed for carbon emissions that would occur naturally

A global study suggests that conventional carbon accounting may substantially overestimate certain greenhouse gas emissions directly attributable to dams.

When a river is dammed, decomposing organic matter in the resulting reservoir can release carbon dioxide and methane.

That is why reservoirs now sit in national greenhouse gas inventories. It is also why some people question hydropower’s green credentials.

But much of the organic carbon carried into reservoirs would have decomposed naturally in rivers and estuaries even without dams.

A new study estimates that dams add about 21.5% to the emissions from the carbon they trap, once a free-flowing river’s own emissions are counted.

For the type of carbon tracked in the study, the net emissions attributable to dams were less than a fifth of conventional estimates.

The research was led by Wenqing Shi of Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology.

The co-authors came from the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, the University of North Carolina’s Institute of Marine Sciences, and Aarhus University in Denmark.

“High carbon emissions from reservoirs have sparked controversy over dams,” the team wrote.

In an interview with Earth.com, Shi noted that a fair test compares the same river with and without the dam, from the reservoir down to the estuary.

“We need to distinguish emissions that occur in a reservoir from emissions actually added by the dam,” Shi said.

Rivers carry about 940 million tons (850 million metric tons) of land-grown carbon to the ocean every year. Some of it decays in the channel on the way down.

Most of it settles in estuaries, where it decays too, releasing the same two gases.

A dam interrupts the trip. More than 70,000 large dams now stand on the world’s rivers, and each one catches carbon that would otherwise have kept moving.

The usual accounting charges every ton of gas rising from a reservoir to the dam that made it. That treats the carbon as if it would have stayed put without the dam.

Shi’s team ran the numbers both ways for 5,346 dammed reservoirs around the world: once with the dam in place, and once with the river flowing freely to the sea.

Methane traps far more heat than carbon dioxide, so the team converted it to a carbon dioxide equivalent, at 27.2 times the warming over a century. That put the two scenarios on one scale.

The two rivers look very different. In the free-flowing version, about 4.9% of the carbon decays in the channel and the rest reaches the estuary.

In the dammed version, 88.3% of the carbon arriving from upstream is caught in the reservoir, 0.5% decays in the channel below, and 11.1% makes it to the estuary.

Nearly every dam, 99.4% of them, raised emissions compared with the undammed river. The average increase was 21.5%, and the team’s uncertainty range runs from 8.3% to 32.6%.

The conventional method counts all reservoir emissions as the dam’s doing. Measured against it, the net effect is 18.6% of the old figure.

“We expected the baseline to matter, but the size of the difference was striking,” Shi told Earth.com.

Shi emphasized that the 18.6% figure covers only the land-grown carbon particles the study followed, not every source of reservoir emissions or hydropower’s whole carbon footprint.

“The emissions themselves have not disappeared; what changes is how much can reasonably be attributed to the dam,” Shi said.

Added up, the world’s dams release an extra 6 million tons (5.4 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide equivalent a year, by the team’s estimate.

Hydroelectric dams account for just over half of that, with irrigation dams next and flood control dams third.

Per ton of trapped carbon, hydroelectric dams add the least, 16.5% against more than 19.4% for every other dam type. They lead the list because there are so many of them and they drain such large areas.

A few dams even cut emissions. On rivers flowing from cool regions toward warm coasts, carbon held back in cold water decays more slowly than it would in a warm estuary.

What a dam changes most is which gas comes out. In reservoirs, slow water lets organic-rich mud pile up and run out of oxygen, and that is where methane forms.

Free-flowing rivers generally have more oxygenated conditions that are less favorable to methane production.

In the team’s model, methane’s share of the warming from decaying river carbon rose from 4.4% without dams to 22.8% with them, more than a fivefold jump.

“Reservoir conditions can favor methane production, so shifting decomposition upstream can still increase the climate impact, even after accounting for the no-dam baseline,” Shi said.

Reservoir depth and how long water lingers behind the dam were the strongest controls.

Shallow reservoirs and very deep ones both pushed emissions up, while reservoirs between about 65 and 260 feet (20 and 80 meters) deep held them down.

Shi said that spread is one more reason not to apply a single correction factor to every reservoir.

The model follows only one kind of carbon, the particles washed in from the land. It leaves out carbon in soil flooded when a reservoir fills, carbon dissolved in the water, and algae grown in the reservoir itself.

All three can add to a reservoir’s emissions. So the team called its 18.6% a conservative figure, and the true share pinned on dams could be higher.

Those other sources, and hydropower’s full life-cycle impacts, still have to be assessed separately, Shi said.

The researchers also treated all incoming carbon alike, though carbon from different watersheds decays at different rates.

No global dataset yet describes how a dam changes the flow of the river below it, so that effect is missing too.

“A priority is to make the estuary baseline more site-specific,” Shi said. That means measuring the carbon arriving, how much of it is buried or decays, and the gases that come off.

The team also wrote that any carbon accounting for a dam should run from the reservoir all the way to the estuary.

Until that happens, the figure in a hydropower plant’s carbon ledger depends on where the ledger decides the river begins.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

At a cliff site in Texas, archaeologists discovered hundreds of bison bones, stone tools and arrowheads, suggesting Indigenous people used "bison jumps" to hunt.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have uncovered an extremely rare example of a "bison jump" in the Texas Panhandle, where a natural geological formation allowed Indigenous people to hunt North America's largest living land mammal for 3,000 years. The discovery confirms that the prehistoric hunting technique ‪—‬ which involved channeling a herd of bison into a stampede off a cliff, akin to "walking the plank" ‪—‬ was not limited to the northern Plains like experts previously thought.

"Bison jumping is an iconic, uniquely North American hunting technique that yielded some of the most productive food-getting events in the history of human hunting," researchers wrote in a study published online Nov. 9 in the journal American Antiquity.

Although jump sites are well known throughout the northern Plains, only one such site had ever been found in the southern Plains. But a second bison jump called Nighthawk has now been identified in Caprock Canyons State Park in the Texas Panhandle, and researchers found that Indigenous people used the Nighthawk bison jump for millennia.

"Returning to the same place over and over again over 3,000 years shows that people had a significant connection to the Nighthawk hunting facility," study first author Gus Costa, an archaeologist at Rice University in Houston, said in a statement.

Nighthawk was found when bison remains began eroding from a bone bed (a place where bones naturally accumulate) underneath a roughly 65-foot-tall (20 meters) cliff spur. Archaeologists investigated and found chipped stone tools near the bones, as well as a few arrowheads. Several of the bison bones had cut marks from stone tools consistent with prehistoric butchery practices. These discoveries added up to a possible bison jump.

Archaeologists found hundreds of bison bones at the Nighthawk bison jump site in Texas.

"The only way bison can arrive at the site is by falling from above, as the site surface is sandwiched between two cliffs," the researchers wrote. Indigenous hunters likely used the cliff's natural spur shape to herd the bison to their deaths. "Instead of a stampede toward a surprise fall, Nighthawk could have operated more like 'walking the plank,'" according to the researchers.

Even more surprising than the discovery of a bison jump site in the southern Plains was the length of time the jump was used.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A series of radiocarbon dates revealed that there were at least seven mass bison kills at Nighthawk over a span of three millennia, between roughly 1550 B.C. and A.D. 1550. One of these events, which the researcher named Kill 3, was responsible for most of the bison bones. That enormously successful hunt most likely took place around A.D. 300 to 400 and would have required an immense labor force and precise coordination.

Archaeologists excavating a bison jump site called Nighthawk in Caprock Canyons State Park in the Texas Panhandle.

"Bison jumping is a complicated community effort," Costa said. "Large scale bison harvests (like jumps) are exciting because they require a large group of people working together to be successful."

It is not entirely clear what the Indigenous hunters were doing with the bison killed in the hunt. In the northern Plains, archaeologists have long assumed that bison jumps were generally performed in the fall and used to provision the community for winter. Bison in the North were used to make pemmican, a shelf-stable mix of dried meat and rendered fat.

But although pemmican was an extremely useful foodstuff and trade good in the North, it was likely too warm in Texas for bison fat to last more than a few weeks, the researchers wrote. This may mean that the southern Plains bison hunts were more useful for displaying power and building alliances.

All of the kill events at Nighthawk were at least a century apart, with an average of 500 years between each bison jump. That points to an infrequent use of the jump but also a clear memory of its utility.

"The simplest explanation for long-lived jump facilities is that these techniques were passed down over long time spans rather than revived again and again," the researchers wrote.

Costa, A. G., Houk, B. A., Lyle, A. S., Bement, L., Lintz, C., Lawrence, K. L., Frederick, C. D., & Culleton, B. J. (2026). The Nighthawk bison jump: New evidence for recurrent Late Holocene bison jumping in the Southern Plains. American Antiquity, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1017/aaq.2026.10229

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6384. Ice baths don’t help your muscles recover after a workout any better than heat-based methods, according to a new study

Despite the popularity of ice baths for post-workout recovery, new research finds that cold-water immersion helps restore muscle strength no better than heat-based methods.

Enduring a freezing ice bath after a hard workout feels like a steep price to pay for better muscle recovery. Now, results from a new study show that cold-water immersion restored strength no faster than sitting in a chair with a hot towel around your neck.

For this research project, forty people wrecked one thigh muscle on purpose. They then spent 15 to 30 minutes in cold water, hot water, hot air, or an ordinary room. Three days later, their strength had come back at the same pace in every group.

The hot water did change the body in ways the ice bath didn’t. Blood markers of muscle damage settled faster after a hot bath, and a protective protein rose more.

Those changes never showed up as extra strength or less soreness. So, for now, the finding is that heat and cold are different, not that either one is better.

Freya Bayne, a lecturer in sport and exercise science at the University of East London, led the study. Her co-authors came from London South Bank University, Maastricht University, and the University of Montpellier, among others.

Each person got one session of one treatment, and the follow-up stopped at 72 hours, so the results say nothing about weeks of regular ice baths.

“Cold-water immersion remains one of the most popular recovery strategies used by athletes and recreational exercisers alike,” Bayne said.

“Our findings suggest that heat-based recovery methods produce different physiological responses following strenuous exercise, particularly in relation to markers associated with cellular protection and muscle repair.”

The volunteers were 40 adults, 31 of them men, averaging 26 years old, who already lifted weights three to five hours a week.

Each one sat at a machine that forced the dominant knee to bend while the thigh muscle fought it, 210 times in all. Contractions like that are what make muscles sore a day or two later.

Right after the session, the thigh could push with about 36 percent less force than before. That loss is what the recovery treatments were meant to undo.

Each person was assigned at random to one of four treatments, ten to a group. One group sat chest-deep in water at 108°F (42°C) for 30 minutes, and another sat in an ice bath at 48°F (9°C) for 15 minutes.

A third sat in a room heated to 86°F (30°C) for 30 minutes, and the last sat in a room at 64°F (18°C) in their gym clothes.

Everyone came back at 24, 48, and 72 hours to push against the machine again. They also gave blood and rated their pain and soreness.

By 72 hours, the hot water, hot air, and plain room groups had all recovered about 88 to 90 percent of their starting strength. The cold water group was at about 82 percent.

The gap between cold water and the rest looks like something, but with ten people per group the uncertainty around it is wide. The statistics could not separate any group from any other.

The authors wrote that the pattern fits other recent work suggesting cold can slow the signals that rebuild muscle, while stopping short of calling it a result.

Three things in the blood told a different story from the strength test. One was a protein called creatine kinase, which leaks out of damaged muscle fibers.

It was back to normal 48 hours after the hot bath and 72 hours after hot air or a plain room. After the cold bath, it was still about 25 percent above normal at 72 hours.

The second was heat shock protein 72, a protein that cells make under stress to protect and repair themselves. Right after the treatment, the hot water group’s level was more than three times its start. The cold water group’s was about one and a half times.

The third, an immune messenger called interleukin-6, spiked highest after the hot bath and then dropped fastest, back to near normal within a day.

Only the hot bath warmed the muscle itself, from 98°F to 102°F (36.6°C to 38.8°C). The cold bath cooled it to 93°F (34°C).

Pain and soreness rose in every group by the next day and were still up at 72 hours. No treatment brought them back to the starting point. The hot air group reported the most pain on days one and two and the most fatigue on days two and three.

Cold water held soreness down on the first day, but it climbed on the second before easing on the third.

“It is important to recognize that these responses did not result in significantly greater recovery of muscle strength or lower levels of soreness over the following 72 hours,” Bayne said.

The study tested a single session of each treatment, and the authors said one session may not capture what repeated use does.

The team didn’t track what the volunteers ate, and only asked them to state their first day’s meals. Soreness ratings were filled in online, and only 29 of the 40 people completed every one.

With nine women among 40 people, the team couldn’t ask whether men and women respond differently to heat and cold. And the blood marker for muscle damage is an indirect one, since no muscle tissue was sampled.

Bayne’s team wants larger groups, repeated exposures, and tests of timing and dose. “Further research is needed to understand whether repeated exposure to heat-based recovery strategies might produce longer-term benefits,” she said.

Until that work is done, heat changes the blood in ways cold does not, and the strength tests show no difference in recovery between them.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Thermal Biology.

#6382. A new AI tool could help fight online wildlife trafficking

Researchers have developed a way to recognize elephant ivory, pangolin scales, and tiger claws in photographs to help investigators flag suspicious online listings.

A new AI tool can identify elephant, pangolin, and tiger products in photographs, even among similar-looking everyday objects.

Tests suggest it could help investigators sift through online listings and decide which items deserve closer inspection.

The research was led by Enrico Di Minin at the University of Helsinki. Lead author Ritwik Kulkarni worked with the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) on the image library and prototype.

Wildlife products change appearance as they become jewelry, ornaments, or medicines. A photograph may show a carved bracelet, loose scales, or a claw, with few clues about its origin.

Illegal and unsustainable trade contributes to wildlife declines. Tracking it online means reviewing large numbers of photographs across shopping sites and social media, often with limited staff.

“Identifying illegal wildlife products, such as elephant ivory, using AI was one of the grand challenges we were facing,” Di Minin said.

“These new tools offer novel opportunities for real-time monitoring of online illegal trade in ivory, pangolin scales, and tiger claws for enforcement purposes.”

The researchers assembled 39,941 images collected through IFAW’s monitoring work in China between 2008 and 2023.

Sources included online advertisements, market inspections, publicly reported seizures, and image searches. This gave the team examples of products as they actually appeared in trade-related photographs.

The library also included objects that could fool a reviewer. Jade bracelets resembled ivory bracelets, while slices of herbal medicine looked like pangolin scales.

Two experienced IFAW analysts reviewed the labels and resolved disagreements. Objects were also marked with boxes, teaching the model where to look within each photograph.

That mattered for crowded product displays and collages. The system needed to locate a suspicious item even when other objects appeared beside it.

The team compared models trained separately for each target group with a model trained on all three. The combined approach performed best overall.

“The best model achieved an overall accuracy of 84% and exceeded 90% accuracy for tiger and pangolin products,” Kulkarni said.

The paper gives the figures as 93.6% for pangolin products and 90.3% for tiger products. Elephant products proved harder, with an accuracy of 71.1%.

Ivory carvings can resemble objects made from bone or resin. The researchers also noted that models may sometimes rely on surrounding visual clues instead of the object’s identifying features.

“When integrated into a research prototype smartphone application and evaluated independently, the tool reached 91.3% accuracy in practical screening tests, highlighting the potential of automated image analysis to help prioritise suspect content for human review,” Kulkarni explained.

The app was assessed using 138 additional images, separately from the initial model tests.

The prototype lets users choose an existing photograph or take a new one. It then returns a prediction, with boxes marking the objects it has detected.

An investigator reviewing online advertisements could submit saved images. During a market inspection, an officer could photograph an item for an initial assessment.

“For these technologies to make a meaningful contribution to conservation, we need to make them accessible and usable by the people working on the ground,” Kulkarni said.

“Our prototype demonstrates how we can bridge the gap between AI research and practical conservation applications. An app built on it could help, for example, conservation organizations and authorities.”

Users can also give feedback on whether the labels and boxes are correct. That provides a way to record mistakes and improve later versions.

A photograph cannot settle whether a sale is illegal. A flagged image gives investigators something to examine, while qualified authorities remain responsible for legal decisions.

Errors create different problems. False alarms send reviewers toward ordinary goods, while missed detections can leave suspicious listings unnoticed.

The aim is to help people decide where to spend their time. Specialists would still need to examine the item, the listing, and any other relevant evidence.

The reported results measure image-recognition performance. They do not show how many illegal sales the tool would prevent or how much it would reduce pressure on wildlife populations.

The researchers plan to improve accuracy, add more species and products, and explore pilots with conservation organizations and online platforms.

They also want secure, ethical procedures for referring suspected cases to authorities.

Continued training will matter because products and their presentation change. A system built from past photographs needs updating as new examples enter the market.

The paper also suggests combining images with information from listing text. That could help when a photograph alone leaves too much uncertainty.

“We are excited to see this research translate into a practical screening tool for combating illegal online wildlife trade,” said Lionel Hachemin, IFAW’s Wildlife Crime Program Director.

“This study demonstrates what’s possible when conservation organizations and researchers join forces. We see this as a practical step toward turning the tide on illegal wildlife trade online.”

The study is published in the journal Conservation Biology.

Astronomers once assumed galaxies were born before black holes, but giant black holes spotted in the early universe are forcing them to rethink their order of events.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nearly every large galaxy is thought to have a supermassive black hole at its center. The Milky Way's black hole, known as Sagittarius A*, is enormous, weighing over 4 million times as much as the sun. But which came first: the black holes or the galaxies around them?

Astronomers told Live Science that they thought they knew, but new observations mean they're no longer sure.

For decades, the prevailing idea was that galaxies came first: Dying massive stars leave behind black holes that can merge and feed until they swell to millions of times the sun's mass, said Joseph Silk, an astrophysicist and professor at Johns Hopkins University.

Then, in recent years, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) began peering back at the early universe. "Recent observations are challenging this picture, or at least showing us that it cannot be the whole story," Roberto Maiolino, a professor of astrophysics at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science in an email. "We are finding extremely massive black holes just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang."

The galaxy GHZ2 (white box) contains the oldest known supermassive black hole. Discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope in 2022, its light had to travel some 13.4 billion years to reach Earth.

Stranger still, some of these black holes look too big for their hosts. In nearby galaxies, a central black hole is typically about a thousand times less massive than its galaxy, Maiolino said, but some early ones "appear to be almost as massive as the stars in their host galaxies." In a study in the journal Nature, Maiolino and colleagues measured one such black hole's mass directly in an object called Abell2744-QSO1 and found that it holds most of the object's mass.

So where could such giants come from? Maiolino outlined several possibilities, and more than one may be correct. Some supermassive black holes may be ordinary stellar remnants that grew much faster than usual. Others may have been "born big," forming from the direct collapses of enormous gas clouds, which "would give the black hole a head start in its growth," Maiolino explained. Another idea is that these monsters were seeded by primordial black holes that formed "shortly after the Big Bang, before the first stars and galaxies existed."

Further complicating the question is that black holes and galaxies also push and pull on each other. A growing black hole can release an enormous amount of energy that heats or expels gas, which, in turn, curbs or shuts down star formation, Maiolino said.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

However, it can also compress gas and potentially trigger new stars. "Black holes and galaxies influence one another throughout their evolution, and neither can be understood entirely in isolation," he said.

A black hole spewing jets inside the elliptical galaxy Centaurus A.

Silk said the balance varies. In giant, elliptical galaxies, black holes weighing billions of suns can have "histories of extreme violence" that helped limit their hosts' growth, while in spirals like the Milky Way, feedback from stars tends to dominate.

So which came first? Answering that question will take far more data from JWST. Right now, "we have samples of tens of objects, maybe 20, 30, 40," Silk said, and astronomers need far more data to tell whether oversize black holes are typical.

If black holes outweigh their galaxies the farther back astronomers look, that would strongly suggest black holes formed first, Silk said; if stars dominate, it would point the other way.

Maiolino suggested the question itself may need rethinking. "Asking which came first may be too simplistic," he said. "The more interesting question may be how black holes and galaxies formed, grew and influenced one another at different stages of cosmic history."

There may be no single sequence. "Different black holes, in different environments and at different cosmic epochs, may have formed and evolved through different pathways," Maiolino added.

For now, the cosmic chicken-and-egg puzzle remains open. As Maiolino put it, astronomers are "beginning to explore a period of cosmic history for which we still have many unanswered questions."

#6379. Astronomers catch ‘galaxy-killing’ wind in the act

In the local universe, it is common to find galaxies that have stopped forming new stars. These so-called quiescent galaxies have lived for billions of years and over that time, gradually exhausted their star-forming gas. By contrast, galaxies that lie at much greater distances — and thus appear to us when they were young, in the early universe — should have plenty of gas and be readily forming stars.

But ever since it first began surveying the cosmos, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has discovered more quiescent galaxies within the cosmos’ first 2 billion years than current models of galaxy formation and evolution predict. Astronomers don’t know why they have stopped forming stars so soon, but they have many theories. Some of them require dark energy to have had a stronger influence in the early universe than previously thought, and thus have profound impacts on our understanding of the universe and its evolution.

Now, a team has found evidence that when galaxies collide — as they frequently did in the early universe — it can trigger a burst of star formation so intense that it generates winds capable of snuffing out the opportunity for any further stars to be born. This could explain the high number of young but unexpectedly quiescent galaxies JWST has found without needing drastic changes to our understanding of dark energy and its influence over time.

In order to form stars, galaxies need reservoirs of gas that are dense and cold, lacking energy and prone to collapsing inward. One way to end a galaxy’s era of star formation — a process that astronomers call quenching — is to trigger strong winds that blast outward from the galaxy. These vast, high-speed flows of charged particles can blow away or heat this cold gas.

Such galactic winds can have two possible sources of energy. One is an actively accreting central supermassive black hole (called an active galactic nucleus, or AGN). The other is the energetic blasts generated by massive stars that form and then quickly die, ending their lives by exploding as supernovae. But astronomers have never caught such a wind in the act of draining its host of gas in the early universe, as it is difficult to get a detailed look inside a galaxy so far away.

To better discern the inner workings of star-forming galaxies in the early universe, researchers carried out a joint survey combining observations taken with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) — a powerful radio observatory in Chile — and infrared data from JWST. They also turned to archival data from the Hubble Space Telescope. A team led by astrophysicist Rebecca Davies of Swinburne University of Technology in Australia spotted one particular galaxy, called CRISTAL-02, that shows what appears to be the first direct evidence of a wind powerful enough to halt star formation in a massive galaxy just 1.1 billion years after the Big Bang. The discovery was published June 10 in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

CRISTAL-02 is part of a larger sample of around two dozen star-forming galaxies at a similar distance (and therefore of a similar age). Observations showed a huge plume of cold gas extending outside the galaxy, almost as large as the galaxy it comes from. The plume is moving toward Earth at some 60 miles (100 kilometers) per second. Finding fast-moving gas so far from the galaxy is a sign the gas is being actively pushed out in a wind-driven process.

But to truly determine the nature of the plume, the team first had to rule out another possibility behind its formation: Because CRISTAL-02 also appears to be in the throes of merging with several other galaxies, the plume could be a tidal tail — gas stripped away by gravitational forces during the interaction, rather than a genuine wind. This was tricky to determine, Davies says, as no single measurement could settle the question of the gas’ origin; instead the team had to combine several different measurements to characterize the plume and confirm its cause.

First, Davies’ team measured how many new stars the galaxy produces each year. Massive stars live much shorter lives than less massive ones, so looking at how many young, massive stars are in a galaxy indicates how quickly it is forming new stars to replace the ones that are dying. So, the team searched for signs of these young, massive stars in the galaxy’s spectrum and measured how bright those features appear.

The researchers also needed to determine how much gas the galaxy is losing. They did so by first using ALMA data to calculate the mass in the plume and then combining it with the gas’ velocity and distance from the galaxy’s center.

The verdict: CRISTAL-02 is forming stars at roughly three times the rate of a typical galaxy its size at this distance, but is losing twice as much gas as the galaxy’s star-formation rate. “If this rapid blowout continues, the galaxy could be dead in less than 50 million years, explaining the origin of the mysterious massive dead galaxies in the early universe,” Davies said in a press release.

Finally, the team turned to identifying the cause of the plume. Was the gas being pushed out by energy coming from the galaxy’s central black hole, or was the galaxy’s burst of intense star formation — and the resulting supernova blasts — the culprit?

Models predict that the most powerful outflows from massive galaxies like these should be the result of accretion onto supermassive black holes, Davies says. But CRISTAL-02 shows no sign of AGN activity in its center. On the other hand, based on the amount of massive young stars in the galaxy, Davies’ team calculated that the energy transferred to the surrounding gas as these stars die and explode as supernovae would be powerful enough to produce the observed plume.

The speed of the gas backs this idea up. Supernova-driven outflows rarely exceed speeds of about 1,550 miles (2,500 km) per second, says Christy Tremonti, an astronomer at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the study. Velocities higher than this usually point to an AGN as the energy source. CRISTAL-02’s outflow is moving around 400 miles (640 km) per second, comfortably within the range expected for a wind produced by a powerful starburst.

Davies says that “the result is surprising,” going against the conventional wisdom that AGN are the cause of star-formation-ending winds. Tremonti notes that  “theoretical models love to use AGN feedback to shut off star formation in massive galaxies — almost every simulation does.” Yet CRISTAL-02’s star formation alone appears capable of triggering a wind that could exhaust its gas supply within tens of millions of years.

CRISTAL-02’s story may not be an isolated case, Davies says. Studies suggest that around 40% of massive star-forming galaxies in the early universe are merging, meaning many of them may be caught in similar growth spurts. If this commonly results in subsequent supernova-driven winds, it could help explain why so many early galaxies burned brightly and died young. “It may be the case that AGN are really important for keeping star formation off, but maybe they’re not the thing that shuts it down initially,” Tremonti says.

The case isn’t entirely closed. Davies says her team cannot completely rule out the presence of an active supermassive black hole — either one too faint to detect, or one that may have flared briefly in the past and pushed gas away from the galaxy before subsequently fading from view. Tremonti agrees this is one of the hardest scenarios to eliminate. Future observations in the mid-infrared, which can peer through dust that might otherwise hide a buried black hole, could help close this gap.

As for CRISTAL-02, its fate is somewhat ironic: The explosive burst of star formation it is undergoing is also the underlying cause of its imminent death.

Shreejaya Karantha is a science writer based in India. Her work has appeared in Sky & Telescope, Phys.org, Live Science US, and The Hindu.

#6378. Benjamin Franklin mocked the bald eagle in a 1784 letter and praised the turkey, but never asked for it to be the national bird

The letter, never mailed to his daughter, was not published in full in English until 1817. The bald eagle became the national bird by law only in 2024.

A popular Thanksgiving story holds that Benjamin Franklin wanted the turkey, not the bald eagle, to be the national bird of the United States. It is a good story, but it is not what Franklin actually wrote.

The story traces back to a letter dated January 26, 1784, and addressed to his daughter, Sarah Bache. In it, he poked fun at the eagle on the badge of the Society of the Cincinnati and said a few kind words about the turkey. In that letter, he never proposes the turkey as a national symbol.

According to the editors of his papers, Franklin never even sent the letter to his daughter. And the bald eagle itself was officially designated the national bird by law only in 2024, more than two centuries later.

When Franklin wrote the letter, the bald eagle was already on the Great Seal of the United States. It had been adopted for the seal on June 20, 1782.

In the winter of 1783 to 1784, Franklin, the American minister, was too ill to travel and isolated at Passy, in France, according to the editors of his papers.

On January 26, he saw the founding document of the Society of the Cincinnati, a hereditary order of American army officers. John Paul Jones had sent it to him along with a pamphlet attacking the society.

The letter that Franklin wrote that same day was, in the view of the editors of The Papers of Benjamin Franklin, a satire meant as a public essay.

Addressing it to his daughter, with whom, the editors note, he never corresponded about politics, made it look like a private note.

He took aim at the idea of passing honors down to children. He objected to “an order of hereditary Knights, in direct opposition to the solemnly declared sense of their country.”

He even did the math. In nine generations, he wrote, a member’s share in his descendant would be “but a 512th part.”

The birds come up near the end, when Franklin turns to the society’s badges, which had been made in France. “To me they seem tolerably done; but all such things are criticised,” he wrote.

Some critics, he reported, disliked the Latin mottos. “Others object to the bald eagle, as looking too much like a Dindon or turkey,” he wrote, using the French word for turkey.

Then Franklin gave his own opinion. “For my own part I wish the bald eagle had not been chosen as the representative of our country,” he wrote. “He is a bird of bad moral character. He does not get his living honestly.”

He described the eagle sitting on a dead tree, “too lazy to fish for himself,” while it watched another bird, which he called the fishing hawk. When that bird caught a fish and carried it toward its nest, he wrote, the eagle “pursues him, and takes it from him.”

He went further. “Besides he is a rank coward,” Franklin wrote. The “little king bird not bigger than a sparrow attacks him boldly and drives him out of the district.”

Only then does Franklin praise the turkey. He wrote that he was “not displeased” that the figure on the badge was not recognizable as a bald eagle and looked more like a turkey.

“For in truth, the turkey is in comparison a much more respectable bird, and withal a true original native of America,” he wrote. Eagles, he noted, “have been found in all countries, but the turkey was peculiar to ours.”

He did not spare the turkey entirely. He called it “a little vain and silly,” though “not the worse emblem for that,” and “a bird of courage” that would attack a grenadier of the British guards who dared to invade its farmyard “with a red coat on.”

Nowhere in the letter does Franklin ask for the turkey to replace the eagle on the seal or anywhere else. The comparison is part of a joke about a badge.

According to the editors of his papers, Franklin showed the letter only to his grandsons before sending it, around March 1784, to the abbé Morellet in France to translate it into French. Morellet advised against publishing it. Franklin agreed and promised it would not appear while he was alive.

A partial French translation came out in Paris in 1790, months after Franklin’s death. The full English text was not published until 1817, when William Temple Franklin included it in his edition of Franklin’s writings.

In other words, the letter that so many people now quote was almost unknown in Franklin’s lifetime.

The bald eagle’s official title came with a bill that Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota introduced on June 20, 2024, exactly 242 years after the eagle was adopted for the Great Seal.

The Senate passed it by unanimous consent in July 2024, and the House approved it by voice vote on December 16, 2024. It was signed into law on December 23, 2024, as Public Law 118-206.

The law adds a new section to the U.S. Code. It reads: “The bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) is the national bird.”

In its findings, Congress noted that the bald eagle is unique to North America and that federal, state and local governments, nonprofit groups and individuals had all contributed to its recovery.

Even so, eagles still face problems, including the lead poisoning that is common in eagles.

The turkey’s history with people goes back much further than Franklin. Scientists have found that turkeys were domesticated at least 1,500 years ago.

The information was obtained from Benjamin Franklin’s letter to Sarah Bache of January 26, 1784, as published by the National Archives in Founders Online from The Papers of Benjamin Franklin, the record of S.4610 on Congress.gov, and the enrolled text of the bill published by the U.S. Government Publishing Office.

The most powerful cordless stick vacuums will easily run you $500 or more, but in my experience, there are plenty of capable cleaners under $300. They may not rival the suction power, battery life, or features of their higher-priced counterparts, but many are perfectly capable of keeping up with typical household messes on hardwood, carpet, and every surface in between.

I’ve spent years testing vacuums for Popular Mechanics, and that experience informs a lot of my recommendations below. Some of these models have been through my own series of hands-on tests, while others made the cut based on my familiarity with their brands and product lines, along with research into their features and real-world performance. From budget-friendly everyday cleaners to options for pet owners, these are the best cordless vacuums that deliver the most for under $300.

The Shark PowerDetect is a feature-packed option for anyone who wants a cordless stick vacuum that does a lot of the thinking for them. The Detect mode automatically adjusts suction based on floor type and amount of debris, and a dual-roller floor head tackles tough messes on hardwood and carpet.

The hinged wand is great for cleaning under furniture and makes it a lot easier to reach hidden areas without having to bend down at all kinds of weird angles. It’s on the heavier side, and the long recharge time is a drawback, but strong pickup and smart features make it a good pick for whole-home cleaning.

Don’t let the price fool you: The Bissell PowerClean FurFinder is a strong and versatile cordless vacuum. It isn’t too heavy to carry between rooms, and the self-standing design means you don’t have to remount it or lay it flat any time you need to pause during your cleaning session.

It has a tangle-free brush roll that does a great job picking up pet hair (as well as your own stray strands around the house). I also like the LED headlights that show hidden dirt, dust, and debris on floors and furniture. The attachments are great for above-floor cleaning, too. Battery life drops considerably when you crank up the suction power, so it’s best for maintenance cleaning.

The LVAC-300 packs cleaning power and everyday convenience into a lightweight machine. It’s easy to maneuver, and it transitions between hard floors, rugs, and low- to medium-pile carpet without scattering debris all over the floor. The tangle-resistant brush roll is a major pro for homes with pets or long hair, and five-stage filtration and washable filters are valuable additions.

It converts to a handheld vacuum cleaner with attachments for upholstery, stairs, and car interiors, and it uses a pleated mechanical HEPA filter with a dense arrangement of fibers to capture even the tiniest dust particles. The smaller dustbin and shorter runtime on max power might negatively impact your overall experience using this vacuum, but still, it’s versatile enough to take care of a variety of common household messes.

The Tineco Pure One Station 5 is the sibling to the Station 5 Pro that I’ve tested and still use to this day. And luckily, this more affordable model doesn’t cut key features that I love, such as the self-emptying and self-cleaning bagless docking station and green laser light for dust detection.

This model also has HEPA filtration and smart features. Internal sensors detect dust and adjust suction accordingly, and the anti-tangle brush roll helps prevent hair buildup. You get a shorter runtime with this model than you do with the Pro (estimated 70 minutes compared to the Pro’s 100), but the automated cleaning capability is hard to beat.

The Dyson V8 is right at the edge of our $300 budget, but it’s a powerful option for homes with lots of carpeting or area rugs. I haven’t tried this specific model yet, but the motorbar floor cleaner is the same design that comes with other Dyson vacuums I’ve tried, such as the Dyson V15 Detect. It works well for hard floors, but I’ve found it particularly useful for dislodging embedded hair and debris from carpet fibers.

The V8 comes with three attachments and converts into a handheld vacuum if you need more portability. Runtime is on the lower end for Dyson, but if you’re looking for a premium design without the premium price tag, the V8 is it.

The Eureka ReactiSense 440 offers a number of features that make vacuuming less of a chore. It has dust detection sensors, automatic suction adjustment, floor head lights, and an anti-tangle brush roll with fins and a comb strip to prevent hair from getting wrapped around it.

I like that this model uses HEPA filtration to capture up to 99.7 percent of airborne particles and odors (which is great if you’re a pet owner). This model is lightweight and portable, converts to a handheld, and provides up to 60 minutes of runtime. Battery life will likely vary if you’re regularly cleaning at high power levels, but I’d reach for this vacuum for daily maintenance cleaning and quick pickups.

#6376. The biggest concern about toddler screen time may be what children are missing

Many toddlers use screens daily, potentially missing valuable opportunities to play, talk, and learn through real human interaction.

At 18 months, children are learning to name things, put words together and make sense of the world around them. Many are also becoming quite familiar with television and smartphones.

In Hungary, researchers found that 49% of children around this age used screens every day.

There has been plenty of debate over how much screen time is appropriate for young children. A new review, however, looks at a different side of the problem.

How much time is left for talking, playing and being with other people?

Krisztina Kopcsó, a researcher at the HCSO Institute for Quantitative Population and Economic Research in Budapest, led the review.

Kopcsó and her colleagues drew on data from a Hungarian national survey and research from around the world published since 2015.

Among the authors was Ákos Pogány from the Department of Ethology at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE).

“Young children learn primarily through actively exploring the world and interacting with others, rather than through screens. One of the greatest risks of introducing digital devices too early is that their use takes time away from precisely these essential experiences,” Pogány said.

Screen exposure before age two is discouraged by the World Health Organization and the American Academy of Pediatrics. Video chatting with distant family members is treated as an exception.

A more restrictive position has been adopted in France. Complete screen abstinence until age three was recommended by an expert committee appointed by the French President.

A recent Hungarian expert guideline also recommends avoiding screens before age three.

Despite these recommendations, early screen exposure is widespread. A 2022 meta-analysis included 63 studies and more than 89,000 children.

Only 24.7% of children under two were found to meet the guideline of no screen use.

In the United States, children under two averaged 63 minutes of screen media per day in 2024. These data were reported in the Common Sense Media census. By age two, 40% of children owned their own tablet.

Objective measurements were used in the Australian EUiLO cohort, described by Brushe and colleagues in 2023. A child-worn device recorded electronic noise for 16 hours on a typical day.

Families with lower educational attainment were oversampled among the 207 children. At 24 months, no screen exposure was recorded for only 2.4% of them.

Mean daily exposure in that cohort was 76.1 minutes at 6 months and 148.3 minutes at 24 months.

The Hungarian data were obtained from the Cohort ’18 Growing Up in Hungary panel study. A representative sample was recruited during pregnancy.

Maternal reports for 2,569 children were collected in 2019 and 2020 and analyzed by Kopcsó and colleagues in 2024. The children were aged between 15 and 23 months.

The database was weighted for maternal age, education, parity and marital status.

Daily screen exposure was reported for 49% of the children. More than one hour of exposure on a typical day was recorded for 37.5%. No exposure was reported for 14%.

Among daily users, mean screen time on a typical day was 122.5 minutes.

Most children were cared for at home. Only 6.7% attended formal childcare at the time of the survey.

Television viewing was identified as the most frequent screen activity. It was watched every day by 43.6% of the children.

Videos on mobile devices were watched daily by 21.2% of children. Active touchscreen use on a daily basis was reported for 18.7%.

Higher screen time was observed in lower-income households and among children of less educated mothers. Both gradients were statistically significant in the 2024 analysis.

A similar gradient was reported in a 2024 German study of 3,035 children by Paulus and colleagues. Parents there described using screens when time was short.

The contexts of screen use were also recorded in the Cohort ’18 survey.

Screen use while having fun with the child was reported by 62.1% of mothers.

Screens were allowed during household chores by 53.5%. Use for perceived developmental purposes was reported by 52.8%.

Background television was reported as a regular practice in 31.4% of families. It was rare or absent in 39.1%. The mother’s own relaxation was cited as a reason by 13.9%.

In Hungary, 19.6% of toddlers watched screens during meals, and 12.4% used them while falling asleep.

Children who spent more time with screens were read to and played with slightly less often, even after accounting for family income and mothers’ education.

However, busy parents may have less time for these activities, regardless of screen use.

A 2017 study linked screen use during more daily routines to delays in social and emotional development.

Another study in 2018 found that children who spent less time with screens at age two had better self-control at age four.

Apps and streaming content for babies are often marketed as educational.

A 2021 meta-analysis published in Child Development examined how well young children learn from videos compared with real-life demonstrations. Children aged 0 to 6 were included.

Less learning was found from video than from equivalent live demonstrations, and the gap narrowed with age.

Word learning from video was supported by adult co-viewing in a 2018 study by Strouse and colleagues.

Video chat was examined by Myers and colleagues in 2017 and by McClure and colleagues in 2018. Reciprocal interaction and joint attention cues are preserved in that format.

Screens were used to soothe or distract the child by 43% of Hungarian mothers. Frequent reliance on this strategy may reduce chances to practice self-regulation, the authors wrote.

Reciprocal associations between device use for calming and emotional reactivity were reported in a 2023 JAMA Pediatrics study.

Children aged 3 to 5 were followed. Similar associations were reported by Konok and colleagues at ELTE in 2024.

Autoplay, infinite scrolling and algorithmic recommendations are listed in the review as persuasive design features. Rapid cuts and high visual salience may also place heavy demands on immature attention.

A parent’s phone can interrupt even the simplest moments with a child. In 2018, researchers McDaniel and Radesky used the term technoference to describe these interruptions.

Studies conducted in restaurants and public places in the United States and Israel found that parents paid less attention to their children while using phones.

Some even responded rather sharply when their children sought their attention.

A 2015 study found that just hearing a phone notification was enough to distract someone, even if they ignored it.

Babies seem to notice these interruptions, too. In a 2018 study, infants whose mothers frequently used phones had a harder time returning to a happy mood, even after their mothers put the devices away.

In the French ELFE cohort, mean daily screen time at age two was 49 minutes in 2013, among 12,099 children.

Television exposure during family meals at age two was associated with poorer expressive language.

Less advanced general cognitive development was found at age 3.5, Yang and colleagues reported in 2024. Overall screen time was not the factor identified.

Earth.com has previously covered how a parent’s own phone use relates to vocabulary growth. The role of eye contact in infant language learning has also been reported.

A harm-reduction approach to infant media use was proposed by Heller in Infant Behavior and Development in 2021.

Age-appropriate limits combined with harm-reduction strategies are recommended in the review.

Background and parallel media use during caregiving routines and play should be reduced. Screen exposure during meals and before bedtime should be avoided.

Caregiver co-use is prioritized when screens are introduced in the second or third year.

Information could be provided to expecting parents through obstetric, prenatal and primary care services. Complaints about the no-screens-before-two rule have also been reported by parents.

The European Union has rules to keep children safe online. Article 28 of its Digital Services Act focuses specifically on protecting young users.

On July 14, 2025, the European Commission also issued guidelines addressing features that could make it difficult for children to stop using digital platforms.

However, these measures do not specifically address the needs of babies and toddlers.

The authors argue that keeping children safe from the potential harms of digital media should not be the responsibility of parents alone.

Reducing screen time sounds like a sensible idea, but researchers still have much to learn about its benefits for very young children.

A 2025 review of experiments involving preschoolers found that programs teaching parents about screen habits helped reduce children’s screen use.

Few studies, however, have tested similar approaches in children under two. Even fewer have followed children long enough to see whether their language skills, sleep or ability to manage emotions improved.

Future studies could test whether replacing screen time with play and reading improves language development in children under two.

For young children, what they do after the screen goes off may be just as important as switching it off in the first place.

The review was published in the journal Biologia Futura.

#6375. Phaethon’s fiery folly

Even the best-laid plans can require a bit of luck to execute. During the solar eclipse of Aug. 12, 2026, in which parts of Iceland, Portugal, and Spain experienced totality, much of western Europe enjoyed a substantial partial eclipse. Astrophotographer Alexandre Tournay set up near Brussels to capture the Moon crossing the disk — as well as a transit of another kind.

“I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy. “Against the odds, one did, passing across the partially eclipsed solar disk with its contrail trailing behind it.” Flight tracking data allowed him to pinpoint the flight: Cargolux 5933, a Boeing 747 freighter from Mexico City bound for Luxembourg.

The work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames. That process brings out the roiling details in the Sun’s chromosphere, but would oversharpen the edges of the airplane and Moon. So Tournay blended a 1,000-frame stack of the Sun with a single frame that preserved the silhouettes and froze their motion against the disk.

He named the resulting image “Phaethon’s Flight” after the boy in Greek mythology who journeyed east to prove that his father was Helios, the Sun god. Phaethon convinced Helios to let him drive his Sun-bearing chariot across the sky, but was unable to control the horses. He blazed an erratic path that brought climatic extremes to Earth — freezing cold and scorching heat — before Zeus intervened and struck him down dead.

“There’s something fascinating about being able to photograph, with modern instruments, a celestial phenomenon that our ancestors could only understand and describe through mythology,” says Tournay. “And then, by pure chance, to have a flying machine cross the Sun at that exact moment, almost as though a modern-day chariot were dragging the eclipse behind it across the sky, made the story of Phaethon feel like a perfect fit. Seeing that plane cross the eclipsed Sun, I can almost hear the ancients screaming, ‘See?! I told you it was Phaethon!’ ”

Mark Zastrow is Editor-in-Chief of Astronomy magazine. He holds masters degrees in astronomy and science journalism and has over a decade of experience covering science in the U.S. and in Asia.
