#6373. A new discovery could give the world 12 months to prepare for extreme El Niño and La Niña weather events

Researchers have found the conditions needed to predict some El Niño and La Niña events 12 months ahead of time.

Most El Niño forecasts are only reliable about six months ahead of time. Predicting a full year in advance has long been considered nearly impossible.

That is because the Pacific Ocean becomes so sensitive to tiny shifts in the spring that forecast models easily lose track of what comes next.

Now, researchers have found that certain 12-month El Niño forecasts really do hold up, depending on the state of the Pacific on the day the prediction is made.

Forecasts issued during a La Niña held up a year in advance in all nine climate models an Australian team tested. Forecasts issued when the Pacific was in neither phase did worse than a forecast built from nothing but the historical odds.

For farmers and water managers, that could mean months of extra warning before some El Niños.

Nandini Ramesh of CSIRO, Australia’s national science agency, and UNSW Sydney led the work. Her co-author Mandy Freund is at the University of Melbourne and the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Weather of the 21st Century.

The team graded about 7,500 past forecasts rather than building a new forecasting system. Ramesh said the researchers are still a few steps from applying the findings to agency models.

In an interview with Earth.com, Freund said the accuracy of forecasts that started during a La Niña surprised the team most. Routine checks of forecast performance, she said, often don’t sort forecasts by their starting state.

El Niño, La Niña and the neutral years between them make up a cycle scientists call the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, or ENSO.

“Separating forecasts according to their starting state, we were able to uncover a much clearer picture of when long-range ENSO predictions can be trusted,” she said.

The warm phase of that cycle is El Niño, when the surface of the central and eastern tropical Pacific runs warmer than usual. La Niña is the cool phase. Both tend to peak around December, and both change weather patterns around the world.

A declared El Niño or La Niña can set off drought warnings for farmers and water managers, the authors wrote. It can move the prices of farm commodities and start public health planning.

By one estimate they cite, seasonal forecasts influence companies worth a combined $13 trillion.

The trouble is the spring. From March to May the tropical Pacific is unusually sensitive to small disturbances. A forecast made before those months and aimed at the winter after them loses much of its skill.

Forecasters call this the spring predictability barrier. It is a big part of why predictions beyond about nine months have stayed so difficult.

The team worked from an archive of decade-long climate simulations run by modeling centers in nine countries. Those include the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan and Canada.

These are physics-based models, which simulate the ocean and atmosphere from physical laws rather than past statistics.

The centers started a fresh batch every year from 1961 to around 2020, and the team used the runs that began between October and January.

Rather than judging the simulations on exact temperatures, the researchers asked one question of each: would the following winter land in La Niña, neutral or El Niño?

They sorted every year into one of those three bins using sea surface temperatures in a patch of the central Pacific. The coolest third of years counted as La Niña and the warmest third as El Niño.

Sorting the years that way left about 7,500 one-year forecasts to grade against NOAA‘s record of what the ocean actually did. Then the researchers split the results by which of the three states the Pacific was in when each forecast began.

In every one of the nine models, forecasts that began during a La Niña scored higher than forecasts that began during an El Niño or a neutral year.

Their skill a year out matched what seasonal forecast models manage three to four months ahead, a range forecasters already rely on.

Forecasts that began from a neutral Pacific did the opposite. In every model, they scored below a forecast built from nothing but the historical odds of one state following another.

Inside a single model, the gap between starting points was larger than the gap between the best and worst models.

“The finding that one-year forecasts starting from La Niña perform well in all nine of the models tested suggests there is something about La Niña conditions that makes the tropical Pacific system more predictable over the following year,” Freund said.

Stronger La Niña events were predicted better than weaker ones. For El Niño the pattern was less clear, though badly missed forecasts of strong El Niños were rare.

The team then asked the question a farmer might ask of any forecast: when a model predicts a particular switch, how often does it actually happen?

In one American model, a forecast of El Niño issued during a La Niña came true 82 percent of the time, a year ahead of the event. The same model’s forecast of a La Niña from neutral conditions came true only 9 percent of the time.

Three of the nine models were right more than 70 percent of the time when they predicted a La Niña would give way to an El Niño. Eight of the nine were at their worst predicting a La Niña from a neutral year, a switch that is rare in the real ocean.

And when a model called for an El Niño from neutral conditions, not one beat the historical odds. Those calls are the likeliest false alarms.

Across all starts from neutral, the models were right 23 to 43 percent of the time. A forecast built from the historical odds alone would have been right 61 percent of the time.

Freund told Earth.com that the weakness from neutral starts remains an important caveat. “Unfortunately, starting from a neutral Pacific, the physics-based models often make the wrong predictions,” she said.

“The system can be very sensitive: it is an example of what is known as the ‘butterfly effect’ where very small disturbances can be amplified over time into huge changes in a system’s behavior.”

Asked by Earth.com what farmers and water managers should take from the result, Freund said the study is encouraging.

Those are people, she said, who rely on knowing about an El Niño much further ahead than forecasts now allow. When a La Niña is under way, a forecast for the following year can be trusted more.

“This gives farmers, water managers and other decision-makers valuable extra time to prepare, including decisions about which crops and seed varieties to plant or how to manage water resources,” she said.

The method itself is simple, Freund said, and would not take much for forecasting agencies to consider. “It could provide this extra layer of confidence we can lay on certain predictions of ENSO,” she said.

The researchers also tested two-year forecasts, and for almost every kind of switch those were wrong more often than right.

The one exception came after an El Niño, when every model did better than the historical odds at saying there would be no El Niño for the next two years. Long stretches without an El Niño have been linked to multi-year droughts across the subtropics.

Why a La Niña makes the following year easier to predict is the open question. The team offered three possibilities.

A La Niña’s cool water tends to linger into spring instead of fading in February or March the way an El Niño’s warmth does. Earlier studies also found fewer random atmospheric disturbances during a La Niña.

And a La Niña is when the upper tropical Pacific refills with warm water, so the state of that reservoir may carry a lot of information about what comes next.

The authors set aside long-term warming trends, slow decade-scale swings in the Pacific and the differences between one El Niño and another.

They also didn’t test the statistical and machine learning methods they suspect would do better from a neutral start. Those methods work from past patterns instead of from today’s conditions. Whether the La Niña advantage holds in the models agencies actually run each season hasn’t been tested.

The team’s next step is to work out which of the three explanations is doing the work. The confidence check it proposes can be run on any model from the forecasts it has already made.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

A stunning new image from the Gemini North telescope captures two spiral galaxies caught in each other's gravity, helping to trigger the birth of new stars.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What it is: NGC 7253 (also called Arp 278), a pair of interacting spiral galaxies

Where it is: 200 million light-years away, in the constellation Pegasus

Picture a spiral galaxy, and you'll probably imagine a swirl of stars. But some galaxies appear to be the complete opposite. One is NGC 7253, which looks more like a bizarre balloon animal than a cosmic coil. In reality, it's two spiral galaxies caught in each other's gravity. As shown in this recent image from the Gemini North telescope on Mauna Kea in Hawaii, the galaxies' once-ordered shapes are being disturbed and disrupted as their mutual gravitational pull stretches and distorts their spiral arms into a tangled arrangement of stars, gas and dust. It sounds and looks chaotic and destructive, but encounters between galaxies don't mean stars are physically colliding; the distances between individual stars are too great. Instead, something extraordinarily productive can happen.

Spiral galaxies contain huge clouds of cold gas and dust, particularly within their arms. When galaxies interact, gravitational forces can disturb and compress those clouds. If enough material is squeezed together and becomes dense enough to collapse under its own gravity, it can produce bursts of new star formation.

Evidence of just that can be seen in this image. Scattered through the galaxies are concentrations of bright pink light. These are H II regions — enormous clouds of hydrogen gas energized by intense ultraviolet radiation from hot, young stars.

The gravitational encounter is rearranging two structures containing billions of stars while simultaneously helping to create new ones. These interactions radically alter the shapes of the galaxies involved and, in time, can ultimately cause them to merge into a single galaxy. For now, NGC 7253 is listed as Arp 278 in the Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies, a catalog of galaxies that are neither perfectly symmetrical spirals nor smooth, spherical ellipticals.

The new image has another story much closer to Earth. It's just been given the Hawaiian name Nā 'Uhane Māhoe Huki Pū i ke Ola, meaning "The Twin Spirits Pulling Together Creating Life." Hawaii high school students participating in the 2026 Project Hōkūlani internship program chose the name. One reason was its position within Ka Lupe o Kawelo, the Hawaiian constellation corresponding to Pegasus.

The "twin spirits" represent both the two galaxies and the twin telescopes of the Gemini Observatory — one in Hawaii and the other in Chile.

#6371. A remote island in New Zealand was supposed to be a safe haven for wildlife

A remote island off New Zealand’s coast reveals the challenges of protecting native birds from invasive predators.

Today’s Image of the Day from NASA Earth Observatory features Resolution Island, a remote expanse of wilderness off the southwestern coast of New Zealand.

Surrounded by deep blue waters and covered in dense vegetation, the island appears to be an ideal sanctuary for wildlife.

Its isolation, however, has not always offered the protection that conservationists envisioned.

For more than a century, Resolution Island has been at the center of an ambitious effort to preserve some of New Zealand’s most extraordinary native birds.

Its history reveals both the potential and the limitations of using islands as natural barriers against invasive species.

The image was captured on December 12, 2025, by the Operational Land Imager aboard the Landsat 9 satellite.

Resolution Island lies within Fiordland National Park, a spectacular region of mountains, forests, waterfalls, and narrow waterways that extend deep into the southwestern coast of New Zealand’s South Island.

During past ice ages, enormous glaciers moved through the region, gradually carving deep valleys into the landscape.

As the glaciers retreated and sea levels rose, ocean water flooded many of these valleys, creating the dramatic fjords visible today.

Resolution Island is the largest island within the national park. Its mountainous terrain reaches an elevation of 3,507 feet at the summit of Mount Clerke.

The island’s varied landscape supports wetlands, ancient evergreen forests, and high-elevation grasslands. These distinct environments provide a range of habitats for native wildlife.

New Zealand’s long geographical isolation allowed wildlife to evolve in remarkable ways.

Before humans arrived, the country had virtually no native land mammals other than bats. Birds occupied many ecological niches that mammals filled elsewhere in the world.

Some species gradually lost the ability to fly, while others developed behaviors that left them particularly vulnerable to ground-dwelling predators.

Among them were kiwi, which forage along the forest floor, and kākāpō, the world’s only flightless parrot.

For millions of years, these birds survived without facing the kinds of mammalian predators found on other continents.

That evolutionary advantage became a liability when people introduced unfamiliar animals into New Zealand’s ecosystems.

Rats, cats, and members of the weasel family brought new pressures that native birds were poorly equipped to withstand.

By the nineteenth century, the decline of New Zealand’s native wildlife was becoming increasingly apparent.

European settlers had introduced stoats and other predators in an attempt to control rabbit populations. Instead, these animals created another ecological problem by preying on vulnerable native species.

In 1872, conservationist Thomas Henry Potts suggested that Resolution Island could provide a refuge for birds threatened by introduced predators.

The surrounding ocean appeared to offer a natural protective barrier, allowing native species to survive without the dangers they faced on the mainland.

Resolution Island became a protected reserve in 1891, making it part of a pioneering chapter in New Zealand’s conservation history.

Long before modern wildlife restoration programs existed, naturalists were experimenting with ideas that would eventually become central to endangered species management.

One of the most dedicated figures in this undertaking was Richard Henry, who became the island’s caretaker.

Henry recognized the urgency of protecting birds that were rapidly disappearing from other parts of the country.

Working in an isolated and physically demanding environment, he transported hundreds of native birds across the waters of Fiordland.

More than 700 birds, primarily kiwi and kākāpō, were relocated to Resolution Island and neighboring islands during his conservation efforts.

Much of the work involved traveling by rowboat through a region known for challenging weather and rugged terrain.

Henry’s efforts represented an early attempt to prevent extinction by establishing wildlife populations in geographically isolated locations.

Unfortunately, the assumption that the surrounding waters would keep predators away proved incorrect.

By 1900, invasive predators had been detected on Resolution Island. Stoats were capable of swimming across the channels that separated the island from nearby land.

The discovery undermined years of painstaking conservation work and exposed a weakness in the island’s natural defenses.

Stoats are highly adaptable hunters. Their ability to exploit different environments makes them particularly problematic in New Zealand, where many native birds nest on or near the ground.

Henry attempted to control the invading predators through trapping but eventually left the island to pursue conservation work elsewhere.

His experience demonstrated that geographical isolation alone was not necessarily enough to protect vulnerable species.

More than a century later, conservationists continue to build on Henry’s original vision.

In 2008, New Zealand’s Department of Conservation launched a predator management program on Resolution Island to improve the prospects of native wildlife.

Maintaining such a program across a large, mountainous island presents considerable challenges.

Dense forests, steep slopes, and remote locations complicate efforts to monitor wildlife and control invasive animals.

Conservation also extends into the surrounding waters, where a marine reserve protects coastal ecosystems near the island’s distinctive Five Fingers Peninsula.

Viewed from space, Resolution Island offers a striking portrait of an apparently untouched wilderness.

Yet beneath its forest canopy lies a complex ecological history shaped by human intervention, invasive species, and generations of conservation work.

The island remains a powerful reminder that protecting nature sometimes requires far more than simply setting it aside.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/ Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey

#6370. The Sky Today on Wednesday, November 25: Uranus at opposition

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 24: A Super Beaver Moon occults the Pleiades

The distant ice giant Uranus reaches opposition tonight at 6 P.M. EST. Opposition is the best time to view a planet in our sky, and it’s visible roughly from dusk until dawn. Because Uranus is faint — magnitude 5.6 — you’ll want to give it a few hours after sunset to climb away from both light pollution and turbulent air near the horizon. Around 10 P.M. local time, you’ll find Uranus midway between the bright star Aldebaran and the Pleiades star cluster in Taurus the Bull, about 60° above the southeastern horizon. It sits some 1.5° south of 4th-magnitude 37 Tauri.

Although Uranus can be visible to the naked eye under clear, dark conditions, the bright waning Moon is nearby, so pull out binoculars or a telescope to view the far-off planet tonight. Once you land on its location, look for a “flat,” grayish-colored star. Uranus’ disk spans 4”, so you will likely be able to tell it is circular, rather than a pinpoint of light like any background stars.

#6369. What makes a hug truly memorable has a lot to do with empathy and how you handle relationships

A survey of 15,049 adults shows most people remember hugs for comfort and support. Empathy, attachment patterns, and hugging habits also play a role.

We tend to think of a hug as a universal source of warmth, yet nearly three in ten adults in a large survey could not recall one that had left a positive mark.

When a hug did stick in someone’s memory, it was much more likely to be for comfort, support, or understanding than for romance.

Whether someone could remember a hug at all came down to a few key traits. The top three were how much empathy they felt, how they handled closeness, and whether they usually hugged their friends hello.

Anna Lena Dueren of the University of Bristol‘s School of Psychological Science led the analysis of 15,049 adults in the U.K. Their answers came from the Touch Test, a national survey on touch that BBC Radio 4 promoted in early 2020.

The study is a snapshot of who remembers what. It can show which traits go together with a hug memory, not what causes one.

In an interview with Earth.com, Dueren put the main finding simply. “Most participants remembered hugs because they conveyed comfort, understanding, or support,” she said.

To her knowledge, she added, it’s the first large study to ask people why a hug stayed with them.

The question was plain: is there a hug you remember because of its positive emotional effect on you? Of the 15,046 people who answered, 10,457 said yes, or 69.5 percent.

People who said yes then picked the single best reason from a short list. Among the 9,703 who chose a listed reason, about a third picked comfort, 29 percent said the hug conveyed understanding, and 20 percent said support.

Comfort, understanding, and support together cover more than four in five of the hugs people kept. Just 147 people, or 1.5 percent of the group, said the hug was memorable because it was physically arousing.

Earlier studies had linked daily hugs to lower stress and better mood, and these answers fit.

Men and women were about equally likely to remember a hug at all. The reasons they gave, though, differed in a small but consistent way.

Among men, 3.9 percent chose arousal as the reason, compared with 0.8 percent of women. Men were also more likely to pick friendliness, 12.3 percent, in comparison to 4.8 percent of women.

Women chose comfort more often, at 34.6 percent to men’s 25.3 percent, and understanding more often too. The team suggested that the nurturing side of a hug may count for more among women.

Dueren’s team noted that only 2,197 men gave a reason, against 7,506 women, so they advise reading the gender differences with caution.

Dueren’s team, which includes researchers at UCL, the University of Sussex, and the University of Greenwich, then checked which traits went with keeping an emotional memory of a hug.

The strongest link was a habit: people who always greet friends and family with a hug were more likely to recall one.

Disliking the feel of being hugged went the other way, and so did finding it hard to know how firmly to hug someone. Asked by Earth.com what someone who dislikes hugging might take from the work, Dueren pointed to the size of the gap.

“In our study, people who disliked the feeling of being hugged were slightly less likely to recall a hug that had a positive emotional effect on them than those who did not dislike it,” she said. “The findings highlight that hugging experiences are not equally remembered by everyone.”

Empathy mattered too, whether measured as reading other people’s feelings or as feeling them alongside someone. Higher scores went with higher odds of remembering a hug.

So did attachment style, how a person relates to those closest to them. Insecure attachment comes in two forms.

People who feel distress at separation, the anxious form, were more likely to hold a hug in memory. People who prize independence in relationships, the avoidant form, were less likely to.

All of these effects were small, and together the traits explained only 10 to 14 percent of the variation in who remembered a hug.

Dueren’s team expected that people who are less satisfied with their bodies would be more likely to remember a hug for the comfort or support it gave. That expectation failed.

A person’s satisfaction with their own body did not influence whether they remembered a hug, or why. However, there was a measure that did.

The team built a five-item scale of how much a person’s sense of their body runs through touch. One item asked whether they choose clothes partly for how the fabric feels on the skin.

People who scored higher on it were more likely to remember a hug, and to remember it for understanding or arousal rather than comfort. The scale is new, and the team called those results preliminary.

Being tucked in with a hug and a kiss as a child had no bearing on whether a person remembered a hug. Neither did how often that person gets hugged day to day.

The people who answered chose to take part and were not paid, so they may care about touch more than average. Three-quarters were women, and all lived in the U.K., where attitudes to touch differ from those elsewhere.

The survey didn’t ask who gave the remembered hug or where it happened, so it can’t say whether comfort from a partner is remembered differently from comfort given by a friend.

Answers were collected between January and March 2020, and fewer than 1 percent arrived after the U.K.’s first lockdown began. So this is a record of hugging before the pandemic changed it.

Dueren told Earth.com that she wants to pursue why the same hug feels so different to different people. “The same type of touch can feel pleasant for one person and uncomfortable to another,” she said. “I would like to better understand factors that contribute to these differences in experience.”

Empathetic people may store up hugs, or memorable hugs may make people more empathetic, and this survey can’t tell which. Settling that would mean following the same people over years, and that study has not yet been run.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS One.

#6368. A Train Carrying Deadly Materials Was on Fire for Nearly an Hour as It Barreled Toward a Small Town. Why Didn’t Anyone Stop It?

A small sensor failed to do its job—leading to one of the worst train wrecks in American history.

Editor’s note: In July 2024, after this story was published, the National Transportation Safety Board released its final analysis on the Norfolk Southern freight train derailment in East Palestine, Ohio. It also released a companion illustrated digest of the incident. The analysis determined that the train derailed after an overheated wheel bearing caused an axel to “burn off.” The punctured DOT-111 tank car leaked butyl acrylates, which are flammable and likely started the post-derailment fires. Further, the decision to intentionally “vent and burn” vinyl chloride tank cars was likely unnecessary and based on incomplete or misleading information, according to the report. The NTSB issued 34 new safety recommendations covering several needs, including defect detection systems, tank car standards, hazardous materials, and emergency response procedures.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

On the frigid evening of Friday, February 3, 2023, at around 8:50 p.m., a Norfolk Southern freight train measuring more than a mile and three quarters long snaked its way through the town of East Palestine, Ohio. The train consisted of 149 cars, pulled by three locomotives—two at the front, one in the middle—and traveled just under 50 miles per hour. Of those 149 cars, 20 were tankers labeled with hazardous-materials placards. Several of the tankers contained liquefied vinyl chloride gas, the combustible and carcinogenic precursor material for PVC pipe; others contained ethylene glycol, a toxic ingredient in antifreeze. Driving the lead locomotive was Tony Faison, the train’s engineer; with him were the train’s conductor and a trainee.

Engineers chart their progress by designated mile markers along the track. About 20 minutes earlier, the train had crossed mile marker 69.0, just east of Salem, Ohio. While crossing that spot, an infrared sensor built into the track called a “hotbox detector” had reported elevated temperatures on one of the front axles of the 23rd railcar. The ambient temperature that night was 10 degrees Fahrenheit. The bearings on the axle had reached an abnormally hot temperature of 103. The car, a hopper designed to hold commodities like grain, wasn’t carrying hazardous materials, but the hotbox detector relayed an alert to Norfolk Southern’s Atlanta command center all the same. No further action was taken.

As the train left East Palestine, it approached Ohio’s border with Pennsylvania, passing within a few hundred feet of the State Line Tavern, a local watering hole. There, at 8:55 p.m., it crossed mile marker 49.8. As the twenty-third car crossed the next hotbox detector, the infrared sensors revealed that the temperature of the axle’s bearings had risen sharply, to over 250 degrees. Faison immediately received an audio message from the locomotive’s onboard computer to stop the train. He reacted quickly to apply the brakes, but it was too late. He didn’t know it, but for the previous 40 minutes, his train had been on fire.

The train took more than a thousand feet to come to a stop. As it did, the compromised axle gave way. The left-side journal box, which held the axle in place, broke off and landed on one side of the track; the wheelset, consisting of the axle with two steel wheels mounted at both ends, ended up on the other. The twenty-third car jumped the rail, and the cars behind it followed suit, creating a tremendous series of crashes that could be heard throughout town. Thirty-eight railcars piled up, including 11 of the hazmat tankers.

Faison leaped from the locomotive to inspect the damage. From his standpoint at the front of the train, he could see flames rising into the night. He immediately contacted 911. So did many of the town’s residents, reporting both the train crash and the fire. One thought a gas station had exploded.

In the next few hours, the toxic flames would force an evacuation of the town. The specter of chemical poisoning lingered over East Palestine for months. And even today, the question of how a system of detectors—expressly designed to prevent this kind of derailment—failed to notice a dangerously overheated train axle remains unanswered.

In the minutes after the derailment, first responders rushed to the blaze, but they were initially underequipped. Serving a town of fewer than five thousand people, the East Palestine fire department was a mostly volunteer force. The sole professional on staff was Chief Keith Drabick, who on that night was almost three hundred miles away, driving through Pennsylvania on vacation. Informed of the crash at 9 p.m., Drabick turned his car around and drove straight back to East Palestine, but he didn’t arrive until five hours later. For the first few minutes, volunteers had to fight the blaze alone. Meanwhile, following protocol, Faison cut the first two locomotives from the train and moved them a mile down the track. In the confusion that followed, some firefighters seemed unaware they were responding to a hazmat site and reported to residents that the burning train cars were carrying only malt liquor.

Some of the train cars were carrying malt liquor, but others contained stronger stuff. As the scope of the disaster slowly became clear, the volunteers were joined by professional firefighting crews from nearby counties, including a special hazmat squad. At 9:45 p.m., concerned about the risks of a vinyl chloride explosion as well as the toxic cocktail of flaming chemicals escaping into the night, officials began evacuating nearby homes. Meanwhile, some of the contents of the leaking tankers began seeping into nearby Sulphur Run, a stream that flowed directly from the crash site through the center of town.

Even before the official order, citizens had started to evacuate. East Palestine resident Jami Wallace had learned of the train wreck from her mother. Wallace, a human resources manager in her forties, had recently gotten engaged. She called her fiancé, who was with a friend at the State Line Tavern. Driving past the burning crash site, he raced home to collect Wallace and their three-year-old daughter. “Grabbed her a couple of changes of clothes and out the door we went,” she told me. “We didn’t even know where we were going. It was the middle of winter and the heater was broken in the car.”

After an hour and a half of firefighting, the Ohio State Police expanded the evacuation zone to one mile surrounding the derailment site. Around midnight, still fearing an explosion, the firefighters retreated. They then began to survey the crash site with aerial drones, in an attempt to determine which specific chemicals were leaking. The survey was challenging: The site was, well, a train wreck, and some of the plastic hazardous-materials placards had melted in the fire.

Eventually, responders determined that three hazmat cars had been physically breached. One contained ethylene glycol, the antifreeze ingredient, which can be lethal in concentrated doses. The other two contained acrylates, used as base ingredients in adhesives and paint. All three materials were burning off, releasing volatile organic compounds into the air. The fire was additionally fueled by nonhazardous but flammable railcar cargo, including several tankers loaded with petroleum lubricants. For days to come, an ominous toxic cloud hung suspended over the site. “You know how smoke, like, moves through the sky? Yeah, this wasn’t moving anywhere,” Wallace said. “It was almost like a green cloud that was, like, hovering.”

Initially, none of the vinyl chloride tankers were breached. (If they had been, a series of explosions might have occurred, and the cancer-causing chemical could have rained down on the town.) Still, five vinyl chloride tankers, containing more than 115,000 gallons of vinyl chloride in total, had piled up in the burn zone. Each tanker had an emergency pressure release valve designed to vent gas into the atmosphere. Over the next few days, as temperatures rose inside the tanks, these valves automatically opened and closed, periodically releasing excess vinyl chloride gas into the air—where it immediately caught fire. In one extraordinary display on the evening of Saturday, February 4, one of the tanker valves vented for 70 continuous minutes, creating a spectacular flamethrower.

With the crash site cordoned off and the tankers burping flames, officials deliberated on what to do. One worry was that the release valves on the tankers were starting to suffer thermal damage. Another was that the vinyl chloride inside the tanks might “polymerize,” forming into chains of PVC, which might cause the valves to stick, sealing the pressure in and causing the tankers to blow.

From the outside, the hazmat experts couldn’t be sure if polymerization was occurring. Eventually they settled on two options. One option was to deliberately puncture the tanks and conduct a controlled burn of the vinyl chloride gas. The other option was to wait it out and hope the tanks cooled down enough so they wouldn’t explode. Chief Drabick was presented with this devil’s bargain: Wait, and potentially watch the exploding tanks rain shrapnel and poisonous chemicals on his town, or release mass quantities of vinyl chloride—a known Group A carcinogen—into the atmosphere. “I was given 13 minutes to make a decision,” Drabick told investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), the federal agency responsible for investigating the wreck.

After consulting with his chief officers, Drabick chose to vent and burn. Following an expanded evacuation order, specialists attached explosive charges to the exteriors of five damaged tanker cars. At 4:37 p.m. on February 6, the charges were detonated, sending twin columns of flaming vinyl chloride gas high into the air and obscuring the setting sun with thick, black smoke. The burn continued through the following day; it was not until February 8, five days after the axle on train car 23 had first started to burn, that the fire was fully put out.

East Palestine soon found itself host to another kind of toxic cocktail, one consisting of corporate communications specialists, blustering public officials, government bureaucrats, and enterprising class-action attorneys. Complementing this splendid company were the more respectable representatives of the NTSB. Leading the agency’s efforts was Ruben Payan, an NTSB veteran with a heavy build, a thick mustache, and a calm and measured voice. Under his patient command, the NTSB began a thorough investigation of the crash site and the events leading up to the derailment.

The agency published the first investigation update to its website in March 2023. And then on June 22, Payan presented his preliminary results at a public meeting in East Palestine. (It was the first onsite NTSB meeting in six years.) Using security camera footage collected from homes and businesses adjacent to the tracks, Payan was able to present a detailed videography of the train’s final minutes. Between the towns of Sebring and East Palestine, more than a dozen surveillance cameras had captured the train in motion; in ten of those camera feeds, the train was plainly on fire. In true-color camera feeds, the lower axle of the twenty-third car glowed a dull orange color; in infrared camera feeds, it blazed an intense white, throwing visible sparks.

The first two cameras to show the fire were in Salem, Ohio, some 26 miles west of East Palestine. The train passed the first camera at 8:11 p.m., 44 minutes before the derailment. That camera, which overlooked an alley of snow-covered cars, caught the train in the far background, its axle glowing orange. The camera was located six miles in front of the Salem hotbox detector—the one that had sent an alert to Atlanta but did not stop the train.

How had the Salem hotbox detector missed the fire? The cameras clearly showed flames and sparks along the length of the bottom of the twenty-third car, but when that same car crossed the hotbox detector 10 minutes later, infrared sensors registered the bearing temperatures at only 103 degrees. This wasn’t a case of a sputtering fire that started and stopped, either—the cameras along the route showed a steady blaze. The NTSB declined to comment for this story, citing the pending results of the final investigation. Norfolk Southern declined to comment as well.

I put the question to David Farwick, a veteran engineer who commanded trains in Ohio for Norfolk Southern for nearly 40 years. He told me that Norfolk Southern’s systems were well maintained and up to date. “Those hotbox detectors, they’re pretty sensitive,” he said. “It’s not like we were working with 1960s stuff. They were pretty good.” The detectors are positioned among the crossties on the track and use infrared sensors to scan the undercarriage of the train. More than 6,000 are deployed across North America. The sensors on the hotbox detectors line up directly with the roller bearings. Farwick seemed flabbergasted that a flaming train had crossed a detector and not tripped an immediate brake alert. “It blows my mind,” he said.

Regulators have also grown concerned in recent years about how long the trains are getting. Farwick told me trains are growing so long that engineers have trouble seeing the backs of them, even on a curve. I asked him whether the train crew would have known they were carrying hazardous materials. “Absolutely,” he said. Farwick explained that the conductor on each train carries a bound paper manifest of the train’s cargo known as a “consist.” In the event of a derailment or crash, a hard copy of this consist is to be immediately delivered to first responders. But Drabick, when questioned by NTSB investigators, said his firefighters never received the consist directly from the Norfolk Southern train crew: “I do not believe that we had any contact with those individuals,” he said. Drabick was only fully informed of the train’s hazardous contents when he arrived on site hours later.

The other looming question about the crash involves the degree of environmental poisoning East Palestine has suffered. In the months following the vent and burn of vinyl chloride gas, Environmental Protection Agency personnel repeatedly visited the town and surrounding areas to take soil samples. Per the EPA’s website, “the sample results indicate that impacts from the smoke and soot were minimal.” The EPA has also monitored the health of the town’s waterways. In the aftermath of the disaster, the agency recorded more than 40,000 dead fish and aquatic animals in the Sulphur Run creek adjacent to the derailment and burn site. While the agency claims that the creek “has not shown any contaminants at levels that exceed health standards since May 1,” it continues to maintain “Keep Out” signs posted around Sulphur Run.

East Palestine is immediately downstream of the crash site, and many local residents believe the creek has delivered poison into their homes. Two days after the derailment, Wallace returned to her evacuated residence to pick up some medication. “As soon as I pulled into my driveway, it hit me in the face—I started coughing ... until, like, I can’t breathe,” she said. “I look over because I know it’s the creek. I look over, and I see these chemicals free-floating down.”

Wallace told me water from the creek regularly seeps into the basement of her residence, and that she has since relocated. She has pushed for the EPA to start indoor monitoring in East Palestine homes; so far, the agency has declined. In any case, the damages Norfolk Southern owes the town are substantial. In June, Norfolk Southern announced that cleanup costs and injury compensation settlements related to East Palestine would cost the company nearly $1 billion, though it anticipated that much of that cost would be covered by insurance.

In a statement a couple of weeks after the crash, Jennifer Homendy, the chair of the NTSB, described the accident as “100 percent preventable,” but didn’t offer specifics. She was likely referring to the “hot axle” phenomenon. Train axles use ring-shaped bearings that keep the axle secure while permitting it and the wheels to rotate. A skateboard’s wheels rotate using lubricated ball bearings inside the wheels. Train cars instead use cylindrical roller bearings, which make contact with the axle, permitting easy rotation.

As of December 2023, the NTSB has not yet made a final determination, but multiple experts I talked with told me that they believed a failed roller bearing was the most likely cause of the East Palestine derailment. About two dozen trains derail this way in North America every year. Bearings can fail for any number of reasons, including insufficient lubrication, contamination, overloading, and, simply, age. Once a bearing fails, the axle begins to grind against the metal, and this friction causes a rapid rise in temperature; this was potentially the source of the fire. “Bearings do break down, but that’s the reason why you get these detectors, right?” Farwick said. “That’s exactly what these things are supposed to prevent.”

The roller bearings on train axles are sealed inside the wheel and can’t readily be accessed. A faulty one can easily escape visual detection. Hotbox detectors, by using infrared temperature sensors to monitor the bearings in motion, offer a second layer of protection. Generally speaking, they work. Since the early 1980s, train derailments in North America have fallen from more than 7,000 annually to just over 1,000, in part because of hotbox detectors.

The place to catch the failed roller bearing was not in East Palestine, but 20 miles west, in Salem, Ohio, where the train had crossed a detector 30 minutes before the derailment. That detector had recorded temperatures 93 degrees above the outside environment and sent a noncritical signal to Norfolk Southern central command in Atlanta. Whether dispatchers in Atlanta relayed this warning to the train crew remains unclear; the NTSB has yet to publish transcripts from the train’s black box recorder, and Norfolk Southern has refused to discuss the details of the accident.

Perhaps it is worth noting that in the days before the derailment, the East Palestine train had already been delayed twice by stops for unrelated mechanical issues.

In March, the NTSB opened a probe into Norfolk Southern’s safety culture. Regulators were concerned not only by the East Palestine derailment, but also two other Ohio derailments in the surrounding months, as well as separate incidents in which three railroad workers on Norfolk Southern lines were killed in a span of 16 months, starting in December of 2021. In a statement announcing the investigation, the NTSB urged Norfolk Southern “to take immediate action today to review and assess its safety practices.”

This October, Norfolk Southern unveiled a new layer of protection: giant metal sheds, festooned with cameras, that each train will pass through at various points on its journey. The shed is described as a “portal,” and its cameras take an average of 1,000 images per railcar, and send those images to an A.I. data center. Deep-learning algorithms are then employed to spot problems that track detectors and overworked railcar mechanics cannot.

Following the derailment, legislators introduced the bipartisan Railway Safety Act of 2023, which proposed decreasing the required distance between hotbox detectors to 15 miles, from an average of 25 miles today. The legislation is well intended, but it’s not clear if it would have prevented the East Palestine derailment: On that track, the hotbox detectors were an average of 16.7 miles apart. Closing the distance to 15 miles wouldn’t necessarily help.

The most striking revelation from the NTSB’s preliminary findings was the sheer number of camera feeds that had captured the train car on fire. It costs about $200,000 to install a hotbox detector, and critics have estimated the cost of compliance for the Railway Safety Act at up to $2 billion. Perhaps wireless video cameras could permit dispatchers and AI to regularly monitor the status of the cars, and would give engineers better visibility to the back of the trains.

Finally, there’s still the problem of the toxic derailment site. It remains a hazard zone, and the nearby State Line Tavern remains closed. Under the guidance of the EPA, much of the topsoil near ground zero was excavated. The soil was supposed to be shipped to a hazardous waste facility in Oklahoma, but that state’s governor, Kevin Stitt, blocked the plan in March. Similarly, the contaminated water from Sulphur Run was drained. The water was supposed to be sent to a treatment facility in Baltimore, but that fell through too.

For a while, the poisoned water and soil remained at the derailment site. “They have these big Shamu tanks,” Wallace said. “They each hold, like, 100 million gallons of water.” Wallace said a neighbor had flown a drone over the tanks, and seen the chemical sheen on top. Nearby, the toxic dirt was piled into giant mounds, and covered with tarps.

However, as of January 2026, the EPA reported that personnel had completed a “site-wide cleanup and restoration,” in which crews cleaned the remaining oily sheens from nearby waterways such as Leslie and Sulphur Runs, and removed more than 38 million gallons of wastewater. They also removed any remaining contaminated soil and debris for treatment or disposal, and completed the derailment site excavation. The EPA is now sampling groundwater, surface water, and drinking water quarterly and will continue monitoring the area. Comprehensive updates of the work are available at the EPA’s website.

#6367. Nov. 25, 1783: The birth of Claude-Louis Mathieu

Born in Macon, France, on Nov. 25, 1783, Claude-Louis Mathieu showed an aptitude for mathematics from a young age. Despite his family’s poverty and his father’s wish for him to be a carpenter, Mathieu moved to Paris in 1801 to study for admission to the prestigious Ecole Polytechnique. He became a student at Ecole Polytechnique two years later and graduated from the school in 1805.

A varied career in astronomy followed, during which Mathieu served as secretary, assistant to the director, and later astronomer at the Paris Observatory, conducting research focused on calculating stars’ parallaxes and determining stellar distances. He also became a professor of astronomy at the College de France, a writer and editor, and a driving force behind the adoption of the metric system in France. Mathieu was elected president of the International Metre Commission in 1870 although he was in his late 80s, and continued to work in that position into his 90s.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6366. Millions of Americans use a form of birth control that surveys have overlooked

More Americans use menstrual cycle tracking to avoid pregnancy than surveys suggested, with use rising in some states.

Tracking the menstrual cycle to avoid pregnancy may be far more common than scientists once believed. Based on national surveys conducted over the years, only a small share of Americans were thought to rely on it.

Around 7% to 8% of US birth control users aged 18 to 44 tracked their cycles in 2022 and 2023. That share nearly doubled by 2026 in three Western states.

Its popularity has also been underestimated because of the way most surveys count birth control users.

The study was led by Chelsea Polis, a principal research scientist at the Guttmacher Institute.

She worked with Rebecca Simmons, a research associate professor of obstetrics and gynecology at University of Utah Health.

No new information was gathered for the project. Data from four large surveys were reanalyzed instead.

Cycle tracking for pregnancy prevention falls under a category of contraception known as fertility awareness-based methods (FABMs).

“I hope that these results are a shock to the family planning community,” Simmons said.

“There’s been a lot more acceptance of FABMs as legitimate methods over time, but most people still aren’t putting them on their radar enough for how important they are in the cultural milieu.”

“This is a really important thing that I’m hoping that people will sit up and pay attention to right now.”

Pregnancy is possible on only six to nine days of each menstrual cycle. These days fall around ovulation, when an egg is released by an ovary.

Some people count days on a calendar to work out when they are fertile. Others check their temperature every morning, and some watch for changes in cervical mucus. A smartphone app is used by some.

To avoid pregnancy, they skip sex on fertile days or use condoms as a backup. People who are trying to conceive can use the same information.

More than a dozen fertility awareness-based methods exist, but they don’t all work equally well.

“FABMs are a method class,” Simmons said.

“They’re not a single method. Within that method class, some of those methods, like the rhythm method, are not very effective, and some are actually comparable to the effectiveness of short-acting methods like pills or patches.”

Two of the surveys covered the whole country. One was the 2022–2023 National Survey of Family Growth. The other was a 2022 survey on access to birth control.

The other two were limited to six states between them. One was conducted in Arizona, New Jersey and Wisconsin. The Mountain West Sexual and Reproductive Health Survey was carried out in Idaho, Nevada and Utah.

Each survey recruited its participants in its own way. The time frame for current use also varied from the month of the interview to the previous three months.

Despite these differences, the four estimates for 2022 and 2023 fell within a narrow band of 6.6% to 8.3%.

The federal survey alone suggests that more than 2.2 million people in the US use these methods.

“Fertility awareness-based methods are used by a meaningful share of US contraceptive users,” Polis said.

“Although many clinicians do not receive robust training on FABMs, our data show that FABMs are more frequently used than several other contraceptive methods that clinicians are routinely trained to provide.”

Gaps in knowledge about birth control are nothing new. Earlier research found that many healthcare providers don’t offer self-injected birth control either.

Picture a woman who keeps track of her cycle and relies on condoms during her fertile days. A national survey would most likely record her as a condom user.

That happens because each person is usually assigned the most effective method they mention. Cycle tracking is ranked low on that scale and is therefore easily missed.

Such combined users made up about a quarter of cycle trackers in three surveys. In the fourth, they were close to half.

When they were added back into the federal survey, the estimate went from 4.3% to 6.6%. The standard approach had overlooked about a third of the people who track their cycles.

People who paired tracking with the pill, an IUD, an implant or sterilization were not counted. They accounted for about one in five cycle trackers, compared with roughly 9% in a 2013 to 2015 analysis.

Several of those methods prevent ovulation entirely. In that case tracking offers almost no extra protection, and the researchers suggested that some users may not realize it.

Cycle tracking appears to be gaining ground, at least in some parts of the country.

Between 2019–2020 and 2022–2023, its use in Arizona, New Jersey and Wisconsin increased from 5% to 6.9%.

A sharper rise was recorded in Idaho, Nevada and Utah. There, the share of birth control users who tracked their cycles stood at 7.5% in December 2022. It had grown to 12.5% by June 2024 and then to 14.5% by January 2026.

Most of this growth came in the first 18 months. The later increase was small enough that it could have been due to chance.

Is the same trend playing out nationwide? That question can’t be answered yet. Because the federal survey has since been redesigned, its latest results cannot be compared reliably with earlier rounds.

Several factors could be involved, according to Simmons. Concerns about hormonal birth control may be one.

The popularity of tracking apps and difficulty getting other contraceptives may be others. None of these reasons was examined in the study.

Social media could be adding to the trend as well. Earlier studies of popular TikTok videos about birth control found cycle tracking was discussed more than any other method.

Among cycle trackers in the federal survey, 63% were married. Only 45% of people using other methods were.

The gap in Arizona, New Jersey and Wisconsin looked much the same, at 60% versus 43%.

Cycle tracking only works when both partners cooperate. Couples in steady relationships may find it easier to decide together when sex should be avoided or a condom used.

A link between relationship commitment and the birth control choices of young adults has been reported before as well.

Some surveys pointed to a role for education too. In Arizona, New Jersey and Wisconsin, 55% of cycle trackers had a college degree. Among other birth control users, the figure was 42%.

No consistent link with religion was found. Cycle tracking therefore cannot be explained simply as a religious practice.

Adults aged 25 to 34 were the most likely to track their cycles in three of the four surveys.

Why more people are turning to cycle tracking is still unclear. Some people might just like it better. For others, getting hold of their preferred contraceptive may have become harder.

“Are people choosing these methods because they’re their preferred method, or are they choosing these methods because they’re out of options?” Simmons said.

“It might be that people are choosing these because they no longer have access to a doctor and they can’t afford the method that they need.”

How people track their cycles is another open question. In the surveys, scientifically tested methods could not be told apart from more casual ones.

Many period tracking apps were never designed to prevent pregnancy. Two apps have been cleared for birth control by the US Food and Drug Administration. Only one of them, Natural Cycles, is still on the US market.

The findings have some limits. All birth control habits were self-reported. Other factors that might explain the differences between groups were not accounted for.

The Idaho, Nevada and Utah survey was also carried out online and in English. Some groups in it were small, so the results may not reflect the rest of the country.

Future research could ask cycle trackers directly what led them to choose the method.

New national data expected in 2027 could reveal whether the growing popularity of cycle tracking reflects a regional trend or a fundamental shift in how Americans approach birth control.

The full study was published in the journal The Lancet Regional Health – Americas.

Astrophysicists have dared to ask a cosmological question never asked before: Do black holes "wear pants"? New research shows how fast-spinning black holes may split apart.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Black holes are known to collide and combine in monstrously violent merger events, but new research suggests these celestial stalwarts can also fragment into smaller bodies, like a cosmic pair of pants splitting down the middle.

In a paper published Oct. 22 in the journal Physical Review D, researchers used several mathematical modeling methods to propose a "pair-of-pants" topology for black holes. The hypothesis suggests that under extremely specific conditions, these dark behemoths could fragment into numerous less-massive black holes.

"Understanding precisely what is forbidden, what is merely unlikely, and what becomes possible once the assumptions are relaxed is the central goal of this work," the researchers wrote in the paper.

Black hole fragmentation could play into other cosmic mysteries. For example, it could help to explain black holes with masses that are too small to be formed through conventional astrophysical processes. These hypothesized black hole "morsels" would be so small that astronomers could see them evaporating before their eyes on observational timescales.

In the new paper, the researchers explored whether black holes' event horizons — the boundaries beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape — could split under various cosmological conditions. These situations included classical four-dimensional general relativity (Einstein's description of our large-scale universe as we currently understand it) as well as cosmologically esoteric frameworks such as higher-dimensional space-time and modified gravity scenarios.

But modeling black hole dynamics, especially the split of an event horizon, is messy work. So the researchers simplified it by comparing discrete slices of space-time, effectively condensing the fragmentation process into static snapshots from before and after the split.

In our classical cosmos, it seems mostly impossible for black holes to split, the researchers found, but they did identify a loophole that might allow it to happen.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The "pair-of-pants" topology for the fragmentation of a black hole.

The first impediment is entropy, the possible arrangements of an isolated system's energy, which cannot spontaneously decrease but only stay the same or increase. This has been theorized by Stephen Hawking and recently demonstrated through detections of ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, suggesting that a black hole's surface area cannot decrease.

For these reasons, splitting a static Schwarzschild black hole — the simplest type of black hole in our four-dimensional general relativity — would be strictly forbidden because it would violate the second law of thermodynamics.

The second impediment is kinematics, the motion of orbital dynamics, which precludes the possibility of a permanent split because the black hole fragments would recombine into a single body incredibly quickly.

But there is a loophole: A rapidly rotating black hole could literally spin itself apart.

"This is why, in four-dimensional general relativity, an isolated black hole in empty space could only split if it spins very close to the maximum rate the theory allows, what we call a near-extremal black hole," study co-author Manuel Del Piano, a theoretical physicist at the University of Southern Denmark, told Live Science via email. "Loosely speaking, the equator of the horizon is then dragged around at nearly the speed of light."

Through this theoretical process, the two resultant black hole fragments could be gravitationally slingshotted away from each other before they could recombine. So under conventional space-time conditions, it seems "black holes do not wear pants."

Then, the researchers mathematically modeled black hole fragmentation in versions of space-time with more than four dimensions.

In models of higher-dimension space-times, a black hole's rotational velocity is no longer limited because gravity weakens with increasing dimensionality. Therefore, any such ultrafast spinning black holes could theoretically fragment, the researchers explained in the paper.

A diagram from the new study illustrating the theoretical pants-splitting method.

In the "black string" model, a normally spherical black hole would become cylindrical or string-like, stretching across any extra dimensions. It could then pinch off to fragment into multiple smaller bodies, akin to "beads on a string."

Additionally, the researchers calculated that black hole fragmentation may be entropically favored in space-time models with modified gravity, which alter the gravitational interactions in extremely warped environments near the black hole.

"The fragments are tiny, though: in one of our benchmarks, a black hole of ten solar masses would favour fragments … a few times the mass of the Great Pyramid of Giza squeezed into a region smaller than a proton, and the heavier the parent, the smaller the fragments," Del Piano explained.

Fragmentation also may be more likely if there is a "bumpy horizon" around black holes, akin to a dense blanket or shroud of exotic matter that acts as a singular-but-gigantic quantum entity. The superfluid qualities of this matter could create strange vortices that eventually cause a black hole to fragment into multiple smaller bodies.

Scientists might see a black hole decrease in size, an actual fragmentation, or simply an indirect gravitational signature, depending on the dimensions and whether it intersects the viewer's "brane," or slice of dimensionality.

The researchers expect that smaller objects — like the hypothesized, miniature primordial back holes that may have formed shortly after the Big Bang — are more likely to split, compared with much more massive astrophysical black holes such as those at the centers of galaxies.

"Overall, we expect small black holes, such as primordial ones from the early universe, to be the most prone to splitting," Del Piano told Live Science.

Gamma-ray telescopes or gravitational wave observatories may one day offer evidence of a signal associated with the supposed split of a small black hole, but the specifics, including whether this actually occurs, are uncertain.

"One important caveat: our analysis shows when splitting is allowed by entropy and conservation laws, not that it actually happens," Del Piano noted. "As we put it in the paper, a shattered glass has more entropy than an intact one, yet glasses don't shatter on their own. Settling the question requires full dynamical simulations, which is the natural next step."

Cacciapaglia, G., Del Piano, M., Sannino, F., & Vellucci, V. (2026). When black holes admit pair-of-pants topologies. Physical Review. D/Physical Review. D., 114(8). https://doi.org/10.1103/cx69-t466

#6363. Scientists find a new way to study some of the ocean’s most elusive microbes

A new study sheds light on the largely unexplored microbial world beneath the ocean and its potential ecological significance.

Most of the microbes living on the deep seafloor have never grown in a lab dish. On the way to the surface, a sample loses the high pressure and steady cold its microbes are adapted to.

The sudden change can kill the microbes before anyone gets to study them.

A robotic system called DISCUSS keeps both conditions in place, from the seafloor all the way to the lab bench where single microbes are picked out. With it, a team grew a bacterium that barely grows at ordinary air pressure.

The work was led by Jing-Chun Feng of Guangdong University of Technology in China. Zhengguang Liu, a researcher in the University of Manchester Department of Chemical Engineering, was one of the paper’s corresponding authors.

“Scientists have long struggled to grow many microorganisms found in nature under laboratory conditions, limiting our understanding of how they live and function,” said Liu.

The deep sea is home to a vast diversity of microbes, many of which have adapted to extreme pressure and near-freezing temperatures.

Some deep-sea microbes even produce enzymes and other molecules.

The molecules that deep-sea microbes create can be useful for medicines, new materials, food and energy.

Scientists say that less than one percent of deep-sea microbes can be grown with normal lab techniques.

“Deep-sea microbes are particularly fascinating because they have evolved to survive extreme pressure, cold and unusual chemical conditions,” Liu said.

The testing of this technology was carried out in the South China Sea at a depth of 4,300 feet (1,300 meters) in a cold seep location.

Cold seeps are areas of the seafloor where methane and other compounds emerge at temperatures similar to those of the surrounding water.

At this depth, the water pressure would be 1,900 pounds per square inch (13 megapascals), which is about 130 times the atmospheric pressure at sea level, and water temperature would be 39°F (4°C).

Before carrying out any sampling procedure, sensors detected the levels of methane, carbon dioxide, oxygen, acidity, temperature, and pressure on the seafloor.

After evaluation by the software, only those locations with scores related to methanotrophic microbes were sampled.

The sealed samplers kept more than 98% of the seafloor pressure on the way up.

In the lab, the system built a virtual copy of the seafloor conditions from the sensor readings. Researchers call that kind of copy a digital twin, and the machine used it as the target to hold.

When a sample moved from one chamber to the next, one pump pushed while another pulled at a matched rate. That kept the pressure from jumping during the handoff.

To grow one kind of microbe on its own, a microbiologist spreads cells thinly across a soft gel. Each cell that survives grows into a small dot called a colony.

DISCUSS performs this task inside a sealed, high‑pressure chamber. A robot arm spreads the cells with a needle, and a camera watches through a sapphire window.

A force sensor in the arm lets it press lightly enough not to tear the gel. In tests, the camera software recognized colonies with 94.6% accuracy.

The needle hit its target within 0.002 inches of the intended spot. Between tasks, the system sterilized the needle using light, keeping the pressure seal intact.

“From an engineering perspective, what excites me most is how intelligent sensing, modeling and automation can help us explore biological systems that were previously difficult to study,” said Liu.

The team recovered 34 microbes and grew each one on its own.

In 11 of them, a gene that scientists use to tell microbes apart differed enough from known reference strains that they may belong to groups not yet described.

The team took a close look at two of the 34. Both turned out to be strains of known species.

One belongs to Pseudomonas songnenensis, and the other, named HP_SR10, belongs to Bacillus cereus.

To test how much each strain depended on pressure, the researchers grew both for 11 days at five pressures, from ordinary air pressure to a little above the seafloor’s.

The Pseudomonas strain grew about as well at ordinary air pressure as it did at seafloor pressure. HP_SR10 didn’t. It grew best at the same pressure as the seep it came from, and poorly at ordinary air pressure.

The authors wrote that this strain can’t be recovered with conventional methods, which grow microbes at surface pressure.

The system also kept a whole community of microbes alive and working for 180 days.

At its center was a partnership between methane-eating archaea, single-celled microbes distinct from bacteria, and bacteria that use sulfate from seawater.

Pumps fed the community methane and nutrients and flushed out waste. That kept sulfide, a byproduct that holds these microbes back at high levels, below 4 millimoles per liter.

Around day 110, both partners became noticeably more common.

The authors wrote that communities like this one typically collapse in closed lab containers with no fresh supply.

Carbon made near the ocean surface can sink to the deep ocean, and scientists still don’t fully understand how deep-sea microbes change it.

Growing a wider range of these microbes under conditions close to home could help scientists study that process.

Only two of the 34 microbes were studied in detail. The study doesn’t describe what the 11 possibly new microbes do, or whether any make useful molecules.

All of the samples also came from a single seep. The authors noted that the design could be adapted for deeper water and for very hot places such as hydrothermal vents.

Next, the team plans to run many plates at once under different conditions and to track dissolved chemicals more closely as they change.

The researchers also plan to automate growing microbes in liquid instead of on gel.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Sensors.

#6360. In a 1996 study, researchers reviewed 22,793 poinsettia cases reported to U.S. poison centers and found no deaths, but the plant can still upset pets

Poison Control says the deadly reputation rests on a child's death over 100 years ago. Tests of about 500 to 600 leaves found no poisonous dose.

Every holiday season, poinsettias go up on tables and windowsills, and so does an old warning: keep them away from children, because they are deadly.

Researchers led by the Pittsburgh Poison Center checked that idea against hard numbers. In a study published in 1996 in the American Journal of Emergency Medicine, they analyzed 849,575 plant exposures reported to the American Association of Poison Control Centers (HRSA).

Poinsettias accounted for 22,793 of those cases. There were no deaths among them.

The researchers wrote that the poinsettia “is a much-maligned plant which is thought by the public and some health professionals to be extremely toxic.”

Their data told a different story. Almost all of the poinsettia exposures, 98.9%, were accidental, and 93.3% involved children.

Most of the people involved, 96.1%, were not treated in a health care facility. And 92.4% did not develop any toxicity related to the poinsettia at all.

“Most patients do not require any type of therapy and can be treated without referral to a health care facility,” the authors concluded.

The study is 30 years old, but the current advice from Poison Control, run by the National Capital Poison Center, says the same thing.

“The poinsettia plant is often considered deadly. That’s wrong,” its guidance states. “Poinsettia can be irritating but it is not fatal if eaten.”

Poison Control says some stories “just won’t go away.” “Over a hundred years ago, a child was found next to a wild poinsettia plant. He died and people blamed the plant. This hasn’t happened since,” it says.

Researchers have even tried to find a poisonous dose. They “just couldn’t, even after reaching experimental doses of about 1.25 pounds (500-600 leaves),” according to Poison Control.

That does not mean the plant is a snack. If children or pets eat it, Poison Control says, they can develop mouth irritation and stomach upset, such as nausea, vomiting or diarrhea.

The sap can cause a skin rash, and Poison Control notes reports of gardeners who work with the plant frequently developing one.

Poison Control describes one real case. On Christmas Day, a 10-month-old put a small piece of a poinsettia leaf in his mouth, and his mother called a poison center.

The specialist told her no problems were expected and advised her to wipe the child’s mouth and give him something to drink.

The plant can also be a choking hazard, so Poison Control recommends placing poinsettias, and other houseplants, where children and pets cannot reach them.

The ASPCA lists the poinsettia as toxic to dogs, cats and horses, and it names the plant’s irritant sap as the toxic principle.

Under clinical signs, the ASPCA describes the plant as “irritating to the mouth and stomach, sometimes causing vomiting, but generally over-rated in toxicity.”

Poinsettias are only one of the season’s concerns for pet owners. Earth.com has looked at how to keep cats safe at Christmas, from toxic trees to dangling decorations, and at festive plants that may be less safe than they look.

The poinsettia is the most popular flowering plant sold in the United States, with more than 70 million sold each year, according to a Clemson Cooperative Extension factsheet last revised in 2015.

It is named after Joel R. Poinsett, the first U.S. ambassador to Mexico. He brought the plant to the Bartram Botanical Garden in Philadelphia in 1828, and a Philadelphia nurseryman, Robert Buist, named it after him, the factsheet says.

The wild plants in Mexico grew 12 to 15 feet tall. The red parts that people think of as flowers are actually bracts, a kind of modified leaf. The true flowers are the small yellow clusters in the center.

If someone does swallow part of a poinsettia, Poison Control’s advice is to call a poison center at 1-800-222-1222, which is free, confidential and available 24 hours a day.

The information was obtained from the study Poinsettia exposures have good outcomes…just as we thought (American Journal of Emergency Medicine, 1996), Poison Control’s page Are poinsettias poisonous?, the ASPCA’s poinsettia entry, and Clemson Cooperative Extension’s poinsettia factsheet.

#6358. The Sky Today on Thursday, November 26: Thanksgiving turkey in the sky

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Celebrate Thanksgiving with a celestial turkey: The famous Orion Nebula (M42) is also playfully known as the Turkey Nebula because it looks to some like a turkey, particularly in deep astrophotos. But whether you’re a photographer or not, this bright deep-sky treat is easy to enjoy tonight while dinner digests.

By about 9 P.M. local time, Orion the Hunter has risen above the eastern horizon, his recognizable three-star belt standing in a vertical line. The lowest star in that line is Alnitak (Zeta [ζ] Orionis), and the Orion Nebula lies just 3.7° south-southwest of this star, to its lower right on the sky this evening. You might be able to spot its glow without optical aid, although the bright Moon nearby may make that difficult. Binoculars or any telescope will easily show it.

At 4th magnitude and spanning some 85’ by 60’, the Orion Nebula is a huge and bright star-forming region that sits roughly 1,350 light-years from Earth. In the brightest portion of the nebula lies a small grouping of young stars called the Trapezium Cluster. Take your time with this gorgeous sight, scanning around the region to pick out detail in the nebulosity. And if you are an astrophotographer, consider turning the view into a Thanksgiving memory to share for years to come.
