#6357. An mRNA shot made hearts pump about 10% more blood after a heart attack, with the effect lasting 12 weeks

An experimental mRNA treatment helped mouse heart cells divide after a heart attack, improving pumping function, but human trials are still needed.

An experimental treatment pushed adult heart muscle cells in mice to divide again after a heart attack, something those cells normally cannot do.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge delivered a modified messenger RNA that briefly switches on two proteins inside heart cells, Myc and Cyclin T1.

Treated mice pumped around 10 percent more blood with each heartbeat than mice given a mock treatment, the university reported.

The gain held when the animals were reassessed at 12 weeks. The work was done in mice, and the treatment has not been tested in people.

An adult human heart can lose up to one billion heart muscle cells in a heart attack. Those cells are never replaced, which weakens the pump and leaves scar tissue behind.

An estimated 920,000 people in the U.K. are living with heart failure, and a transplant is the only cure, according to the British Heart Foundation (BHF).

“Getting the human heart to repair itself is the holy grail for cardiologists,” said Professor Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the BHF.

Myc is better known as a cancer gene. Switching it on makes liver cells multiply within days, yet in the heart it does almost nothing.

A 2020 mouse study explained why. Myc protein binds DNA in heart muscle cells but cannot turn genes on, because the heart is short of a partner protein, Cyclin T1.

“When the Ccnt1 and Myc genes were expressed together, the heart switched into a regenerative state,” said Dr. Megan Bywater, a senior research officer at QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute and first author of that work.

The new experiment turns that finding into something closer to a therapy. Instead of altering genes, it uses mRNA, the kind of instruction a cell reads and then breaks down.

The team injected 100 micrograms of modified mRNA straight into the heart muscle during surgery. Injections guided by ultrasound did not work efficiently.

Myc and Cyclin T1 protein showed up in heart tissue one hour and four hours after the injection, and had gone by 24 hours.

A fluorescent version of the molecule, used to track where it travelled, was still visible around damaged heart cells 24 hours after the injection.

The university says the brief, localized signal is not expected to cause any permanent modification, which is meant to limit the risk of overgrowth.

Ultrasound scans tracked each animal on days three, six and 28 after treatment.

Ejection fraction, the share of blood the left ventricle pushes out with each beat, dropped by 26 percent in treated mice by day 28. In untreated animals it fell by 37 percent.

At 12 weeks the decline was 7.1 percent in the treated group, against 16.1 percent in controls.

Markers of cell division rose in the treated hearts, and the number of heart muscle cells had climbed by day five.

Tagging cells and their descendants showed 41.5 percent of labeled heart muscle cells sitting in adjacent pairs after treatment, compared with 5.5 percent in control hearts.

A genetically engineered version of the same approach did even better, holding the day-28 decline to 9 percent against 23 percent in controls.

Scar tissue told a different story. By day 28 the scar was no smaller in treated mice, although the volume of working muscle in the left ventricle had grown.

Waiting did not ruin the effect. In the transgenic model, switching the two proteins on seven to eight days later held the ejection fraction drop to 14 percent by day 36, against 30 percent in untreated animals.

No tumors were found in the treated animals at either checkpoint, and laboratory tests found no added capacity to transform cells.

Switching Myc on across the whole heart, by contrast, killed seven of eight mice in the transgenic version of the experiment, which is why the team confined the signal to the injured area.

Among the animals that received the mRNA, survival across 12 weeks did not differ significantly from controls.

Human heart muscle cells grown from stem cells in a dish also showed more signs of division after treatment.

The Cambridge group is now refining the treatment with BHF funding.

Larger animal studies, and then human trials, are needed to establish safety and effectiveness before the approach could help a human heart heal after a heart attack.

“These are really exciting results,” said Dr. Catherine Wilson, an associate professor of pharmacology at the University of Cambridge and co-senior author of the study.

“We’re not just treating the symptoms of heart failure – this approach could help the heart to repair itself,” Wilson added.

“That makes it exciting when studies like this are able to reignite regeneration in heart muscle cells,” Williams said.

The study was published in the journal Nature Cardiovascular Research.

Archaeologists discovered a stash of Celtic coins ahead of a construction project for an electrical substation in Hungary.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Hungary have discovered a stash of more than 200 Celtic silver coins that are over 2,000 years old. It's one of the largest hoards found there in decades.

Researchers unearthed the coins during excavations ahead of construction for an electrical substation in western Hungary between 2023 and 2025, according to a translated statement from the power company E.ON. The hoard dates to sometime between the late second century B.C. and the early first century B.C.

The coin cache weighs roughly 4.4 pounds (2 kilograms). In today's market, it's worth more than $2,000 as raw silver alone, but its rarity and historical value effectively make it priceless, the statement said.

The site was once part of a farm, and plowing there had unearthed several individual coins in recent decades, the statement said.

During the latest excavations, archaeologists initially found a few coins and then searched the area with metal detectors, which led them to the coin hoard. The treasure had been packed inside a small ceramic vessel and sat about 16 inches (40 centimeters) below ground.

"This is a rarity in Europe," Eszter Kreiter, an archaeologist at Hungary's National Archaeological Institute, said at a news conference, according to local news outlets. She added that the last similar find was made in Hungary in the late 1960s.

The hoard's silver coins are modeled on Greek tetradrachms — a very early type of large silver coin that was introduced in the late sixth century B.C.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The newfound Celtic tetradrachm copies are a type known as "Velem," which are named after Velem-Szent Vid, a fortified Celtic hilltop settlement, or oppidum. Similar coins have been found at that site, which is located about 10 miles (15 kilometers) to the west.

Each coin has a stylized head on one side that probably depicts the Greek god Apollo, and portrays a helmeted rider and horse on the other side.

Artifacts from more than 7,000 years of occupation have been found at the site, including a glass bead (bottom, center) thought to be about 2,500 years old.

The excavations have revealed evidence of more than 7,000 years of occupation at the site, officials wrote in the statement. The artifacts include a nearly 7,000-year-old polished stone chisel used for woodworking and a glass bead with a peacock's eye pattern that seems to have been part of jewelry from the sixth or seventh century B.C.

A Roman-era villa was built at the same site in later centuries, without disturbing the hoard of buried silver, Kreiter said at the news conference.

The site in Hungary's western Szombathely region was excavated between 2023 and 2025 ahead of the construction of an electricity substation.

The villa has long since been demolished, but the excavations enabled the archaeological team to reconstruct its floor plan, including its underfloor heating system, she said. They also found a Roman-era brick with a dog's paw print.

The artifacts from the site will become part of a museum exhibition.

According to Museum Wales, the Celts were loosely related Iron Age peoples descended from Proto-Indo-European speakers. Emerging in Central Europe, Celtic groups occupied much of Central and Western Europe from about the 10th to the first century B.C. The Celtic Gauls were finally defeated by the Romans, led by Julius Caesar at Alesia, now in eastern France, in 52 B.C. The Britons were also Celtic, though most people of Celtic descent would not have recognized that name.

Several modern ethnic groups, including the native Irish and the Bretons of coastal France, trace their descent to the Celts. Regions with strong Celtic origins are sometimes called the "Celtic fringe" of Western Europe.

Writing in the Journal of Roman Studies, the British coin expert Christopher Howgego, an honorary curator and professor emeritus of Greek and Roman numismatics at the University of Oxford, stated that Celtic tribes in the Carpathian Basin, now in Hungary and Romania, started minting their own silver coins after Celtic mercenaries had seen them when serving with Hellenistic armies in Greece and Macedonia.

Howgego has written that the Greek-inspired Celtic coins included adaptations of classical Greek portraits, as well as distinctive Celtic designs. These copycat tetradrachms held very high value for their makers, so they were rarely used for everyday purchases. Instead, they were often hoarded as wealth or buried as ritual offerings.

#6355. Nov. 26, 2018: Mars InSight lander touches down

InSight, short for Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy, and Heat Transport, landed on Mars Nov. 26, 2018, tasked with a simple yet challenging mission: unlock the mysteries of Mars’ interior. Top priorities included uncovering Mars’ internal structure by measuring the thickness of the crust, obtaining the size and density of the core, and sussing out the structure and composition of Mars’ mantle.

In addition to bountiful seismic data, which included more than 1,300 marsquakes, InSight recorded about a year’s worth of weather data at the lander’s location with unprecedented accuracy, according to Bruce Banerdt, the mission’s principal investigator and principal research scientist. The InSight lander also took the first magnetic field measurements on the surface of Mars and measured several properties of the soil around it.

Not everything was a rousing success, however. Most famously, the mission’s “mole” subsurface probe only penetrated about 16 inches (40 centimeters) deep, despite being designed to burrow to a depth of at least 3 feet (10 meters). It turned out that the soil beneath InSight’s struts was unlike any previously encountered on the surface; it simply didn’t cooperate with the instrument’s design. But even that cloud has a silver lining, as it provided scientists with important details about the terrain upon which InSight landed.

InSight’s successful initial two-year mission was extended to run at least through the end of December 2022. But the stationary lander relied on power generated from its two large solar panels, which steadily gathered dust. That dust reduced the panels’ efficiency over time, forcing mission planners to make tough choices regarding power allotment. In May of 2022, engineers placed the craft’s robotic arm into a final resting pose and turned off all its instruments, save one: InSight’s seismometer continued to operate on what little power was available, running about half the time, according to Banerdt. InSight last contacted Earth Dec. 15, 2022, after which two attempts were made to raise the lander. Both failed, and a few days later, NASA officially brought the mission to a close.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6354. Extreme weather in India and China shared a hidden atmospheric connection

A new analysis reveals how atmospheric circulation connected extreme heat in India with a rapid shift from flooding to humid heat in southern China.

India baked under a stubborn heat dome while southern China lurched from flooding into dangerous, humid heat.

A new analysis links the May 2026 extremes to the same sprawling high-pressure system.

Meng Gao from Hong Kong Baptist University led the analysis, with collaborators from the Chinese Academy of Meteorological Sciences and Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology.

For much of early May, temperatures across the Indian region studied had been below normal.

Starting on May 17, that changed sharply, with temperatures staying over 1°C above the recent May average.

The researchers combined weather observations, atmospheric reanalysis, and climate simulations to trace the change.

Their maps showed daily average temperatures exceeding 40°C in some locations.

May 20 stood out. Across the region studied, it was the hottest May 20 in the record stretching back to 1979.

Humidity added to the strain. The wet-bulb temperature, which reflects the combined effects of heat and moisture, ranked third-highest for that date.

For people working outside, particularly in northern India, the combination made an already difficult season more dangerous.

The developing El Niño offered part of the explanation. By May, the central and eastern equatorial Pacific had entered El Niño conditions.

Atmospheric circulation shifted far beyond its shores.

The researchers linked this developing El Niño to a stronger western Pacific subtropical high. This broad area of high pressure also stretched farther west than usual.

Meanwhile, a persistent wave pattern in the upper atmosphere strengthened another high-pressure system over the Iranian Plateau. That system moved eastward.

Over India, the two highs joined, creating a stable “heat dome.” Air sank beneath it, warming as it descended and helping keep skies clear.

With more sunshine reaching the ground, temperatures continued rising. Warm waters in the northern Indian Ocean also helped strengthen the Pacific high, further supporting the persistent heat.

In southern China, the same Pacific high helped produce a different sequence of hazards.

Guangdong had endured repeated downpours since early May.

Particularly heavy rain between May 19 and 23 brought widespread flooding, followed almost immediately by humid heat from May 24–29.

The abrupt switch followed the high-pressure system’s movement northwestward. Rain eased, sunshine increased, and descending air warmed the region.

The atmosphere, however, remained laden with moisture after the downpours. The result was a “rainfall-to-deadly humid heat” sequence, with little time between the two emergencies.

The paper reports dozens of heatstroke ambulance calls in Shenzhen and thousands of livestock deaths in Maoming.

Such dangerous combinations of heat and humidity arrived one to two months earlier than usual.

Air temperatures alone did not explain what happened in Guangdong. Readings were near the top of the historical range, but comparable heat had occurred before.

The difference was the moisture accompanying them. Relative humidity during the dangerous hours averaged about 60%, compared with roughly 50% during similarly hot hours in earlier years.

Humid air makes it harder for sweat to evaporate, limiting the body’s ability to shed heat. That means familiar thermometer readings can conceal much greater physical strain.

For several hours, conditions exceeded a modeled threshold for safe, sustained activity among healthy adults aged 65 or older. That applied even to sitting quietly or standing with minimal movement.

That threshold describes a particular group under specified conditions. Heat tolerance varies with age, activity, and exposure to sunlight.

The timing was exceptional too: these conditions appeared earlier than in any year of the available 2011–2025 comparison record.

The team also asked how human influence had changed the likelihood of India’s heat.

Using 11 climate models, the researchers compared simulations including human influences with a preindustrial climate.

Their central estimate suggested human influences had made a similarly intense Indian heatwave roughly 27 times more likely.

The estimated range was wide: about 16 to 52 times, at a 90% confidence level. The authors caution that differences between models and limitations in correcting their biases affect the result.

The authors describe the finding as evidence of a likely human contribution, with the precise scale still uncertain. The estimate applies to the Indian event, not to the entire sequence across both countries.

A common atmospheric influence helps explain why distant places suffered heat at nearly the same time. Whether those heatwaves also reinforced each other remains unresolved.

For southern China, the order of events matters. Flooding can damage electricity supplies and other infrastructure, leaving residents without reliable cooling when the heat follows.

Warnings therefore need to account for what happened in the preceding days.

A heat forecast issued during flood recovery may reach people whose homes, workplaces, and access to electricity are already disrupted.

The researchers call for stronger infrastructure and better preparation in vulnerable regions.

In places facing rapid weather reversals, flood response and heat preparation may need to happen at the same time.

The study is published in the journal Advances in Atmospheric Sciences.

#6353. The Maya People Loved the Color Red. Scientists Say It May Have Helped Bring Them Down.

The reddish pigment cinnabar was so popular that it seeped into the water supply around Maya settlements, setting off a disastrous downstream effect.

The Maya people had a toxic relationship with the color red—quite literally, according to fresh research. The new analysis of the Yucatán Peninsula during the Maya era identified astronomically spiked levels of mercury, which might have contributed to the collapse of Maya culture.

“The mercury data was crazy,” Matt Waters, an environmental sciences professor and paleolimnologist at Auburn University, said in a university statement about the unexpected discovery on the peninsula. “Off the charts. These mercury levels aren’t normal.”

Matt Waters led a study published in Science Advances that explored sediment samples collected at two lakes—Lago Coba and Cenote Xcach—showing the intense spike in mercury (Hg) levels ranging from around 40 C.E. to 800 C.E.

“We show that Classic Period Hg concentrations in sediment cores from two lakes on the Yucatán Peninsula exceeded modern sediment Hg toxicity thresholds by orders of magnitude for centuries during ancient Maya occupation,” the authors wrote, adding that the heightened pollution coincides with aquatic food collapse, “confirming that Hg toxicity was an additional environmental stressor for Classic Maya populations.”

While Waters isn’t saying mercury caused the collapse of the Maya civilization, he also doesn’t want to ignore its impact. “It’s been confirmed that drought was an issue, deforestation was an issue, erosion was an issue, overpopulation was an issue, and feeding the population was probably an issue,” he said. “This study adds the impact of water quality. Let’s put that in the list. That’s what our study does. It establishes that list and moves it forward.”

The study actually began as part of a National Science Foundation project focused on harmful algal blooms, but a then-graduate student and study co-author, Savanna Wooten, suggested also testing for heavy metals. Sediment coring from the lake bottoms pulled up mud from thousands of years ago that contained the intense mercury spikes during the Classic Maya Period, which were then followed by an abrupt decline.

The powerfully high mercury concentration lasted for hundreds of years, and Waters believes the sudden change at the base level likely moved up the food web, impacting fish and other larger creatures. Not only would eating fish or drinking water have exposed humans to the toxic levels, but there may have even been fewer fish to catch. “They would have seen a strange color change in the water,” Waters told Live Science, “and a drop in its productivity, such as fish for protein.”

Waters linked to a study he’d worked on with a team from the University of Florida in the late 1990s that found a gap in ostracod shells during a specific period from Coba, correlating the missing shell timing to the rise in mercury. Further investigation into the cores found that declines in biological markers occurred throughout. “The algae was killed,” he said. “The cyanobacteria, they tanked. Purple sulfur bacteria, vanished. The biological community completely changed.”

The people “experienced this for decades and, in one case, for centuries.”

The source of that mercury was cinnabar, they believe, a vibrant red mineral made up of 86 percent mercury that Maya culture viewed as a sacred pigment. “This was not like mercury raining down from the sky,” Waters said. “This was not a regional thing. It was concentrated.”

Maya loved cinnabar, using the bright red in pottery, murals, temple walls, and burials. To keep up with demand, they heavily imported it, especially around Coba and Xcach. “It’s common knowledge that there was trade in obsidian, in jade, and beautiful stones, and weaponry,” Waters said. “I think this could start a conversation that cinnabar could have been a major trade commodity.”

It may also show a highly toxic love affair that contributed to Maya struggles.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

#6352. The closest exoplanets may host magnetic fields

In all the universe, Earth is the only planet known to have life. A big part of the reason life is possible here is our planet’s magnetic field. It acts like a shield, deflecting harmful energy from our Sun as well as cosmic rays from deep space that could otherwise erode Earth’s atmosphere and irradiate the surface, a death sentence for evolving life-forms.

But Earth is far from the only planet we know of. As of this writing, there are more than 6,300 confirmed exoplanets on the roster, with more added by the day. Scientists have discovered stars with as many planets as our own Sun hosts. In other systems, planets as big as Jupiter whip around their sun in only a few days’ time. Astronomers have even discovered planets that orbit multiple stars at once, and they recently caught a glimpse of a possible atmosphere around a rocky, Earth-sized world in its star’s habitable zone. But until 2026, they had no compelling evidence that any terrestrial exoplanets had magnetic fields of their own.

Because of their protective role, magnetic fields have major implications in the search for life beyond Earth. Astronomers have long suspected that part of the reason Mars now appears dead is that its magnetic field fizzled out billions of years ago. This let the solar wind strip the water and other volatile compounds from its atmosphere, leaving it cold and barren.

Beyond the solar system, in 2019 researchers reported “indirect detections of exoplanetary magnetic fields” in four hot Jupiters. Then, a 2021 study found a strong signature of a magnetic field around HAT-P-11 b, a Neptune-like planet. Two years later, a pair of studies detected possible signs of a magnetic field around YZ Ceti b — this time, a rocky, Earth-like planet roughly the same size as, and only a bit less massive than our own. But this find has not yet been confirmed.

In July 2026, a study published in Astronomy & Astrophysics found possible evidence of magnetic fields around two rocky exoplanets. Not just any exoplanets, either — Proxima Centauri b and d, the closest confirmed planets beyond our solar system, orbiting the red dwarf Proxima Centauri 4.2 light-years away.

Proxima b, roughly Earth’s mass and size, orbits every 11.1 days. Proxima d, likely a quarter to a third of our planet’s mass and 70% its size, orbits closer in with a period of 5.1 days. Because Proxima Centauri is smaller and less massive than our Sun, Proxima b is inside the habitable zone, where temperatures allow liquid surface water. A third planet, Proxima c, was tentatively detected in 2019 but is still unconfirmed. Astronomers don’t yet know if any of these worlds host atmospheres.

The new study, led by María Rosa Zapatero Osorio of the Centro de Astrobiología in Madrid, Spain, used 117 separate observations made with the Echelle SPectrograph for Rocky Exoplanets and Stable Spectroscopic Observations (ESPRESSO) instrument on the Very Large Telescope atop Cerro Paranal in Chile. The research followed up on previous studies conducted with ESPRESSO in 2020 and 2022, which focused on confirming the presence of planets around Proxima Centauri. Zapatero Osorio and her collaborators used the data to identify a peculiar correlation between the timing of flares emitted from Proxima Centauri and the orbital periods of its planets.

“We detected low-energy flares occurring with a characteristic period of about 5.1 days,” Zapatero Osorio says. “This is very close to Proxima d’s orbital period.” But flares did not occur during every orbit of Proxima d, so the team ran statistical analyses to determine whether the flares were preferentially occurring at particular phases of the planet’s orbit. They found strong statistical evidence “that the occurrence of the flares is not randomly distributed over the planet’s orbital period,” Zapatero Osorio says. “Instead, a significant number of flares tend to occur at particular times in Proxima d’s orbit.” This is a possible indication that Proxima d could be interacting magnetically with its parent star, which would be likely to happen if the planet has a strong magnetic field of its own.

Using a model adapted from the physics of solar flares, Zapatero Osorio’s team calculated that Proxima d could have a magnetic field anywhere from 8 to 230 gauss in strength, with the best median estimate limited to around 16 gauss. This is about 27 times more powerful than Earth’s magnetic field (0.6 gauss), which protects life on Earth from the worst of the Sun’s energy.

Their model assumes that the star and planet are magnetically connected, Zapatero Osorio says. Each sustains its own magnetic field, and these fields are interconnected. As a result of this connection, stress builds up on the stellar surface. From time to time, this stress is released in the form of low-energy flares, whose period is closely tied to the planet’s orbital period.

Although there was not as strong a correlation between Proxima b’s orbital period and the stellar flares, the team did find that Proxima b could also be interacting with the star, albeit in a lesser capacity. This suggests that although the finding is less sure, Proxima b may also sustain a magnetic field.

There are alternative explanations for the findings. One possibility is that there could be intrinsic, long-lived active regions on Proxima Centauri itself that account for the peculiar timing of the flares. Another explanation is that gravitational interactions between the planets and Proxima Centauri could induce disturbances on the star without requiring a strong planetary magnetosphere, although the team suggests this is less likely. It’s also possible that when Proxima’s stellar wind reaches the planets, it interacts with them in a way that mimics the effects of a planetary magnetic field without requiring one.

Like most red dwarfs, Proxima is a highly active star, regularly belching out intense flares that would be hazardous to any fledgling life-forms on the worlds in close orbit. Because Proxima is so close to Earth and has at least one rocky planet in its habitable zone, it makes a perfect testbed for studying how stellar flares could affect habitability around red dwarfs — the most common stars in the universe.

Astronomers looking for habitable worlds around these stars must contend with the likelihood that any planets would be effectively sterilized by the intense radiation in the flares constantly washing over them. Now, though, there is a glimmer of hope. If Proxima b and d do have magnetic fields, as this research suggests, they could act much like Earth’s own protective magnetic shield, deflecting enough harmful stellar radiation that life might just be able to take hold.

“Earth’s magnetic field plays an important role in protecting life and supporting human progress,” says Zapatero Osorio. “It shields our planet from the solar wind and energetic particles, and it has also played an important role in navigation.”

Unfortunately, Proxima d is so close to its host star that it is likely too hot to sustain life as we know it. Proxima b, however, lies within the habitable zone. “Based on the results of our study, both Proxima d and b may have magnetospheres capable of providing some protection against their host star’s activity,” Zapatero Osorio says.

The importance of this find goes deeper than simply a pair of neighboring planets. In the last few years, evidence has emerged that gas giant exoplanets similar to Jupiter and Saturn host magnetic fields. These are the easiest types of planets to detect and study, but while magnetic fields around such worlds are certainly fascinating, the implications for planetary habitability are limited.

But as the number of known planets continues to swell, so, too, does our sample of Earth-like worlds. And if the two closest rocky planets beyond our solar system do indeed have magnetic fields, then perhaps these features are common. If true, it increases the chances that rocky worlds across the galaxy could be habitable — at least, for life-forms as we understand them. And the more planets capable of hosting life, the more likely it is that we might someday discover we are not alone.

Nick Oakes is a science writer for NASA’s Heliophysics Education Activation Team at Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.

November's full Beaver Moon rises on Tuesday, Nov. 24, giving us a preview of the spectacular Christmas Eve supermoon coming next month.

Editor's note: This article was updated on Tuesday (Nov. 24) to indicate that the full Beaver Moon rises tonight.

November’s full moon, known as the "Beaver Moon," will rise in the east at dusk tonight (Nov. 24), marking the first of three consecutive supermoons.

It will be the third and final full moon of fall in the Northern Hemisphere and the first in a series of unusually close full moons that includes December's spectacular Christmas supermoon — the closest full moon since 2018. These bright moons are just some of the many winter skywatching highlights headed our way in the coming months.

The Beaver Moon gets its name from the time of year when nocturnal beavers in North America traditionally build dams and prepare for winter under the full moon, according to TimeandDate. Other nicknames include the Frost Moon and Snow Moon, and the Anishinaabeg people in North America call it Baashkaakodin Giizis — the Freezing Moon — according to the Center for Native American Studies.

The moon will reach its full phase at 9:53 a.m. ET on Tuesday, when it will be below the horizon in North America. The best time to see the Beaver Moon is at moonrise that evening, as it rises in the east around the same time the sun sets in the west. That's when the moon will appear against a relatively bright twilight sky, making it easier to appreciate its size and color.

The moon will appear full on Monday and Wednesday as well, but Tuesday offers the best opportunity to see it rise during twilight.

The Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, according to EarthSky. A supermoon occurs when a full moon coincides with the moon being relatively close to Earth in its elliptical orbit. The moon's distance from Earth changes throughout the month. On average, the moon is 238,900 miles (384,472 kilometers) from Earth. When a full moon occurs near perigee, or its closest point during its orbit, it appears slightly larger and brighter than usual. #6350. The Government Tested How Dangerous AI Could Get—Then Four ChatBots Helped Plan a Terrorist Attack

The Government Accountability Office secretly tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok and found that all four would help make plans when prompted.

The dawn of artificial intelligence brings with it both rewards and risks. With the ability to sift through unfathomably large data sets, AI could help detect cancers in their infancy, unlock some of the most enduring mysteries of mathematics, and even help contain the beating nuclear heart of future fusion reactors.

Unfortunately, the risks of this technology are far from minuscule, including its impact on human education, the environment, and potentially the survival of the human race (an all-too-plausible scenario put forward by AI tech CEOs). Even the everyday LLMs that now litter our digital lives—Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Grok—can aid and abet some of the most dangerous actors on the planet.

At least, that’s the latest conclusion by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan watchdog housed in the legislative branch of the U.S. government. Typically, GAO turns its investigative gaze on efforts to limit fraud and wasteful spending in the government itself, but in a new tactic at the urging of U.S. Senator Maggie Hassan (D-NH), the office instead performed real-world tests on the platform to see if these four popular AI models would aid in planning a terrorist attack.

“A terrorist can log onto an AI platform and in less than 12 hours walk away with a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack,” Hassan, incoming Chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, said in a press statement. “Today’s new report makes it clear that the AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical.”

GAO conducted this test in the spring this year, and earlier this week reported some disturbing results. Two of the platforms, according to an official GAO release, provided guidance on building and detonating an improvised explosion device, or IED, and two other AI models showing differing methods for targeting the electrical grid. Within 12 hours, all four models also gamed through potential locations and methods for carrying out such an attack.

Although these violent lines of questioning triggered each platform’s safeguards, GAO got around them using common safeguard-bypassing techniques. Additionally, they confirmed the validity of the information provided with experts. The results of this investigation were published in a 61-page report that will be central to future senate hearings on AI safety.

“We set out to do two different types of evil,” GAO director Kevin Walsh said in an interview posted on YouTube. “The first type is we wanted to create a bomb. And we didn’t just want to know how to create a bomb, we wanted it to help pick out a target, a location, and a time, and to give us instructions all the way…Evil scenario two, we wanted to do a bunch of economic damage, and in both cases that ended up being targeting the electrical grid.”

In one case, Walsh reports that one AI model would refuse to answer questions or divert the user to more safe behaviors but said that “it wasn’t always successful.” Walsh says that companies theoretically call law enforcement when suspicious activity is detected, but whether that occurs and at what frequency is uncertain.

“As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards,” the report concludes. “However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security.”

The GAO officially released these terrorist-abetting findings on November 18, 2026, the same day Anthropic, creators of Claude, went public on the stock exchange. Despite the company’s own admission of AI being an existential threat to humanity, its IPO at one point reached a meteoric a $2 trillion valuation before dipping back down to a (measly) $1.6 trillion.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6349. The Sky This Week from November 27 to December 4: Brilliant Venus

Friday, November 27As fall deepens and winter approaches, the wintertime star patterns are reappearing in our evening sky. One is a large asterism called the Winter Hexagon, now fully above the horizon by about 10 P.M. local time. You should be able to spot this shape even with the Moon nearby, as each point in the Winter Hexagon is a bright, well-known star.

Look east late tonight to locate the waning gibbous Moon near the border of Gemini and Cancer. This will help you find the first point in the Hexagon, the pair of stars Castor and Pollux, the heads of Gemini the Twins, glowing just above the Moon at this time. From there, look upward for another bright star in neighboring Auriga — this is Capella, the next point in the Hexagon. From Capella, look left and down just a little to find the V-shaped face of Taurus the Bull, where the bright star Aldebaran shines, marking the next point. Then it’s down to Orion’s bright knee, Rigel, before you drop down and a little left, close to the horizon, to land on Sirius, the brightest star in the sky and the nose of Canis Major. The Hexagon closes out with the luminary of the Little Dog, Procyon.

Sunrise: 6:59 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 7:53 P.M. Moonset: 10:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Saturday, November 28Saturn remains a bright naked-eye object all evening, setting around 2 A.M. local time. Around 8 P.M., you’ll find it high in the south, to the left of the Circlet of Pisces and above the body of Cetus the Whale.

Tonight and for the next few nights, Saturn’s strange, two-faced moon Iapetus is skimming north of the planet, making it easier to find. Now glowing at 11th magnitude, it is heading west toward a late December western elongation, when it will shine about a magnitude brighter but sit far from Saturn. Once you’ve got Saturn in your scope, look about 2’ northeast to land on Iapetus. Over the next few nights, it will move westward, reaching inferior conjunction and standing due north of the ringed world by the 30th.

If you can catch 11th-magnitude Iapetus, you’ll also see four brighter moons: 10th-magnitude Dione, Rhea, and Tethys closer to Saturn; and mid-8th-magnitude Titan, about 3’ to Saturn’s west. The latter is the planet’s largest and brightest moon, easy to spot in any size scope and often even binoculars. If you keep returning each night to track Iapetus, also keep an eye on Titan, which is moving eastward toward the planet and will pass south of Saturn on December 2. Dione, Rhea, and Tethys have smaller orbits and shorter periods, so they move visibly over the course of several hours, frequently swapping places and passing in front of or behind Saturn. For example, Dione disappears behind Saturn’s southwestern limb in an occultation around 12:20 A.M. EST on the 29th (still late on the 28th in time zones farther west).

Sunrise: 7:00 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 9:10 P.M. Moonset: 11:09 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (73%)

Sunday, November 29Have you ever seen your shadow by planetlight? Venus reaches greatest brilliancy at 2 P.M. EST, now shining at magnitude –4.9. Rising nearly three and a half hours before the Sun, Venus will be so bright that it could potentially cast a shadow if you’re in a location with particularly dark skies (Bortle 1 or 2).

Even without perfect viewing conditions, this morning star can’t be missed. By an hour before sunrise, Venus is roughly 25° high in the southeast, blazing just to the lower left of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo. Far to Venus’ lower left, closer to the ground, Mercury stands nearly 5° above the horizon, shining at magnitude –0.7.

Compare the two planets through a telescope. Venus is a 27%-lit crescent, but its disk stretches 40” across. Mercury, by comparison, is much smaller, just 6” across, but its phase is 82%. Now through the first week of December is the best time to catch the solar system’s smallest planet, as it remains bright but appears to sink toward the horizon day by day. By the 5th, Mercury will be less than 2° high an hour before sunrise, making viewing challenging both because of potential obstacles on the horizon as well as the more turbulent layer of air near the ground.

Venus, meanwhile, stays at roughly the same altitude an hour before sunrise all month, its phase growing to nearly 50% lit by the end of the year. Earth’s sister planet will remain prominent in the morning sky through the first half of next year.

Sunrise: 7:01 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 10:25 P.M. Moonset: 11:43 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (62%)

Monday, November 30Venus remains a brilliant and unmissable morning star, but it’s not the only object worth paying attention to before dawn. Leo is hosting a celestial get-together this morning as the Moon joins two planets and the star that sits at the heart of the Lion, just beneath the Sickle asterism.

The waning gibbous Moon is the brightest object here; next brightest is Jupiter, located to the Moon’s upper right and glowing at magnitude –2.2. The gas giant stands nearly side by side with Mars (to Jupiter’s left); the Red Planet is fainter but still a respectable magnitude 0.4. Both planets are slowly growing in brightness and size as they approach opposition early next year. Through a telescope, Jupiter stretches 39” across, offering excellent views of its alternating light and dark cloud bands, and Mars is now 8” wide.

Shining between Mars and the Moon is 1st-magnitude Regulus, often drawn as both the heart of Leo and the base of the Sickle asterism’s handle. The curving backward question mark of stars that forms the Sickle’s blade and the Lion’s head in profile lies above the grouping in the sky before dawn.

Sliding along the ecliptic, the Moon passes 1.2° south of Jupiter at 4 A.M. EST, then 1.1° south of Regulus at 10 A.M. EST and 3° south of Mars at 3 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 7:02 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: 11:36 P.M. Moonset: 12:11 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (51%)

Tuesday, December 1Last Quarter Moon occurs at 1:09 A.M. EST. A few hours later, asteroid 2 Pallas reaches a stationary point at 7 A.M. EST. Located in Cetus, it is visible all evening, setting around 1 A.M. local time. It stands highest around 8 P.M., when it’s roughly 30° above the southern horizon, about 4.2° southeast of 2nd-magnitude Diphda (Beta [β] Ceti).

Glowing at magnitude 9.0, Pallas is easy to find with a small scope. It sits near a neat triangle of 5th- to 6th-magnitude stars, which lie about 1.5° southwest of the asteroid and act as a great reference point to find it tonight. Pallas is 1° east of the easternmost star. Previously, Pallas was closing on that star, moving westward. But after tonight, it will turn and move slowly eastward again, pulling away from the little triangle night by night.

Drop about 5° south of this region for an added treat: 8th-magnitude globular cluster NGC 288, just over the celestial border in Sculptor. Spanning about 13’, this ancient ball of stars lies nearly 49,000 light-years away. It’s also near another deep-sky target, the 7th-magnitude galaxy NGC 253. Often called the Silver Coin or Sculptor Galaxy, this stunning edge-on spiral lies about 1.7° northwest of NGC 288 and can be viewed together with the cluster in wide-field instruments such as binoculars or finder scopes.

Sunrise: 7:03 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: — Moonset: 12:35 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (40%)

Wednesday, December 2It’s now asteroid 4 Vesta’s turn to reach a stationary point at 11 A.M. EST as it, too, swims through the domain of Cetus the Whale. Visible in the evening sky, Vesta sits more than 40° above the southern horizon around 7 P.M. local time. Previously moving retrograde, or westward, it will now begin moving prograde, or eastward, against the background stars.

This month Vesta is located roughly halfway between bright Saturn to its northwest and magnitude 3.6 Theta (θ) Ceti to its southeast. Saturn is impossible to miss, as it’s the brightest object in this region of the sky. To locate 7th-magnitude Vesta, find Saturn early in the evening and slide about 8.1° east-southeast to land on the main-belt world. There aren’t a lot of background stars in the immediate vicinity, so try to match your view to the star chart above to locate the asteroid in your eyepiece. Because it’s moving slowly, you’ll need to come back every night or two to check out the view and note the light that’s shifted position — that’s Vesta.

Sunrise: 7:04 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: 12:43 A.M. Moonset: 12:58 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (30%)

Thursday, December 3Look north a few hours after sunset to find the W-shaped star pattern of Cassiopeia on her head, looking more like the letter M as this circumpolar constellation swings above the North Celestial Pole. Just 1.9° northwest of Navi (Gamma [γ] Cassiopeiae), the midpoint of the M (or W), is a lovely open cluster cataloged as NGC 225 and known as the Sailboat Cluster.

Longtime Astronomy contributor Rod Pommier gave the cluster its nickname because he saw an arc of stars within the cluster that looked to him like the sail of a boat catching the wind, connected to a straight line of stars forming the mast and another eight stars outlining the vessel itself. The stars of the cluster are roughly 2,100 light-years distant, and this grouping was discovered by Caroline Herschel in 1783.

For added visual interest, the cluster is set against a complex of dark nebulae made of dust, which block the starlight behind them.

Sunrise: 7:05 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: 1:49 A.M. Moonset: 1:20 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (21%)

Friday, December 4The waning Moon puts even faint deep-sky objects within reach on these early December evenings. Tonight, let’s look toward a distant elliptical galaxy nestled in the far southeastern corner of Lacerta the Lizard. Cataloged as NGC 7426, this 13th-magnitude stellar smudge sits close to a lovely pair of contrasting stars, making finding it a rewarding sight for all: While you do need a larger scope to track down the galaxy, the stars are visible even through smaller instruments, offering something for everyone.

Around 7 P.M. tonight, our target is still more than 35° high in the west. The zig-zagging figure of Lacerta sits just above cross-shaped Cygnus as the Summer Triangle sinks toward the western horizon. To Lacerta’s left (southeast) is Pegasus, and we’ll use 3rd-magnitude Matar (Eta [η] Pegasi) as our jumping-off point. From here, slide about 5° north-northeast to find a pair of stars, 6th and 8th magnitude, roughly 1’ apart. The brighter star glows blue-white, while its dimmer neighbor shines orangey-gold. NGC 7426 lies roughly 4’ east-northeast of this pair, appearing as a faint, grayish-white smudge. It measures roughly 2’ by 1.5’, its compact size helping to keep its faint light confined to a relatively small area.

Sunrise: 7:06 A.M. Sunset: 4:34 P.M. Moonrise: 2:54 A.M. Moonset: 1:44 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (14%)

#6348. Solo meerkats can find their way back home

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Meerkats live, forage and raise their young in large groups. But they’ve still got solo skills

To test meerkats’ solo navigating skills, researchers outfitted the animals with GPS trackers, separated them from their packs, and followed their journeys back home.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

The animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, says Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin says. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

Meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she says. But that’s not what the team discovered.

In separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin says.)

Neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin says. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

It’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she says, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

M. Martin et al. Ubiquitously efficient solo navigation in group-living meerkats. Journal of Experimental Biology. 2026. doi: 10.1242/jeb.252200

#6347. This week: Lame duck kicks off with Hegseth impeachment effort

Departing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the new Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected next speaker of the House, said Sunday that he would support the Hegseth impeachment.

“I'm a hard 'yes' on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said on ABC’s “This Week.” “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.”

Departing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.

It’s also orientation week on Capitol Hill for new members of Congress. House orientation got underway Sunday.

The Senate, meanwhile, looks to take up a bipartisan permitting bill that has the backing of President Donald Trump.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Senate negotiators over the weekend released text of an amendment seeking to address remaining concerns.

“I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves [the bill] and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Senate Environment and Public Works ranking Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island said in a statement. “Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs.”

Beyond the permitting bill, the Senate Republican majority may seek to use its remaining time trying to confirm more of Trump’s nominations before the control of the floor agenda passes to the Democrats.

"We've got the farm bill, the NDAA, and we have that third reconciliation bill that we need to get across the finish line, and there are so many things that we need to get done and buttoned up," including nominations, departing Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in a weekend Fox News interview. Blackburn, one of the Republicans who had success at the ballot box, is now governor-elect of Tennessee. But it's an open question how long lawmakers will want to stick around.

There’s also the matter of an imminent fight over funding the government and laying the groundwork for the new Congress. Republican leadership elections are scheduled for Tuesday, while Democratic leadership elections are expected in December. Democratic senators-elect are due on Capitol Hill Monday and Tuesday, according to the office of Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer is widely expected to be the majority leader in 2027.

There have been some calls for Senate Republicans to delay their elections, though current Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has been widely expected to remain as the Republican leader.

“One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability,” Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., said in a Sunday night statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward.”

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has also been circulating a letter calling for a delay, and he has argued the election should not be held, in part, because the makeup of the Senate Republican Conference is not yet final. Senate races are still not called in Alaska and Mississippi.

Absent this week will be Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who recently had a stroke.

“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” Murphy said in a Friday statement.

#6346. This Company Wants to Make Fuel From Carbon Dioxide—Using the Power of a Nuclear Reactor

AIRCO hopes to make a carbon-neutral fuel from captured CO2 and hydrogen. Some sustainability experts are skeptical.

The fossil fuel industry is the largest contributor to climate change, and it’s not even close. According to the United Nations, the industry is responsible for 68 percent of all greenhouse gas emissions and an incredible 90 percent of all carbon dioxide emissions. Stick a stake in the vampiric heart of fossil fuels, and beating back the worst effects of global warming becomes suddenly much more possible. But as the recent climate summit at Antalya, Türkiye, this month displayed, the industry shows no interest in giving up its polluting ways, leading some countries to say the world is now “held hostage by the oil mafia.”

Despite this unwillingness to change, some companies are trying to find ways to make some good out of a bad situation. One of those companies AIRCO (originally named Air Company), based out of New Britain, Pennsylvania, did just that by developing a technology that creates jet fuel of a thin “air”—well, kind of.

Instead of making fuel at a massive refinery and transporting it long distances, the system is designed to produce fully formulated synthetic jet or diesel fuel closer to where it will be used,” Nick Steinke, the company’s director of programs, government and defense, said in a recent interview with Waste360. “It takes captured CO₂ and hydrogen and integrates the conversion process into a modular, containerized system.”

Instead of relying on centralized fuel producers, the idea is that synthetic fuels could be created on-site where they’ll be used directly, circumventing the climate impacts of transporting the fuel entirely. Also the ingredients AIRCO uses also aims to come from green sources by leveraging carbon capture technologies for the required CO2 and using electrolysis to supply hydrogen from water.

Chemical & Engineering News reported earlier this year the company hopes to supply the U.S. military with a complete reactor system by 2027 that will be powered on a government site using a small nuclear reactor (SMR), and supply a sufficient flow of energy required for both carbon capture and electrolysis to provide the volumes of ingredients needed to make these mobile, fuel-creating systems viable. It’s a task that at least one expert says sounds easier said than done.

“The technology seems like it holds a lot of promise, especially on the fuel-conversion side, but the part that I have a lot of questions about is, where are you getting the carbon from?” Sarah Gleeson, a materials scientist at Project Drawdown, told WHYY, a local radio station. “Because if they’re saying that there’s some kind of direct air capture functionality in this really mobile device, I would be skeptical at the capacity and efficiency of it.”

Carbon capture is central to the company’s promise of its technology’s carbon-neutral nature with the company’s CEO telling WHYY that “using more CO2 in our production process to make the fuel than we are putting out in the entire process.” Carbon capture, as a broad technology category, still remains unproved even as some climate models rely on its implementation (and the fact that the oil industry likes the technology is concerning to say the least).

If humanity hopes to secure a healthy planet for future generations, ending its reliance on fossil fuels is priority number one. But step one in the process is first limiting—and eventually eliminating— new fuel from being extracted from the ground in the first place while the advancements in green chemistry try to put to work the carbon dioxide that’s already here.

Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity.

This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern, a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery.

Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79.

"It's not something that as a geoscientist I would have said would be predicted," said Sune Nielsen, a geochemist at the University of Lorraine in France who was not involved in the study. "Very far from it."

A fish in the genus Pseudoliparis in an image taken during during a dive by the Jason/Medea ROV at 20,659 feet (6,297 m).

The Challenger Deep is in the remote western Pacific at the southern end of the Mariana Trench. There, the Pacific oceanic plate pushes under the Mariana oceanic plate in a process called subduction. At the trench where the two plates meet, the ocean floor plunges down 6.8 miles (10.9 kilometers). Mount Everest could fit in the chasm, with room to spare.

Geoscientists aren't sure why the trench is so dizzyingly deep, but they have turned up some clues. For instance, there is a tear in the Pacific Plate that allows one narrow strip of the plate to subduct particularly rapidly. The curvature of the plate is also very steep, perhaps because the rocks of the Mariana and Pacific plates aren't very strongly connected to each other, allowing the Pacific Plate to dive steeply and flex freely.

The new findings, reported Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, suggest that volcanism and magma also may play a role, Stern said. The researchers were exploring a segment of the Challenger Deep's forearc, a roughly 120-mile-wide (200 km) expanse that sits between the trench itself and the volcanic arc created by the subduction zone. These volcanic arcs are standard subduction zone features; for example, Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier are part of the volcanic arc of the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But though there are some volcanoes north of Challenger Deep along the Mariana Trench, the Challenger Deep segment of the trench is odd in that there is not an organized volcanic arc there. Instead, there's an ocean ridge. Regardless, the space between this ridge and the trench was expected to be volcanically quiet because there is not usually enough heat in that region of a subduction zone to melt magma.

Nevertheless, the cameras on the deep-diving remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea, which went to the site in 2014, caught strange, pancake-like rock features at three different spots in a 60-mile (100 km) stretch of the trench. Samples brought on board the ship revealed rock embedded with volcanic glass and a pyroclastic flow texture.

A sea cucumber in an image from the Jason/Medea dive at 12,726 feet (3879 m).

The researchers are currently getting the rock dated, but volcanic glass usually erodes quickly in the ocean, Stern said, so the presence of glass suggests the eruptions were fairly recent. "They're not yesterday," he said, "but I don't think they're a million years old."

The pressure of the water at the depths of the flows is equivalent to 592 atmospheres of Earth stacked on top of one another. Typically, that kind of pressure keeps a lid on the dissolved water and carbon dioxide in magma that expands rapidly to cause explosive eruptions. Thus, Stern said, the eruptions by the Challenger Deep may have been driven by a supercritical fluid ‪—‬ a weird state sort of in between a gas and a liquid.

"We just don’t know how those magmas will behave at those water depths," said Stephen Self, a volcanologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the study.

The mission's observations also suggest that the crust of this region is extending, or stretching, in two different ways. To the east, the stretch is caused by a mechanical pulling apart of the crust. To the west, volcanic eruptions are stretching the crust. It's a perplexing finding, Nielsen said, without a clear explanation.

Stern and his colleagues suspect that the two plates are starting a new subduction zone in this western part. That would be an exciting finding; subduction zones move around over tens of millions of years, and researchers don't know much about how new ones start. The geochemical studies of the rocks that Stern and his team pulled up could answer questions about where the lava that made the pyroclastic flows came from and why this bizarre region can generate magma where none should be.

"This region is really, really unusual for our planet, and there is quite a bit of, 'What, really? Wait, how is that? OK, yeah, I guess maybe.'" Nielsen said. "So obviously, I find it super interesting."

Stern, R. J., Pujana, I., Anderson, M. K., Chin, E., Dygert, N., Harigane, Y., Le Roux, V., Leybourne, M., Ohara, Y., Okumura, T., Segee-Wright, G., & Etheridge, E. (n.d.). ROVing in the deep: Tectonic and magmatic complexities of the challenger deep forearc segment, southern mariana convergent margin. Frontiers in Earth Science, 14, 1929806. https://doi.org/10.3389/feart.2026.1929806

#6343. ‘Political malpractice’: Calls grow to delay Senate GOP leadership elections

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

“After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said on Monday evening.

Asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”

Though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

“Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I said, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”

Johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

Also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”

Kennedy said Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he said, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”

But Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, said she has seen such requests launched in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

And several Senate GOP aides said that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the plans and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

That includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”

Republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott said. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

An online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”

Banks similarly said Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”

One senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” said Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”

#6342. A fast-growing heart is good for the Grinch. People are another story

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Unlike in the Dr. Seuss tale, a swollen heart can be an alarming sign of stress or disease

The Grinch’s change of heart turned him from grumpy to radiating joy. Is such a transformation possible in real life?

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In the classic Dr. Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations. Poised to throw it all off a mountain, the grumpy loner has a change of heart as joyous song rises from Whoville.

“They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” says the narrator of the 1966 movie version. With a beatific smile, he pulls the stolen goods back from the brink and returns everything.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Would a too-small heart make you grumpy like the Grinch? And what would happen if your heart went from too small to really big in an instant? The answer depends on what causes the heart to shrink or swell, experts say. And whether or not you are a snake.

Heart size is generally pegged to body size, says Michelle Kittleson, a cardiologist at Cedars Sinai Smidt Heart Institute in Los Angeles. Bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. But some people, she says, have hearts that are naturally bigger or smaller than average for their bodies. It’s not clear why. However, she says, “there are negative consequences of having a too-small heart.”

In one 2025 study, researchers looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people in Australia. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts, the team reported in JACC: Advances.

Smaller hearts may not pump blood as well as larger ones, making it harder for people to exercise. And if the Grinch didn’t exercise enough, maybe “then that made him really tired, and that made him grumpy,” Kittleson says. “Or maybe he did the research, and he found out that his life expectancy was shortened because of it, and that made him even grumpier.”

But would rapidly increasing his heart’s size be good for the Grinch?

As the Grinch slides downhill toward Whoville, pulled by a sled piled high with presents he’d stolen and now was returning, he physically undergoes a change. What started as a heart two sizes too small swelled three sizes, both curing his grumpiness and giving him super strength. Or so the classic tale goes. A person going through such a dramatic change may not fare as well.

There are many ways a heart can grow, says Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder. With vigorous exercise, “your heart gets bigger in good ways,” Leinwand says. That can be true for athletes who do lots of cardio, such as swimmers and marathon runners.

“Their heart gets bigger and thicker,” Kittleson says. “But it’s a good thing in them because it helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.” Pregnancy also makes the whole organ expand to boost blood to the developing fetus. If people stop exercising, or give birth, their hearts will shrink back to normal size within months.

Some diseases, though, can enlarge hearts in deadly ways. “If you’ve got untreated high blood pressure,” Leinwand says, “you can get a huge heart, and it’s not good for you.”

Stress, bad heart valves and some genetic diseases can also result in bigger, but weaker, hearts. In those cases, the heart muscle grows in order to pump more blood. At the same time, the inside of the left ventricle — the heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood to the body — can shrink. That makes it harder for the heart to push blood out. This kind of growth takes time, Kittleson says.

There is one rare condition in which the heart can inflate suddenly. Called takotsubo or stress cardiomyopathy — or in some cases, broken-heart syndrome — it is brought on by extreme stress. That can include positive things like winning the lottery or entering a surprise party or negative stress such as break-up or losing a job.

A surge of epinephrine, or adrenaline, from stress can make the left ventricle bulge into the shape of a pot used to catch octopuses. (Takotsubo is Japanese for “octopus pot.”) That causes immediate heart failure as the heart chamber gets too big to pump blood.

So instead of becoming super strong, the Grinch “would have keeled over and collapsed,” Kittleson says. (People can survive with prompt medical care and their hearts can return to normal size in a few months.)

Given the Grinch survived his rapid growth, there’s another possible scenario: Maybe his heart is more like a snake’s.

Pythons’ hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day after the snakes eat a large meal — sometimes as big as an adult deer. And the bigger a python’s meal, the more its heart grows. Larger hearts pump blood with more force, Leinwand and her colleagues reported in 2024 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The researchers don’t know if this makes the snakes stronger overall.

Once a meal is digested, the heart shrinks again. Snakes can go through many shrink-and-grow cycles with no ill effect. Leinwand hopes that studying these snakes will lead to treatments that make human hearts healthier.

But becoming kinder, like the Grinch? Maybe not.

Notes Leinwand, “our snakes, when they eat a lot, they get rather aggressive.”
